If you love sandboxes, and the feeling of awe that comes from huge landscapes and spaces in general - if you love the idea of gradually coming to understand the aliens you meet - if you love gathering rescources, either by hand or by constructing a farm - if you like starships - if you like naming stuff (star systems, species, planets, ships) - if you like the feeling of wonder that comes from finding something you sometimes didn't even know existed - if you like cool tech - if you like building your own base - if you like settling in systems with other players, or doing quests with them - and if, like me, you're a hopeless romantic (in the literary sense) and your heart melts when you come across a beautiful or weird landscape or structure, and if you can feel immersed enough in a game to feel, every time you take shelter from a storm inside a tiny NPC base, that you've come home... then this game is for you. 

Lots of people won't like it, because it's not their type of game - and that's alright. You don't have to like exploring even though you've theoretically seen everything in the game, just not these combinasions, and you don't have to like it when the story is too cryptic to be easily understandable, and you don't have to like the graphics and you might get impatient when you don't understand a word an alien is saying. If you are worried about these things, this game might not be for you. 
But despite its mediocre start, this game has risen to be one of my favorites, one of the ones I'll always come back to. For all of the reasons in the first paragraphs, for some people, this game will be an unforgettable experience. 

...And also, if you've has enough of game maps that have bounds. This game's map is awfully big (and I love it, personally). So if you were feeling trapped in other games, in this one you'll never feel free-er :)

(Note to new players: before anything else, get sodium and oxygen)

No Man’s Sky is a game geared around space exploration. And, for a gamer who spends most of his free time in a claustrophobic corner clicking away at buttons, the game was a breath of fresh air. Unfortunately, that breath was ultimately very short lived. 

No Man’s begins the game by giving you a “multi-tool” which drills and identifies objects (among other things), a breathing apparatus, and a small ship. Although players are free to follow the pseudo-quest line should they choose, the game is ultimately more fulfilling by simply going your own way. Such immersive and overwhelming freedom was nice to begin with, in part because of the sheer magnitude the game has to offer. 

Each planet on No Man’s is procedurally generated, which means no life form or plant look exactly identical. In fact, the combinations are virtually endless. This is an aspect which I appreciated greatly. Despite this, I quickly got bored. 
The game consists of an endless universe of regrettably desolate planets. Sure, you might bump across the occasional space station or hostile enemy. But these bits of flavor quickly run their course. And while each planet looks distinctly different, few have anything meaningful to offer. For a game so driven on creating a massive, beautiful universe, all I really did was get lost in the bleak vacuum of space over and over again. 

There are some things to do, however, I just found all of them boring. Aside from exploring simply to explore, you may also upgrade your ship, build multiple bases, and even play cooperatively with another player. Once I dabbled in the above to-do list, I quickly got bored of the game however. No Man’s is an expansive space exploration game with absolutely nothing else to do.

UGH what a lifeless grind! If this is the "much improved version from the original state" I shudder to think of what it was before. There are only two good things I have to say about this game:
1. The large-scale procedurally-generated universe is probably impressive from a software engineering/architecture point of view.
2. The flight mechanics/controls are way more usable and pleasant than in some other games. (e.g Elite Dangerous, which i happened to have tried right before this one.)

The gameplay is atrocious though. You will (literally. I'm not exaggerating.) spend at least 50% of your time holding down the laser button, vaporizing everything in sight. Whether you'll be pointing at poor defenseless animals, or vicious robots, or innocuous rocks, or bushes, or trees, this is apparently the main point of the game. Just vaporizing. There is maybe a list of 20-30 different types of components you can get through the forementioned vaporizing, and the combinations of the components will vary slightly from rock to rock or tree to bush, but of course you won't be paying attention because you're just holding down the laser button, rotating your cursor all around for like 2 minutes. Then run forward a bit and repeat the process. Then you check your inventory and think "oh! i got myself enough carbon so that i can recharge my laser and vaporize some more!" So now take this idea, and multiply it by infnity for every planet in this universe. Some of the planets' trees and rocks have components X and Y, others have Y and Z, and while the trees and rocks are slightly different shapes and sizes on different planets - ultimately it makes no difference at all to you. Because you're just doing the exact same thing on every planet, reducing all components to dust using the exact same game mechanic.

So what about the other 50% of the gameplay, you ask? Well, you'll spend at least 20% flying around on your ship from planet to planet, or from farming spot to another farming spot, (which was fine, because at least the flight controls were good, but it does get old quickly enough). Then at least 10% of the time you'll spend "learning the language" at the space stations, and this consists of coming up to every NPC and clicking through the same dialog options of "gibberish"->"please teach me something"->"random word learned". Now multiply that by infinity for every NPC on every space station. Another 10% of the time you'll probably spend looking through the vendors' inventories, hoping to find something significantly different but never actually finding it. And now multiply THAT by infinity for every vendor on every space station. And then the rest of the 10% you'll maybe actually have SOME fun, as you upgrade your character and ship, and maybe build a base. But this last 10% melts away fast, since once you have all the fancy upgrades and you built everything you wanted in your base - you're basically done.

Well, but what about all the exploration, you ask? This so-called exploration got incredibly old after the 4th or 5th planet. Because there is never anything more. Never anything exciting. It's the same planet with a slightly different skin and weather, over and over and over again.

Well then, you say, this criticism is not very constructive, and you (as in I) are just complaining a lot. Here's some constructive criticism: don't use the same tool with the same mechanic to do ALMOST EVERYTHING in the game! We're already stuck with the same tool when we interact with games in general (that tool being mouse+keyboard), we need an illusion of diversity to help us forget it, instead of reinforcing it. Trees are chopped down with axes. Flowers are picked by hand. Rocks are broken down with pickaxes. And yes these are the non-spacey examples, but there are so many things that could have been done to make the farming/gathering aspect of the game less lifeless. And the other constructive criticism is - never take one idea and multiply it by infinity. That's how you get wallpaper. You know, the stuff that's in the background in old houses that you never pay attention to after the first few moments.

Anyway, the only place this "game" has is MAYBE in some computer science research class, with open source code, and some architecture discussions on extra large procedurally generated worlds. But not on a (virtual) shelf in a video game store, next to games like Subnautica, Don't Starve, Terraria, etc. The only reason why I have so many hours on it is because I kept trying to justify the price I paid for it. But now looking back on it - I see that whatever I got out of the game in the first hour of playing - is all I was ever going to get. So that was a waste of both time and money.

No Man's Sky has been on my radar since before it launched, in that notoriously botched state, back in 2016. As a space junkie, already sick and tired of waiting for Star Citizen to ever condense from vaporware to liquidware, I was hungry for some cool space exploration and trading game. No Man's Sky looked like it could be it. Then the "event" happened. No Man's Sky had a catastrophic launch, the game was a litany of broken promises and missing features that shocked the gaming world and a huge backlash followed. Of course, I had not pre-purchased this game, remember kids "don't pre-purchase", so for me it was just a matter of reading the reviews, sighing audibly and removing the game from my wishlist.

At that point, I thought that was the end for No Man's Sky. Indeed, if this was a typical gaming story it would have been. Many developers oversell their games, release them in sorry states with not even half the promised content and then run away with the dough Peter Molyneux-style. Indeed, Hello Games went silent for a while after the release, seemingly confirming the rule. But this game was to be an exception. The developer went silent because they had decided, finally, to let their actions do the talking. In the months and years that followed, they continued developing the game and without asking for extra money, they fixed most issues and added most of the missing features, plus many new ones. I was impressed.

Unfortunately, the game itself did not interest me as much anymore. Yes, I still love space, but No Man's Sky seemed to be primarily one of those pesky open-world/survival-crafting games. Between the release of No Man's Sky and today, I have been burnt too many times by such games to be able to ignore this. They usually lure me in by having traits I like, like being set in great worlds to explore, but their primary gameplay loop simply drains me. Use stuff to gather stuff, to be able to keep using stuff to gather stuff. It feels extremely disrespectful towards my relatively limited free time. But, because of the developer's conduct I bought the game anyway. Perhaps, I thought, the exploration/space part would be enough to offset this. It wasn't.

For people that do enjoy survival/crafting games, I think No Man's Sky has a lot to offer. There are several different types of worlds to travel to, filled with flora and fauna for you to name... and of course resources to gather, so you can travel to the next one. The player is initially very restricted, but as you build up your base and repertoire of known technologies to craft, more and more playstyles become possible. Trading, doing missions, multiplayer hubs, it's all there (at least now). On the other hand the exploration aspect doesn't disappoint. Amazing vistas, big underground caverns, extreme weather effects, space stations with several sapient alien species, speaking their own languages that you have to learn. Those are but a sample of the things on offer.

My playtime may have been rather short, but I did get some great moments out of this game. The first time I went to space, or landed on another planetary body. The first time I spoke to a Gek with their funny unintelligible language and even funnier faces. The first time I travelled through the rings of a planet. I do hope to play some more from time to time, when I feel less drained by the routine. At the end of the day though, I am content to admit that this game just isn't for me. I certainly don't regret buying it, the primary reason after all was to reward the developer for their recent conduct. Nevertheless, to fans of space games that also happen to enjoy the open-world survival/crafting gameplay loop, I can, in good conscience, recommend trying No Man's Sky.

No Man's Sky is an awesome sandbox space exploration game. I saw it on half price during the Winter Sale and liked the look of it so I tried it out. The first few hours of the game are challenging, you start on a harsh planet with a weather condition that is fatal if you don't protect yourself, but the game helps you through how to survive this. Throughout the start of the game it gives you very useful tips and playing through the story can also help with learning how it works. The way the menus work is quite different, and took a bit of getting used to at the start, but once familiar with it, it is a very efficient way to move items around. The space aspect of the game is epic. Leaving/entering a planets atmosphere and reaching space is so seamless, and the travelling through space is well designed, as travelling between planets in a star system isn't too fast, but at the same time doesn't take too long. Using the galaxy map can be daunting at first, but is a great way of plotting your journey through the galaxy. The art style of the game is great, it looks fine on standard graphics and awesome on high graphics. The characters and ships look great, as do structures, but most of all space itself is amazing, the faint distant stars, the lighting caused by the star of the system your are in and the occasional gas clouds really make it a sight to behold. Base building is very well done, the build menu making it easy to find the parts you are looking for and the modular feature of large structures and the position snapping makes it very easy to build a good base.  The player customisation is great, with a large range of colours and lots of starting cosmetics there are lots of options for making a character you like. There are also unlockable cosmetics to equip if you don't like the starter ones. As a singleplayer game, there is so much fun to be had. I can't comment on multiplayer as I haven't tried yet, but the anomaly provides a great lobby to meet fellow explorers.

In summary, No Man's Sky is a truly awesome game, with so many tools to use to have fun in the game, and an excellent sci-fi feel, it is a must have for anyone who likes space and sandbox.

There's some interesting ideas, but everything the game does feels very shallow at best, and unfun at worst.

The thing that bothered me the most was the alien languages, because it had so much potential to be fun and unique -- instead you run up to "alien.obj" and press the "dispense word" button.

Gameplay is just busywork, and pretty light on the "exploration" part, which is a shame. But the story is downright boring. If the game is not going to be mechanically engaging, at least make an effort to make it mentally so! 

Audio is pretty rough, the moment you get down on a planet, expect to hear constant stampedes as the game spawns mobs around you. Sound effects are just off in general -- turning your ship, excavating terrain, interacting with objects... a lot of things just don't sound good. OST is mediocre.

The game, when the procedural generation allows it, is very pretty. And the premade assets, things actually look really good! One exception is player animations.

I do appreciate Hello Games for actually delivering on the promises made after the infamous launch this game had, but as it turns out the game they had planned was just kind of a boring mess. 

I wanted to say that if you're curious you should still buy, because even if you dislike the game you're supporting a developer that tries to deliver on their word. But I really can't. This game as a whole feels like the most basic, barebones implementation of features possible so it can be added as a bullet point in the back of the box.

So, I was incredibly hopeful after reading some positive reviews about the game finally looking up to it's promises on release. But no, it's a massive disappointment for me. Sure, the game is [b] better [/b] then on launch, but that's hardly any praise. 

The first 2 hours were okay. The mechanics are allright, and the game is visually quite appealing with a unique artstyle. 

the second planet a landed on things were already slightly off. For a game that boasts about a massive variety in biomes, creatures and well, worlds in general, the second world was just a palette swap of the first. The third one was too, apart from that fact that this one had grass growing on it. 

A couple planets later and it start becoming very apparent that the variety just isn't there with [b] anything [/b]. 

The creatures are about 7-8 skeletons that have different animal parts strapped to it. They are basically all quadrupedal or bipedal reptile looking goofs, apart from the rare crab creature or tentacle monster. If you scan all of them you get some in game currency, and you can feed them something to ride on them for a bit. That's the end of animal interaction basically. You have some predatory animals that look completely the same on every planet, its always the same cat like beast. 

Biomes I would have to call pretty basic for a game that boasts that every atom is procedurally generated. What bothered me most about this is that the planets are the same biome all the way around, making exploring very non rewarding. If you saw the landing zone you picked, you basically saw the whole planet. There's some good variety here and there between them. The grass worlds look nice the first 2-3 times I guess, but the fact remains that every planet is pretty much functionally identical, apart from it's 1 of 4 flavours of hazardous weather and a difference in resources.

Plantlife is even more of a facade, with each planet having the same 3 basic "hazardous" plants including a venus flytrap, a exploding poisonous zit looking thing and some poison spewing underground bulbs. These are the same everywhere, not even a palette swap here. Furthermore there's a few different looking boulders and tree looking contraptions around for you to study if you're into that kinda thing. 

Spaceship variety is sort of interesting at first but it falls off real quickly, basically the same concept as animals but with ships. Buying them is done by waiting for them to land at a spacestation o outpost on a planet, which is kind of a neat concept in theory but in practice it gets tedious really quickly if you're looking for a specific ship type that just won't show up.

The flying mechanics are overly simple, especially if you're used to games like Elite Dangerous or any kind of flight sim. Space combat is just pointing and holding down m1 since the ships themselves are super slow relative to their size. Landing is done by just pressing the landing key, instead if doing it manually, and taking off isn't much more exciting. Landing animation also looks incredibly flat compared to Elite Dangerous's satisfying CLUNK and the ship suspension moving and  hissing. 

Space stations are the same everywhere, literally. No variety whatsoever, except for the npcs inside, who can be 1 of the 4 sapient races. Trading items between these station is guaranteed profit and 100% risk free, 

The base building is honestly pretty good, as one of the standout things. There's a good variety of parts and equipment, but most of the fun stuff is locked behind an incredibly tedious grind for currency. 

The story missions have an incredibly confusing narrative, and are basically just point to point flying trough space to look for people. The multiplayer missions are buggy as hell. I had to restart the first one I attempted 5 times for it to actually work and the missions themselves are pretty bare bones "fly here and do this" type stuff. 

All in all, I don't see what the hype is about. I want to like this game, I really do. The artstyle is cool and the concept itself is something that could be tons of fun, but it just isn't there for me.

There's a reason this game is always in the nominations list for the 'labor of love' during the Steam Awards. But everybody knows the 'zero to hero' story about the game's release, so I'm gonna skip that.

If I have a gripe with NMS, it's with the Survival mode. My original save file is a Survival mode file, and most of my time played is on Survival difficulty. But it wore me down, eventually. It's not the higher resource requirement that got to me, in the end -- it's the fact that all of the planets begin to have extreme weather at ridiculously close intervals, all but eradicating the ability to do the thing the game was built around the premise of doing: exploring weird places. The tack-on ability to build bases is great, but also requires being outside, and if you like to build grand things that's probably going to involve a lot of tinkering, moving things around, taking a step back to survey and consider, etc. On Survival, you can forget about that. Bookending five minute intervals of clear weather (and sometimes not even that, I have a video clip of a my ship announcing another incoming storm before the previous storm has even fully cleared), you have extreme storms that are going to chew through whatever protections you've scraped together the resources to fuel in your suit.

For me, that's not an added level of challenge, it's just a time sink, and not an especially rewarding one, as it nets you nothing that you couldn't get by playing in a non-Survival mode. Your mileage may vary, of course.

NMS has come a long way, and it's a fun way to spend some time. I do wish there was something more to the gameplay loop, but in its current state it's an entertaining way to pass the time, and I admire the hell out of their commitment to fleshing it out and giving their players more.

Having avoided this game when it came out due to all the bad press, I'm glad I eventually gave it a try. My favorite genres have always been open-world exploration/survival RPGs and city building/management simulators, and have previously fallen HARD into games like Fallout 4 that incorporate some of both, playing for hundreds of hours and maxing out all achievements. I can already feel this game sucking me in.

After only 7 hours played, I'd describe it as mostly a cross between Spore and Subnautica, with a bit of Minecraft thrown in since you can freely manipulate the terrain as well as building structures.

From Spore, it takes the randomly-generated creature designs, as well as the space-stage gameplay of flying around in your solo ship scanning creatures and plants on the random planets you find, building bases on them in order to further your production and trade with alien species (who themselves sound a lot like the synth-voiced alien species from Spore as well), and if the achievements are anything to go by, you're also trying to reach the center of the galaxy in this game. There are references to hostile aliens, who very well might be trying to stop you from doing that. There are a few other discrete species of intelligent aliens in the area, who are color-coded just like Spore and seem to each have a specific civilization focus on trade or military just like Spore. I haven't spent a ton of time in space yet in No Man's Sky, but what little I've seen and been hinted to me feels a LOT like Spore's space stage.

From Subnautica it takes its starting conditions of being an amnesiac shipwreck survivor needing to rebuild by harvesting the most basic materials from your surroundings in order to both keep your own life support systems functioning and build the technology needed to harvest more advanced materials in order to build even more advanced technology, using blueprints that you have to essentially find scattered around on the planets you explore, and building custom bases from specific parts to have a place to protect your tech from the elements. In fact, the basic gameplay of being planetside in No Man's Sky is so similar to Subnautica that I had to go and look up both of their release dates to see if No Man's Sky came out first and Subnautica just stole most of its gameplay from this game or vice versa (from what I can tell, No Man's Sky was announced the same year Subnautica entered Early Access, so that point is a bit unclear).

Though I'm already liking this game better than Subnautica, mostly due to not needing to scour the galaxy to find specific blueprints hidden in specific locations as in Subnautica (I was stuck for HOURS swimming aimlessly in that game looking for the tech I needed to move forward), because in No Man's Sky you merely collect blueprints as a currency that you trade in for the tech you want back at your base. The ability to dig and reshape the terrain is also incredibly powerful. I've merely scratched the surface of this so far, and piloting my spaceship still makes me pretty dizzy, but I'm getting the hang of it and enjoying every minute.

The one thing I'm not such a huge fan of though is the lack of flexibility on when I'm allowed to save. Apparently only in my base or at designated save points? Guess that means one of my inventory slots is forever going to be a portable save point so that I can stop playing at any time, something that almost every other game I've played since the PS1 era lets me do....

I hadn't played for a year or so, so decided to check out the game again. I remember why I stopped playing. I think this game shows an inherent problem with procedural generation - nothing is interesting.

Once you see a toxic planet, it seems as if every other toxic planet is the same. Likewise for Lava Planets and so on. Don't get me wrong, there are pretty views that are well worth it, just there isn't really a drive to explore.

During these eight hours I played, I came across more sticking points, like how annoying it is to get fuel to jump between stars and pulse engine being just a timer with nothing to do while travelling. It's all resource bars, all the way down. You move like a slug on land (until I learned the Shove + Jetpack trick), even when sprinting, which I guess is to encourage exploration in ships, but then you see, to find and tag points of interest, it seems you have to get out the ship and look around with a scope before getting back in (Though the markers show up in the ship, you may just fly past them or lose them as soon as you seem them).

Getting a new ship felt fun, finding a crash site and trying to fly a broken clunker around was enjoyable and thrilling, but then you look at the costs of repair and lose hope, as other ships cost anywhere from a few thousand to a million, often for what feels like minimal upgrades. I'm not sure how the hell I am meant to make that kind of money, asides from the game saying "Trading and Missions" then running into the hills. Same goes for the Laser pointer you start out with, where new ones which seem to be only marginally better are so much more costly than what you already own.

Even though people talk about how the game has changed, which I can see by the amazing things people have built and some of the screenshots they take. The Core gameplay still is rather lacking, where nothing happens and you stare at rocks and trees for a few hours before flying to another, samey planet, sometimes making the police force angry and being chased across the hills by them because you touched their stuff.

[b]Negatives: [/b]

    [*]Exocrafts have no use. ExoMech is impossible to use because it can't change direction without moving forward for some reason. I understand why they implemented the exocrafts but they did not balance the game in that regard so they offer nothing of value.
    [*]Updates are very surface level like "volcanoes", "giant worms" or "a living ship!". I understand that Hello Games are a small developer but still, all these features should have been in the game at launch, and much more satisfying stuff should have been added later with paid DLCs.
    [*]Base complexity has a lot of issues, game has issues loading a lot of parts all at once. Sometimes you fall through floors because they don't load fast enough, other times some elements like lights or decals never load etc. (big base problems.)
    [*]Game is very lonely and can get depressing with all the reminders of impending death (extreme night temperature - thermal protection falling - warning: incoming storm - sentinel force activated - shields depleted etc) and especially the story.
    [*]Although procedural generation is good, there are not enough parts in my opinion to make really distinguished visual styles. In my opinion, they should have added many more parts for procedural generation to combine, and limit their usage styles based on maybe 1000 light year intervals so the more you move towards the center, the gradual change in visual style would motivate the player to seek what else might be out there. Ships and planets feel very samey.
    [*]There are still bugs, especially with terrain editing and resource spawning. For example if someone has an excavated base, you might find it buried underground, or if you don't, there will be rocks floating where the surface used to be. 
[/list]
[b]Positives: [/b]
[list]
    [*]Moddable.
    [*]Smooth and fun gameplay.
    [*]Feeling of awe and wonder.
    [*]Complicated crafting system.
    [*]Good trading foundation is in the game (there are systems with different economical focuses which you can exploit to gain money) although a little surface level, could be expanded upon in the future.
    [*]Fun playing with friends.
    [*]Unique game implementation (half online half offline, local save but serverside discoveries and bases etc.) Some people might list this in the negatives but because there is no competition and structured pvp in the game, editing of local saves don't affect other players.
    [*]Freighters are fucking cool. Watching them jump into the system and battling around them are fun, and they give a sense that there is life and activity in the galaxy.
    [*]Procedural generation is very good. Animals and plants are so many.
[/list]
I think negatives outweigh the positives in this game,[b] but I still recommend [/b] because you will get your money's worth of entertainment.

Reviews.114363:
A game designed around a most boring busywork loop, but still dangerously addictive.

At it's core are two elements I hate the most in gaming; resource gathering and timers. Luckily there are ways to avoid the former mostly, and get rid of the latter entirely. Left is then a tremendous game, that keeps me coming back day after day.

I bought the game around launch, but forgot from where. Played it then for 5 minutes and once I realized the entire gameplay would be "move and loot at the same time, or game over", I quickly deleted it. This year (2021) having seen the game bubble up on Steam's popularity chart, I read some of the reviews. And they were good!?

So bought it again, and what a second impression. Fantastic visuals, jaw dropping scenery, and a very polished and seamless experience overall. It seems the years have reshaped this from a turd of an experience to the gem of 2021.

The timer and resource gathering mechanics are still in, but having patched those out myself, has left me with what is probably the best space exploration game I have ever come across.

I look at this title from the lens of Elite Dangerous. This game is for sure dumbed down when it comes to flight mechanics, as well as less realistic, but it more than makes up for it in the quick and seamless flow of going from point A to B, and things to see. Where it takes ages to traverse from one port to another in Elite, here it can literally take seconds. This allows me to explore orders of magnitude more planets than in Elite. Every time I do a takeoff -> jump -> land loop, I smile to myself and make a finger gesture at my Elite box.

It feels like the devs of No Man's Sky looked at Elite and asked themselves; what makes this such a boring and/or slow experience? And then they came up with solutions to those design problems!

Examples of what I find awesome in this title:
[list]
  [*] Streamlined. Already covered above. I can have a meaningful game session in 10 minutes here. In "other" space games I need to set aside half a day, something I can't afford (socially or economically; family mad when no food on the table).
  [*] Visual style. Graphics though not state-of-the-art in texture detail, has a very nice artistic style to it. Overall the game looks incredibly eye pleasing which helps with immersion.
  [*] Parts of the Physics. The feeling of flying your ship down towards a landing pad on the ground, then doing a sharp horizontal turn/yaw because you missed it by a few meters is absolutely nailed. The craft slides in a motion that in a split second conveys both ship mass and a sense of air resistance. Difficult to describe, you just have to try it yourself.
  [*] Space legs (elite joke). You can walk most everywhere. On space stations as well as worlds, including those with "no atmosphere, light atmosphere and earth like planets".
  [*] Being able to perform dramatic terrain modification.
  [*] Different fast travel options a'la Stargate.
  [*] Jetpack!
  [*] Base building... Anywhere!
  [*] Surveying and mining on planets.
  [*] Good enough FPS combat.
  [*] A range of different biomes, weather, storms, scolding, freezing and what-nots.
  [*] Under water biomes. Once I jumped in a lake by mistake, I realized the world under the sea is almost as detailed and interesting as on land. Blew me away.
  [*] Humor. E.g. when analyzing a mean looking critter, and getting a behavior description that simply states "Evil".
[/list]

The game borrows shamelessly great ideas from both movies and other games. It does it to such a degree that it's almost comical; some internal joke from the NMS studio I guess. I think Elite and Star Citizen in particular are the butt of those jokes. And rightly so. It makes fun of them in the best way possible; implementing concepts from those other games better than the originals. Even implementing ideas that the other studios are still just talking about.

My Hat's off to the developers, even though my wife hates you, because I apparently spend waaay too much time in your "stupid game".

In conclusion I'd say that this game is the most fleshed out universe exploration experience I've come across, and it has so many elements to it that now seems the time for the devs to patch out the timers and resource gathering entirely. The title can stand on its own without those gimmicks. No Man's Sky of 2021 is a completely different game from the title with the same name launched in 2016.
Reviews.114366:
If there was a Phoenix Metaphor in game development. I think Hello Games has one on its hands. I heard nothing but bad things about this game at launch. And when I finally got around to playing it I was pleasantly surprised to see they are still at it. Making it a much better experience overall.

Coop survival in this game is really fun, I played this in a party of four with friends, and we got to explore a lot of different systems together as we did the main story. Even if the game kept taking us back to the same home system over and over. (It turned into injoke, haha)

However this game is still far from flawless. Multiplayer has a lot of bugs that made us drop it for the day. Most of them had to do with the carriers you can purchase and customize, a lot of the times, other players visiting the carrier would just phase through the floor as they tried to enter the main area from the hangar, killing them and damaging their suit upgrades. Other bugs included a now patched bug in Multiplayer that made ships double or quadruple in size, clipping into a space station and making interacting with pilots, or even getting to the vendors upstairs. Impossible. 

This other part is more of a nitpick, but Ive always been one to play Mouse and Keyboard over a controller when I play PC games. Not there is anything wrong with controller Im just more comfortable with it. No Man's Sky's menu and gameplay are very, very much more optimized for a controller and it shows. I don't recommend playing it on Mouse and Keyboard at all.

I recommend this game to anyone who has played Elite Dangerous, and is looking for something to do while waiting for its new expansion, or anyone who is wanting a space exploration game with colorful landscapes, rather in-depth base building, and interested in a light but gripping space odyssey story. Im looking forward to any future updates that are planned and ill be following the development of the game from here on.

Bought and played since dec 2020 and currently 50+ hours of playtime;
At first i was pleasantly surprised by NMS, as after years of skepticism I decided to try it out and found it quite entertaining. Almost immediately however, the polish of the game was revealed to be extremely thin. 

*COOP/MULTIPLAYER being the part of the game that always drew me towards it turned out to be almost nonexistant and what was there seemed to be a superficial afterthought. Simple missions that are pretty much pointless, no combined base building, no coop story sections at all, no trading of items, money, nanites, tech unless you group up and dump item stacks in a refiner and let the other person pick that stack up, etc. Some of these issues are small i know, but this is a game that has been out for 4 YEARS AS A SUPPOSED MULTIPLAYER GAME!!!

*BASE BUILDING turned out to be a bug ridden mess that has resulted in me spending BY FAR more time researching fan/player suggested fixes and workarounds to SIMPLE BASE BUILDING bugs than i have spent building both of my bases!
The simplicity of the issues is the most frustrating and even mind blowing part of my frustration with the game, for example;
Pretty much give up building your base out of wood/metal/concrete unless you love constant issues.  Lighting, temperature, power, storage, all an exercise in frustration due to mind boggling decisions on the devs part. 
Want ceiling lights in your custom base? Too bad. 
Want storage for your single story high base? Too bad.
Want a large base that holds atmosphere? Too bad.
Want a roof made out of flat metal panels? Too bad.
Want a trade terminal in your custom base? Too bad.
And by god i could continue for pages. 

Simply put, i have enjoyed hours of no mans sky play, yet the deeper i get into it, and the more i try to do, the more i find either bugs, glitches or nonexistant features. So much of what irritates my about this game is SO basic. The frustration of trying to work with a friend on a combined base was amplified by the fact that this is not a new game. This has been a sold as a "complete" game for 4 YEARS! 
I wont even touch on all the lies we were given during years of developement and even after release as, to their credit, the devs have done so much to fix what the game but the amount of bugs this game has displayed has frankly surprised me. The lack of so many basic features that almost any other multiplayer game has had for years continues to leave me wondering, WHY? 

In conclusion; So much potential here, So much that can be enjoyed, yet SO much that still seems like an early access game just released. 
The main reason i am so frustrated is that I can see that the issues that ruin my experience here are simply addressed in many other titles, eg; subnautica, breathedge, etc. 
Until they show more basic fixes, rather than meaningless cosmetic content or slightly different ships/transports/tech/etc, i cannot recommend this game in any way.

[b]NMS has lots of things to do, it is like a vast lake, but as soon as you go in, you realize it's only deep enough to wet your feet.[/b]

NMS has lots of mechanics, most of which are extremely shallow. There is a story, there is resource gathering, there is combat, there is resource gathering, there is exploration, there is resource gathering, there is equipment, there is resource gathering, there is base building and there is multiplayer. Oh, and also resource gathering.
Out of all of those the most fleshed out is - you guessed it - Base building. So let me go through those mechanics and how I feel about their implementation within the game one by one to give you an accurate idea of what you will be doing if you decide to spend your free time playing this game.

[h1]Resource Gathering[/h1]
Yes, playing NMS and trying to engage with most of the mechanics requires copious amounts of resource gathering, and all that gathering is in the game is shooting a laser beam at things until they die or get destroyed and those resources get transported to your inventory. Let me remark: all that is is staring at something with your button (mouse, controller, w/e) clicked, until it disappears. That's all. And you will have to do it all the time.
"There is no way that's all there is to it", I hear you saying, and you are right, but that is about 95% of it. There are some other ways to get resources but you won't engage with those nearly as often.

[h1]Base Building[/h1]
Easily the best implemented mechanic in the game. You can go deep with this, and while there are some annoyances, you won't necessarily run into them often. There are lots of different assets for you to play with, and you can really get very creative with this mechanic. There are even assets for water submerged buildings! 
There are games that implement base building with a modular block system: You build rooms and may equip them but you don't design the shape of the room; think Subnautica, and there are base building implementations in which you have - or are encouraged - to build each room yourself, to your liking, and instead of rooms you manage floors, walls, roofs, etc; think Fallout 4. NMS has both of these systems, so you can get a quick setup going by using the modular rooms, or get really intricate and personal by chosing to design each room yourself. 
And the decoration has lots of options too! Chairs, tables, lockers, even flags; you name it, there are probably several options for you to chose from.

[h1]Space Exploration[/h1]
There is this persistent aspect to NMS which is procedural generation. When done right, procedural generation can be amazing. Here it is lackluster. There is a handful of planet archetypes; say radioactive, hot, cold, toxic, earth-like, etc. The first time you visit each of these archetypes, you will experience something relatively different to what you've seen before, and it will probably be exciting, but keep in mind the amount of assets for each planet is [b]very[/b] limited, say up to 20 plants, 20 creatures and 20 minerals, usually less than this, and you must keep in mind that a good portion of each of those are specific to each biome of the planet (water, simple surface, mountain surface or caves). So you will only experience a handful of those assets copy pasted over and over and over again. Some biomes are super similar independently of the planet archetype, like caves or water biomes, what will differ the most with each archetype are the surface biomes. Within each planet archetype, assets get heavily reused, and it's very noticeable.
Basically, as far as planet exploration goes you will have experienced all there is to it by the time you visit your second or third iteration of each archetype.
Other than planets, there are some other things to see in space: some story related entities, which always look the same inside and out, occasional frigate encounters, which look different in the outside but are all the same in  the interior, system space station which also are usually somewhat different on the outside, all the same in the interior, and the Space Anomaly, which is a multiplayer hub.

[h1]Combat and equipment[/h1]
There is combat when on a planet and combat in space. When in space, you will shoot ships with your own ship and get shot at. There are a few different weapons, but combat is so extremely unchallenging that you won't need to use anything other than your base weapon. If you do use something else, its all very similar: 
You can shoot explosives so you deal a large amount of damage in long intervals, or small amounts of damage in short intervals, or continuous laser beams which deal nearly continuous damage. The DPS is nearly the same, and nothing else really changes. 
Enemy ships will always react the same way to your attacks, and there is no other system that will intervene, like if the laser beam dealt more damage to the shield but less to the ship itself. In space there is only 1 type of enemy, which are simple ships, they can be pirates or sentinels but they act all the same.
Within a planet, there are a few more enemy variants. Sentinels, which are robotic creatures present in every planet, can be simple (floating) drones, dog-like 4 legged drones, and bipedal tall robots. The drones shoot small bullets at short intervals at you, they don't do much else other than that. They can have 1 health bar or 2 if they are 'armored'. The dog-like drones are all the same: they can jump at you for melee damage, or shoot a short lived continuous laser that follows your movement. They bipedal robot only shoots the laser akin to the 4 legged drone, but it will require you to use explosives to kill it as it has some more advanced armor.
Other than that, some planets have aggressive fauna, which means that the carnivours of that planet will attack you on sight, and that entails just jumping at your or biting you in melee range. There are also "monstrosities" at abandoned buildings, which can do the same as aggressive fauna, but also they throw some kind of acid bolts at you in a ranged sort of fashion.
That's all there is. Did you count? If you count the different types of damage/weapons you will be facing, there are about 5: Short interval burst of bullets, short lived continuous laser beams, jumping at you melee, close range melee, and a weird bolt. There is no variety or changes from enemy to enemy, those are carbon copies over and over, unlike a ranged enemy in, say, an FPS game which might have different types of projectile weaponry, which have different interval, damage, armor penetration, burst, etc, characteristics.
You can alter your stats, those of your ship or of your land vehicles through equipment. The equipment you can apply occupies slots where your gathered resources could go, which is a fun mechanic as you have to decide if you want to lose capacity in favor of  capability. Visually, nothing changes. The appearance of your character, your vehicles or your ships are independent of the equipment you have. If there was more of an RPG theme to this, and you could armor your character with different equipment that you could see and had different characteristics, that would be cool. Instead, all equipment does is alter some base stats, which means that you maybe will survive a couple of more enemy bullet bursts, or your enemies will survive a couple of bursts less from you... or, alternatively, your ship will move slightly quicker, or your jetpack will last slightly longer. That's about the depth of the equipment system, and that's disappointing.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
At the end of the day, NMS attempts to do a little of everything and ends up doing very little well. When you start playing and every mechanic and concept is novel, it's all very exciting, but as soon as you delve with each of those mechanics as they are presented you realize how shallow it all is.
If you are really curious about it, I'd recommend you get it on a discount.

Played the game originally shortly after the release date. The game seemed fine, just not really for me was how I described it to others. Oddly, it didn't feel like there was a ton to do ... besides traveling to the 98 gazillion planets and scanning everything in the name of research. It was fine, just a bit slower than what I'm normally into (Souls, fps, and sports for the most part).

Recently repurchased the game on sale and it is both completely different and exactly the same as it was before. In a very good way. The game remains the same in principle, with the majority of your time spent travelling through space and collecting materials - just like before. The game still looks great, just as it did. However, there is just more to it now than there was at launch. 

From quests to NPCs, there is simply more content to experience now than there was originally. And they managed to keep all of the positive aspects of the game (random and procedurally generated locations/plants/animals, space exploration and flying your starship) and add to it without harming the core that was there. From base-building to added storylines, there is a much more complete feel to playing the game (especially early on) than there had been initially.

I've played the game for roughly 75 hrs now (this 2nd time through) and I'll admit that flying around in my ship just exploring planets and collecting materials is more fun than I'd originally given it credit for. I honestly think I would have liked the game at least a bit more had I given it more of a chance the first time. However, the game has improved markedly and that really helped to get me going early on. Had THIS been the version of the game to launch initially, the reception would have been very different and in a positive way. 

I really like the game now. If you're on the fence as a previous player, I'd say wait for a sale and go for it. If you've never played and want to fly around in space, check out some alien creatures and locations, maybe converse with the locals a bit - this game is definitely worth your attention.

Latecomer to this game, only picked it up recently. Overall there's lots of potential for growth, feels like a solid foundation and can see a LOT of content opportunities. 

Pros: 
- Very good progression 
- Really enjoying freighter/frigate element and base-building / passive income and hotspot mining is very cool.
- Materials collecting and crafting is accessible and not grindy

Cons:
- Non co-op multiplayer doesn't really seem to be there yet (Nexus missions multiplayer doesn't really seem to offer much over soloing missions)
- Blueprint-locked crafting is kind of annoying. Finding blueprints to enable a crafting recipe in a singleplayer experience feels tedious and unnecessary if there's no player-driven economy at stake

Wishlist: 
- System commodity buy/sell lists visible in galaxy map would really de-grind commodity trading
- Automated crafting at bases via
     1) enabling pipe connections to large refiners to create crafting chains / automatic storage 
     2) enabling hirable automated NPC ships which could ferry goods between planetary bases
- Multiplayer challenge missions like: 
     1) Instanced team co-op raids on planetary bases / sentinel compounds
     2) Freighter boarding raids / capture
     3) Planetside-style missions to unlock systems which become taken over and blocked off by enemies
- More meaningful character creation - currently seems character species is totally aesthetic 
- More ship role bonuses. Class bonuses currently exist but don't appear to affect gameplay too much (just my opinion)
More developed planetary NPC tradeposts and bases - not clear why planetary bases need to be scanned for instead of a few major ones just appearing as destinations for trade like surface stations

Reviews.114689:
I had an extremely mixed experience with this game. There were many aspects of it that I really enjoyed, but there were also many areas that were irritating or frustrating, and the cons eventually overwhelmed the pros, leading me to give this game a negative rating.

The graphics for this game were quite impressive, for the most part. It usually looks quite good, with countless fascinating planets, cool ships, and a ton of different things to see and explore. The optimisations taken to allow such a vast universe to be rendered are quite apparent though, with obvious texture pop-in, very inconsistent framerates, and limited render distances, which did put a bit of a damper on the experience.

The story and lore were very interesting, and this was one of the parts of the game I enjoyed the most. However, this also had some major caveats, as much of the dialogue in this game was either in another language or was written in such a way that made it difficult to read. I wanted to know more about the universe of this game, but struggled to understand what was happening a lot of the time. Additionally, I was not impressed with the ending of the main quest (major spoilers ahead, so be wary). Once you finish the main quest, [spoiler]you are given the opportunity to start in a new galaxy. However, it isn't clear at all what the consequences of such a decision are. It turns out you spawn in an entirely new region of space, and while you keep your ship and freighter, all of your upgrades on your exosuit, ship, and multi-tool break, and you are only able to get back to your previous bases if you're able to teleport to them.[/spoiler] Being vague with such a major choice with absolutely no warnings about the consequences of your decision is just completely unacceptable, and left me feeling quite betrayed.

The gameplay is alright, but it gets very repetitive very quickly. Gathering resources is a chore, hostile creatures almost immediately became trivial to defeat, ship fights are usually fairly trivial as well, and base building would be cool if there weren't so many arbitrary restrictions on how things can be connected. I also tried the game in VR which would have been really cool, but the game didn't run very smoothly in VR and I got motion sick pretty quickly.

Despite everything I've mentioned up to this point, I probably would have given the game a positive review if it weren't for this game's horrendous stability. I honestly feel lied to, as I saw many reviews that stated that this game had improved greatly from it's horrendous state five years ago, and how it's actually a good game now, but my experience (and the experience of the three friends I played with) tells a different story:
[list]
[*] Bases were a nightmare to construct, as terrain edits didn't save properly, the requirements for building components was wildly inconsistent, and plants frequently respawned inside of bases.
[*] Workstation inventories (such as refiners) were frequently wiped, leading to loss of resources, and they often showed they were running when they weren't, or vice versa.
[*] Repairs sometimes inexplicably listed the incorrect materials to repair.
[*] Base computer quests constantly pointed to a different base computer, sometimes pointing to nowhere at all.
[*] Quest icons were sometimes duplicated, or rapidly flashed, making it difficult to navigate to them.
[*] Using the pulse engine was infuriating when multiple icons were in close proximity, as it was often impossible to target the correct one.
[*] The main quest become impossible to complete for me at one point, as the necessary items did not spawn.
[*] It was fairly easy to clip through some objects and fall through the surface of the planet.
[*] Terrain editing was very inconsistent, as it didn't work if you were too close to the ground, terrain could break through other terrain, and breaking terrain sometimes created holes in the ground texture.
[*] Some buildings and landmarks spawned far in the air, while other spawned below what could be mined.
[*] Animals and sentinels sometimes clipped through objects while in dialogue.
[*] Ships sometimes got stuck inside a freighter after exiting a pulse or stuck inside a planet after using a star chart while flying towards one, with no way to escape.
[*] Ships sometimes inexplicably exited a pulse, drastically extending the time it took to fly somewhere.
[*] NPCs sometimes spawned at a 45 degree angle or inside the ground, and trying to talk to them in this state softlocked the game.
[*] Bases didn't sync properly between multiple players, and my friends often clipped through parts of the base or were stopped by things that didn't exist.
[*] My friends randomly got dropped from our group without reason, which also prevented them from getting the rewards for quests in progress, and these quests often didn't sync up properly, requiring steps to be completed multiple times.
[*] Some sound effects were extremely loud and were much louder than the rest of the game.
[*] Crashes to desktop occurred, although infrequently.
[/list]
I continued to try to give this game more chances, as I did enjoy the game for the most part, but as more and more bugs were discovered, I simply couldn't enjoy the experience. The final nail in the coffin for me was when a bug occurred in the main quest, and it became impossible to complete. The only way I found to solve this was to use an external utility to edit the save and skip that step in the quest, which took a number of hours to figure out. After this I simply couldn't bring myself to give this game any more of my time.

[b]TL;DR[/b] While this game shows a lot of promise and has certainly improved in recent years, the poor communication of the story and lore (especially the ending), the repetitive gameplay, and the massive number of bugs and issues encountered lead me to avoid recommending this title.

You start this game off with a tutorial that makes you more confused about what little you know about the game coming in. The UI is super text-heavy, but for no reason. It explains super obvious things in great detail and non-obvious things not at all, not even in the guides. You’ll spend a lot of time on forums, google, etc, is this what a career in development is like? The UI especially when building is the most confusing thing I’ve ever seen in my life, it really doesn’t need to be this difficult to use. The 'quick menu' is also not very intuitively organised, it's just random things stuffed under there it seems.

Controls with K+M for the ship is something you need to get used to, it’s weird. But you get used to it and then you start to kind of like it. The controls for the Exocraft for the Minotaur are disgustingly terrible. Take every logic about movement, and now throw it out of the window, I honestly think you need to control it while being drunk because that’s how its movement feels like. The car has pretty much no physics and now I’m scared to unlock the rest.

Speaking of Exocrafts, they have a resource scanner but no visor ability. If the intention is to explore the planet but you can’t actually find useful POIs because you can use the visor inside a vehicle, what’s the point? You’re better off unlocking some movement upgrades like the jetpack jump, you’re faster than a vehicle and can use the visor at any time.

I had a tiny glimmer of hope that maybe you’re able to fly your freighter, or be able to fly large ships in which you can walk around in, but unfortunately that doesn’t exist but would be cool. Also, the entire UI talks about Freighters but when you see a freighter just like yours, it’s called a Frigate. Very confusing stuff.

Anywhosle, you use your spaceship, a lot and it amazes me that you’re not able to customise the ships' appearance, at all. You’re able to extensively customise your character down to the last detail, you’re able to change the colour of your freighter but not your ship, the one thing you see he most. Really hope this gets added in with an update, you find your perfect spaceship, you buy the doodoo colour special editon thinking you can change it and now you’re stuck with the yellow and green highlighted doodoo tin.

The main mission is incredibly boring, every mission within it is exactly the same, it's almost like you can feel the devs really not wanting to include a story mode but then being pushed by their investors because it generates more in-game use time. Construct a signal booster to find a bigger signal booster to talk to a guy to fly somewhere just so that you can repeat this again 50 times.

Then of course when you see the second main mission, the atlas path you think to yourself - wow, this looks really interesting, let me get a beer and dedicate my whole night to this one mission only to find yourself flying through 5 galaxies (and no, you can't jump directly because the end-galaxies are purposely out of jump range forcing you to fly through 5 galaxies every time) talking to the atlas dude, 11 times in a row where the only exciting thing is the atlas orb’s different animations, you feel a special kind of hatred coming up for the main missions to a point where you contemplate why you bought this game but then you remind yourself that you’re not actually obligated to do these missions.

Which then brings me to the reason why I’m giving this game a thumbs up - after unlocking nearly everything and playing the game how I want to play it, I can safely say that the game does not force you to complete main missions in order to progress with unlocking parts, receipts or generally interfere with your quest in selling as much chlorine to stations as you can in order to get rich and retire.

Although, the game seems to trick you into thinking you need to proceed with the main mission to unlock things, you only really need to get to the nexus and then you're all good. Everything else can be unlocked by finding buildings using a space map, nanites or units.

In short, this game is logical when it doesn’t matter and illogical when it does matter. The UI is very pretty, the UX not so much. However having played the game when it first came out, it’s unrecognisable in a very positive way, I actually enjoy it now. The online community of this game is incredible, I've never come across such a giving and non-toxic community.

A really nice game, full of potential. The player can do much - exploration, combat, base building, learning alien languages, crafting, manufacturing... you name it.

Sadly the game seems to have lost its depth somewhere in the broadness of its content. While you can do virtually anything, most of the actions are a bit ragged around the edges and seem to lack any significant impact on the game other than entertaning the player with yet another self-contained mini-game and a bit of cash for the effort.

Which brings us to the biggest flaw of this nice game - tech progression tied to story progression. Key elements of the game are locked behind the story line. And I don't mean just an "intro story" - the game *is* the story. Each time you unlock some new mechanic, you can bet your hat that this feature will be incomplete unless you move on with the story. 
- Want to build a base? Weell, turns out you can't build 95% of stuff until you finish the linear part of the quest.
- Want to explore and chat up aliens? No problem, but some of them keep asking about some "weapons terminals" and really wish to get hired.. if only I knew what this terminal is. Of course it is unlocked after some more story.
- Planetary vehicles: Still don't have them after 40 hrs. Can't be obtained without doing a lot of story (I guess).

Furthermore, the campaign requirements are done poorly, since you can spend dozens of hours building a perfect relationship with the aliens only to have a mission have you "do a quest for them to earn their trust". I've really missed fixed requirements that would simply accept that I already qualify instead of having a 30 hour long mega-tutorial. And boy it does feel like a tutorial. Fetch that. Take a mission. Look, a module - better install it. All this while you already have several bases, a fleet of ships and nearly maxed out gear.

This brings us to the conclusion:
This game is nice. Really nice. You can do nearly anything. So play along and enjoy it.
If you treat NMS as an open world and roam about, you will get punished by not having key technologies due to them being bound to story line and you will suffer.
If you focus too much on a specific aspect of the game, you will eventually find it lacking and not quite what you wished for - and you will suffer.
The only way to not suffer is to play along. Play the story campaign. Do a few things along the way. The game is made to please. Stay on track and let it please you - and it will. Just don't expect it to be a well working open world.

This game is... neat? I guess that's the best word for it.

As a bonus, there are currently occasional bugs that can prevent you from being able to teleport to a friend's base, further complicating any intentions of doing activities together.

In some ways this feels like a new age or supercharged Minecraft in space. I like how huge this universe is even though I have only partially explored a handful of systems (okay, maybe 2 or 3 handfuls) so far. I am overwhelmed with options to explore, so many missions and things I want to do, it's hard to decide and remember which to pursue.

As a new player, I kind of like how the terminals and attendants to those terminals can help guide you forward in developing technology, but I also feel like in my scatterbrained efforts to figure out what to pursue, I didn't use them very well because a number of technologies they guide me through I had already learned and built.

I have been avoiding the web to some extent because I want to discover on my own, but I feel like I'm missing a lot this way. For instance, I didn't realize I could expand other tabs of storage in my exo-suit and not just the main one until I happened upon this implication in one of my rare web visits, and I didn't find any drop pods to help on this task until I stumbled on one at about the same time after about 70 hours of play after having already expanded my primary exo-suit storage almost fully on space stations. So some of the fundamental ways of progressing are still not quite clear enough if I pick the wrong missions to pursue (drop pods became more obvious when I finished the exo-craft terminal missions). I'm divided on whether I like discovering this on my own at the risk of missing major aspects of the game versus having more guidance down a path where I spend less time on silly and futile efforts. I still don't fully understand the different kinds of maps I can get, and should probably be using those more. I've accumulated more navigation data than I can hold in one high-capacity inventory slot and wondering if I should be doing more map trading or what else I can do with navigation data.

As I said, there are just so many options, and it's hard to choose between them and pursue one (and be unsure about whether it's the best pursuit), but most of them are enjoyable regardless. Few games offer this much freedom and exploration, and those are among my favorite aspects of any game.

Just a couple things bug me about this game. There are still some glitches like the fact that it told me the wrong recipe to refine Deuterium and I had to resort to a web search to figure out how to refine deuterium. The blueprints for doors in some cases don't make a lot of sense and in others flat out don't work. And there have been multiple occasions where relatively valuable artifacts have been buried beneath bedrock making them entirely inaccessible. Also, I can't run this game full screen on my high resolution monitor while my second monitor is plugged in. I have to either use windowed mode, unplug my second monitor, or drop the resolution of my primary monitor. I guess these are small prices to pay to play such an addictive game (I run windowed mode in a relatively large window).

Unbelievable.  This has everything you could imagine wanting out of a game like this and more.  Just as one example, planets with oceans or lakes have different underwater biomes, you can build your bases underwater, and even build a submarine to explore.  It's like they've taken every good element from every survival game ever made and jammed it into one game.  Creative and flexible base building, ground combat, space combat, trade, branching story, missions, base industrial automation.  You can buy capital ships and build a fleet and send them out on tasks.  You have control of how much multiplayer you turn on, you can pick which of your bases, if any, you want to open up to be seen by other players, and if you fully enter multiplayer the game plays like an MMO.

Having so many elements though does mean things like the space combat are obviously not going to be as good as a game where the devs spent 100% of their time just working on space combat.  You pretty well just blow up pirates, but there are enough ship types and ways to customize your weapon loadouts and upgrades to make it fun.  The underwater stuff is cool, but it doesn't go all that deep, and there aren't that many types of underwater biomes, but the fact that they even have one is better than what most survival games have.  There are only a couple industrial buildings, this is not Factorio, but there is enough that I had to think about where to build my bases and when to build stuff to optimize revenue.

Most of the game elements are like that, not the best ever done, a bit shallow, but enough to sink your teeth into, but all of it works together really well to make a great game, and the MMO element is a giant amazing cherry on top.  If there was any word I'd used to describe this game it would be vast, there is so much to do, you could explore until you find the ultimate paradise planet and literally spend the rest of your IRL life exploring it, or explore until you find a hellscape planet and build a base on the side of a volcano, or do what I did and randomly run into a 1000 foot icewall in the middle of an artic planet so cold it'll kill you in 30 seconds without the proper protection and build a replica of castle black, and if you get bored with that maybe go find an Atlas factory and see if your weapon loadouts are good enough to take out one of those giant mechs, jump onto multiplayer and see what cool things other people have built, get some friends together and build a giant base and fly around and go hunt some pirates.

Reviews.114967:
I really struggled with whether or not I should recommend this game or not.

"As broad as an ocean, as shallow as a mud puddle." That really sums it up. Even years on, with (admittedly) laudable efforts from the developers to try to make good on the game they sold people on. 

Don't get me wrong. The devs have done a good job of trying to fix the game and add content. And I've spent a couple hundred hours playing it, so by no measure can I say I haven't gotten my money's worth. I have.

The thing is, though...

There's no point. To anything. The game is almost insultingly overbearing in how little point there is to anything. Even avoiding story spoilers, which is a whole 'nother can of worms... Once you start to realize the "broad as an ocean, shallow as a puddle" problem, the game just sort of collapses. Why spend time gathering resources to make or buy more anti-matter, to warp to planet #4324... Which is just going to be another slight variation on a handful of planet types, with a handful of "skins" each. 

Yeah, great. This planet has flying squirrels instead of flying lizards. This planet has green grass instead of red grass. This planet has radiation storms instead of fire storms. This planet is owned by the frog-people instead of the robot-people. None of it matters. The planets are all the same. There's nothing new to find. After you've explored one system, you've explored 90% of the game. And after a while, spending hours flying around trying to find juuuust the right combination of critters and trees and sky colors to make your base stars to get tedious and feel pointless.

And when you do make a base? Again, pointless. You don't really gain anything from it. The base building interface is oddly buggy, There's no way to make your base feel alive. You can't populate it with NPCs or anything - well, a small handful, that do nothing but stand at their specific work bench. There's a fairly limited number of parts to build with, and a very small amount of furniture and decorative stuff. If you really, really like building games with pre-made, snap-together parts, maybe that part will tickle your fancy, but there are so many games that do it better. 

The multiplayer is glitchy when it isn't obnoxious, cheating is rampant and unchecked, and... Again, not to beat the same dead horse, but there's no point to it. You can't even hardly cooperate - all vehicles are one-player only. Yeah, there are a few missions you can grind with people... But you don't have to, most of them can be done just fine solo. And the only reward is currency to spend on a few cosmetic items. If you want the satisfaction of saying you ground them out, rather than just cheated them in, because your save file is local and easy to modify.

I feel really bad giving this game a "not recommended" review, because the devs have been an sterling example of how devs should be... But I can't honestly recommend the game, either.
Reviews.114968:
Since this game's launch I've been a fan of it and have been following and playing the game. It's quickly risen to one of my favourite games ever.

Which is why it pains me to say that this game still leaves a lot to be desired. 

Inventory
Absolutely everything in this game requires inventory slots. I often find myself, and I'm a few slots short of a fully upgraded exosuit, in need of extra inventory slots. One of the issues here is that there are so much seemingly redundant variants of resources. There's Cadmium and Activated Cadium. Both can be regarded as completely different from one another, even though it's not quiet clear how exactly they are different. Why are there two Cadmiums? 

Freighters
You can't properly build a base in a freighter, because it resets when you buy a new freighter. This effectively stops me from upgrading my freighter again, because I like my freighter base now and don't want to redo it.

Frigates
The frigate rating system is weird. Effectively, sending a two-star fleet on a two-star mission is just a tad too difficult for them. 9 out of 10 times my frigates come back with damage, and nowhere in the game does it communicate to me what it is I'm doing wrong. And sending a two-star fleet on a one-star mission feels like I'm missing out on greater rewards.

Story and identity
Finally, I'd love to see more of the individual races. I'd like to see more places that are important to the lore, more characters that are important, that were modelled uniquely. To really get into the lore that is so rich and beautiful. What if I warp into a system and a big freighter like I've never seen before warps up in front of me and it's owned by an important Vy'keen warlord who invites me to prove my worth to him? What if that ship has Vy'keen shopkeepers that sell uniquely Vy'keen items and upgrades that you can't get on space stations? What if I can meet up with Apollo and join him in space battles? There's still so much that's possible in this regard. I think it's important to take a break from the algorithm every once in a while. That Vy'keen warlord I talked about? Model him. Don't let him be procedurally generated. The reason I say this is the fact that the procedural generation produces things that are just weirdly random enough that in the end they turn out looking rather same-y, and that loses a lot of the magic over time. I think that's rather much of a shame. Because the character design itself is incredible!  
I would love to see more historically important places. Settlements and maybe cities made by the races, that are important to them. 
The ships for all races look the same. Sure, there are differences between systems and types of chips, but I can't tell by being shown a ship whether that ship is a Korvax or Gek ship or whether it's a C class or an A class. It would be really cool if there was a way to acquire rare ships through missions, very particularly Korvax ships or ones that are uniquely Vy'keen. Maybe Hirk's old ship or multi-tool are somewhere at the bottom of an ocean, waiting for a Traveller to come along and fix them. In-game unlockables that can't be acquired through just flying around and talking to NPCs.

Minor UX improvements
Finally, there are some UX problems that bother me. The Galaxy Map for instance. Sometimes when I click and hold a galaxy, it selects that galaxy. And sometimes, it warps immediately. Since warp cells are not the easiest resource to come by, especially early on, it's rather annoying when you're warping somewhere you didn't mean to warp to. 
Lastly, there are some issues with quest wording still. Some quests for instance require you to find "a Korvax cartographer". What you meant was, you wanted me to find one very specific korvax cartographer but didn't word it that way. This creates an opportunity though; if you want me to find a specific character, why not make it a special character in the lore? Model this person so they stand out from the rest and let me meet another interesting person in the lore, rather than interact with yet another character that looks the same as the others.

As you read these things, remember that I think this game is incredible. I think, in terms of quality per person that worked on the game, it's probably one of the greatest games ever. But that's why it frustrates me even more that I'm missing something. And that's also why I'm hoping people will play this game and enjoy it as much as I do. Let's let Hello Games know that we care and that we are waiting with arms wide open for all that is to come.

Reviews.115015:
It delivers on exploration, immersion and generally is fun enough to keep me busy.

It does get a bit repetitive action wise but currently still outweighed by the different planets, biomes, etc with a variety of different items, building options etc.

The biggest problems are with multiplayer quest issues (especially the Specialist quests bugging out and not being able to be completed until starting a solo game) and with general graphics and quest glitches.
Graphics are constantly loading at low quality, and there is frequent clipping issues (this is both on PC and PS4 for context). Flying accidently into a flower or mushroom on a planet will often result in your ship getting fully stuck and then you die. Quests will often bug out on dialogue options or fully freeze (especially in multiplayer when 2 people access terminals at the same time), updates to quests are inconsistent (exploring/identifying quests are a prime example), warping into a planet because it didn't stop when on hyperdrive...
For base building, flatting the ground or taking a mountain out of the way however is a huge problem. The removed mountains will spawn back in at some point and just mess up your whole base. On top of that, it'll create clipping issues where you can just fall straight through.
This all combined can make the game extremely frustrating. Saving often thus becomes a must.

I would still recommend the game as it is fun to play with friends. Because it's cross platform, it's one of the few games my wife and I can play together. And because of the reputation that HG has build back up, I trust that over time, things will continue to improve (and likely break when new features are launched) but it has been worth the money I spend on the game.
