The game is good fun alright, but Hello Games is getting too much credit for it. In lots of places, the work they've put in feels rather sloppy, because there's lots of glitches everywhere, even with things dating back to the release version.

- Capital ships spawning on top of you, trapping your ship inside their hitbox, you have no choice but to let yourself die, or potentially lose a lot of progress depending on your last save.
- Getting stuck in dialogues, again losing progress.
- Ship getting stuck in mid-air in the "landing sequence", again losing progress.
- Digging underground sometimes teleports you to the surface, or creatures to underground.
- Ships landing inside of each other, luckily they don't have physics.
- The PC version has free-look inside ships now, but it's got dreadful mouse acceleration and letting go of free-look violently steers the ship into the direction you were looking at.
- Ship control in general is... I'm at a lack for words, both in "tethered" and "normal" modes (keyboard&mouse).
- Inside view of all Exocraft has dreadful mouse acceleration.
- The Exocraft control feel is alltogether... questionable, at best.
- Freighter interior visually glitching, openings look like walls from one side, and an open path/room/doorway from the other.
- Auto-holstering of the weapon makes it impossible to take careful aim at flying creatures or targets at higher angular velocity with hitscan weapons before firing.
- Hit boxes of creatures are really crude.
- Buying a large figure of items from the market? Have fun weighing down your E key for 10 minutes /facepalm /consolefied

I could list more if I had taken notes of everything. I'm not seeing the great redemption that word of mouth has delivered so far, I see unpolished updates being chucked into the game, and then left at that state.

Going through the interface (inventory, dialogues, et cetera) is somewhat tedious to go through, especially repeated ones ("Practise language skills", or where it closes without letting you choose other available options), forced animation sit-throughs (e. g. when initiating a dialogue).

Sure I've played 56 hours so far, but what have I achieved in that time? If you design a game to be drawn-out and grindy, with somewhat repetitive content, you can play for hundreds of hours without having seen all substantial content. That's not overwhelmingly great game design.

But it's good fun alright. There's enough oddities to be discovered, I just wouldn't wholeheartedly recommend it straight-away. And some things need fixing or adjusting, or the ability to opt-out of them (e. g. animation wait-throughs).

I was never into this type of games (first-person view), more into strategies of all kinds. But I have to say I falled in love with this game right after I started playing it this year!

It is for sure different from the standard strategies but in a good way which makes it addictive. It gives you so much freedom in the playstyle, what to focus on and what to ignore. There is even free-explorer mode where you are not "bothered" with the main story. But even when playing the normal game where you follow the main story you are not forced to, you can fly around, explore, research, build... There are endless possibilities. Most pieces in the game are generated with a little random seed so it does not become just a drill after a while. But the play style is the key, there is no wrong way to play it, you just play it on your own pace, you are not punished for your way of playing so everyone just finds the way he/she likes to play it and enjoy it. That is tremendous difference to  other games where you have to play it the given way to advance to next level and any side "decision" you make have no real effect on the outcome.

In this game, if you want to be an explorer then be it, just explore every planet, every animal, every plant in every system you find. If you want to be a trader then just collect as much as you can and sell it so you become richer and richer. If you like to fight there are sentinels or pirates everywhere. Or just be a one of each a little and enjoy in any combination you like.

Yes, there are also drawbacks in the game. The most annoying is the save of your game... game tries to help you so you do not need to bother but it does the opposite... saving is either when you exit your ship or when you find a "save beacon" on a planet. So you cannot save when you want... for that you have to build a special piece of technology and carry it with you all the time (yet still working on planets only). If only we had the old good Save Game option... Also, most of the things are generated so little random each time, but some mission type are just exactly same which becomes tedious (crashed frighter always has pods on exactly same places).

All in all there is so much in the game to explore, build, fight, choose... even "cooking" is available so you are not bored for quite some time and you can chose what to focus on and what to ignore and still can just enjoy it.

No Man's Sky is essentially Stardew Valley or Animal Crossing in space, but instead of the charming verdant nature of either game it is replaced by vast expanses of cosmic aesthetic that occasionally crosses into the macabre, and most of the time this does work in its favour heavily. You can lose hours to this game just wanting to accrue the necessary financial assets just so you can buy an S-Class Star Ship.

However, if you are looking for something in the vein of the Culture Series, Spelljammer, Warhammer 40,000, or the Xeelee Sequence where science fiction is exaggerated to ludicrous heights this game is not it. You will not be ascending to sublimity. You will not be casting technological spells from your codex of digital souls. You will not be breaking worlds or calling in orbital bombardments to shatter your enemies asunder to the solar winds. Why? Because there is no reason to. There is no real endgame to savor. The sentinels, try as they might, are hardly anything more than a nuisance, and both flora and fauna do not extend to any sort of real hostility. Indeed, there is no Catachan to be found in this game. Finally, pirates are a complete joke and a half and one can easily take on a dozen merely by doing the Parthian Shot technique on their ass.

Don't talk about Abandoned Freighters, they're fun to do but after two or three I have come to realize they are mostly the same and the X-class modules are just stat upgrades, which is the opposite of exciting.

Combat is just above the definition of barebones, danger is simply not there, and after only 36 hours I feel that I've reached the end of what a player can do. Wide puddle, and so on and so forth.

pros:
-the spectacle is top-notch. awe-inspiring environments and visual features such as glowing plants
-simple and infectious minecraft-style "i need more" mental contaminant. you need more units. you need more materials. stuff like that.
-the most fun i can see having is finding funny starships and collecting those that have rare configurations. the starship generation is pretty expansive and is the number one pro for me
-i guess the story is good.
-warping in your freighter is really fun
-abandoned freighters are fun
-minotaur mechs are fun
-base building seems to be incredibly good and a major selling point, although i find construction to be tedious (good thing they added the freighter)

cons:
-too many rare items where you just sell them. you telling me i cant use the whispering egg to make an alien module where i can shoot out alien sperm that melts anything it comes in contact with?
-pirates are a joke
-sentinels are a joke
-animals still seem functionally useless
-cant color my spaceship
-exploration is ultimately still very shallow. i mean yea there's robot animals but they don't do anything. these sandworms don't do anything. these items i pick up don't do anything. this wolf looks cool but it doesnt do anything.
-combat frigates are so fuckin useless in battle it hurts fuck you dawg why does shooting the friendly sentinel drone cause me to gain wanted levels fuck you
-ultimately there was this breaking point where there i felt like there is nothing to do.
-cant collect animals
-cant use animals like pokemon
-no bosses or anything like that, sentinel walkers are kinda daunting but it literally takes like two plasma grenades
-three quarters of these space encounters dont even do anything lol why am i even slowing down


if you are looking to become a god like you do in terraria eject those expectations from your mind right now. (all current "terraria-in-space" games also suck, including you starbound lol)

do i recommend at full price: hell no
do i recommend at 50 percent off: very yes
final score: 6/10, minus one because i can't collect animals

tl;dr stardew valley in space, i dont find it as good as its fans seem to do when they say WOW THIS GAME IMPROVED SO MUCH i mean i guess when you go from a 2/10 to a 6/10 thats a big deal.

If I could middle-vote, I would for NMS. But, up is better than a down vote.  At 76 hours, I've basically quit NMS.  It's the kind of game that you're not sure if you like or not and end up spending a lot of hours figuring it out.  If you want something to just chill, explore, super low stress, grinding and running in a circle for a few hours, this is the game for you.  Here's what I loved and didn't.

Planetary exploration is top notch. There's a good variety of landscape types and fauna/flora to seek out.  But, after a while, you'll noticed the repetition and exploring a planet becomes a grind.  Still, it is well done and enjoyable.  If anything, this should be THE #1 feature you're looking for when buying this game.

Space exploration, however, feels like its on rails and is basic.  If you're looking for a deeper space exploration and ship flight game, I highly recommend Elite Dangerous instead.  Space exploration in this game is basic, feels on rails, and basically exists as simply a way to get from planet A to planet B.  There is some ship combat, but it is gimbled and arcade-like.

Crafting and base building is about as complex as the game ARK (without mods).  (Conan Exiles still has the best base building.)  Terrain shaping is the best feature of base building and the dev's achievement.  It is extremely easy to get back to your base and other star bases you've been to, but getting back out to exploring the black is a pain since you can't easily access the galaxy map without getting in your ship and flying off.  You'll spend most of your time grinding materials and searching planets for materials to build stuff.  I didn't like spending nanites (form of cash) to unlock crafting patterns when later unlocking them again via base terminal missions.  I would play the game differently if I ever started over.

Combat is very basic.  The very first time I died, I killed myself with a mining blaster because I was too close to the blast.  Bots, ships, and fauna are all very simple to kill.  There's a reason an "iron man" one-life mode exists; it's easy and low stress.

You can unlock a frigate to run missions for you, but it is a "set and forget" gameplay that has very little impact on your overall game experience.  If anything, I wish you could make it your main base and teleport back to it from any station.  A mobile base would be awesome for the greater galaxy exploration game.

Overall, its worth $30 (on sale) to play around with.  The game is NOT realistic at all, even as a "survival" game, so you have to just go with it.  The game crashed once or twice, and frames slowed down after a few hours, but it was mostly stable.  Also, the game is not truly as "single player" as one expects.

B+: would play casually for a few hours when I'm bored of other games again.

Reviews.115167:
Graphics
Graphics are nice and vibrant, The different planets feels like separate eco systems to a point. 


Crafting
Easily the best part of the game. Deep system that lets you set up farms that grind mats offline. Worth sinking many hours into allthough once you've got your setup right the issue of money becomes mute and you can grind hundreds of millions each week with no effort.

Basebuillding:
Not a lot to do here. You get the basic options of walls, floors, doors etc but no real diversity of furniture. In multiplayer you don't really share bases. 
Exploring
You'd think with such a vast galaxy to explore this would be a great selling point. Its not. The planets have generic animals that look different, but have no personality or interaction. They are there to shoot for missions and thats it. The various planetary systems are inhabitet by different humanoid races, which brings me to my next grief.

Ships:
There are tons of ships to aquire. They look different and have cool weapons to craft and upgrade. Flying them on PC with mouse and keyboard is a complete joke. Why on earth the developer thought NOT incorporating joystick options was a good idea is beyond me. Why why why why! You create an entire game, release several (free!) DLC's but you refuse to let us use joysticks? In a space game no less? Get out of here. Later on in the game you can get your own fleet and grind out missions and stats for it, I just couldn't be bothered at that point. 

PvE / interaction
There is little to no interaction with any elements of the game. All npc's in the entire game serve as text bots. Thats it. Period. After you have spent tens of hours crafting great equipment and want to go out and use it, there is nothing to do. Shoot animals all day long, or trigger the sentinels. You kill the sentinels in about 30 seconds. Then repeat. Utterly boring and uningaging. Massive fail. Space is no different. Get a A / S class fighter with nice stats and you are God. Waves upon waves of pirates that are killed in 20 seconds each. Then repeat. Yeah...
Missions are expected to be done in a surten order. If you choose to ignore the storyline and go out exploring and crafting on your own, the game mission mechanics throw a hissy fit and the travel indicators disapear or wont light up at all. Once you are synced this straightens out again, but its a huge pain in the ass. Now I hate hand holding in games in general BUT the mission texts in this game leaves ALOT to be desired. The mission log text leaves out what material you are fetching / bringing back so you sell it. They leave out the name of the system and planet you are traveling to. Sure you figure it out in the end, but the flow of the game is interupted. You get use to it, but its a drawback. 


Multiplayer
Make no mistake. NMS is a singleplayer game with multiplayer added on as an afterthought. All the systems under the hood gives you an indication that you are REALLY playing a single player game. Once you get to the Nexus multiplayer hub it really gets laughable. All the co op missions are just singe player missions with better rewards. They are grinded out in anything from 20 seconds of actuall mission time to 5 minutes. It takes longer to travel to the mission site than to actually completing the mission. Not worth spending time on at all. As a multiplayer game I cannot stress how bad this game is. I mainly play co op with two other friends and after about 50 hrs of singeplayer crafting grinding we were all looking forward to finally do some actual co op in this game with our shiny equipment. The main selling point of the game, which is complex procedurally generated worlds to explore - falls extremely short of my expectations. The reason being that the procedural generation is too simple, and after visiting a few planets it becomes clear that the only differences are basically in colour.

- All planets are basically mono biome. You will never see a planet that contains a jungle and a desert and a polar cap. You basically see the entire planet the moment you land.
- Landscape features are very uninteresting. There are mountains of various intensity and occasional stationary bodies of water on some planets, that's it. This, again, reinforces the whole perception that there's nothing to see outside of your landing zone.
- The universe is empty. I understand this is a bit of a plot point, but it doesn't really make the game more interesting. There's like 3 spacefaring civilizations, and nothing else. No primitive societies on some worlds, no ancient ruins of forgotten civilizations. All the artefacts you find look the same and don't tell any stories.
- Even flora and fauna is repetitive. Sure, you get weird critters on some worlds, but the "dangerous flora" like the venus flytraps or the explodey gas blobs - are exactly the same on any planet. No need to cautiously approach a strange plant on a jungle world wondering if it might be carnivorous.

I feel like the game could use another 5 years of development focused entirely on procudural generation before it can actually be interesting as an exploration game.


TLDR - No copeling story or drive to play the game other than flying ship and seeing around 4 different types of planet being water, desert, rock and polar.

Reviews.115200: I would like to start by saying No Man's Sky has been quite the rollercoaster of a game. When it first came out way back in 2016, it was total garbage! However, now I think this game has really come into its own! Since its initial release, the developers of this game have seemed to take development extremely seriously, as there have been numerous major updates and patches, to make the gameplay of No Man's Sky much more fluid and enjoyable. And just like any game, I have pros and cons for the overall experience. The first thing I would like to say, is the art style in this game is radically different based on where you are. Flying through space the color palette is gorgeous, and it really feels like you are flying through the eagle nebula in our own universe. However, once you reach any planet, 90% of them have radically different art styles. In my experience the art styles of these planets are very harsh and disturbing, radically different from the interstellar and inter-orbital environment just above the planet. Overall, however, I do believe that this game has come a long way since its initial release, as planets now seem different even though each planet is procedurally generated and uses similar if not the same assets. The gameplay is rather smooth, I think the control scheme is better suited for first person than third person. And the combat mechanics have come a long way however, the positron ejector still seems quite overpowered. After having around 107 hours in this game, I have yet to come across a challenging dogfight in space! I think part of that is because the positron ejector gun, can take out essentially any ship in two clicks of your mouse. Overall, I would say that this game is not for a person who likes linear storylines, as this game is more suited for someone who enjoys exploration and discovery. The building in this game however, feels like an afterthought, as I have found that I rarely ever build buildings or structures in this game, nor have I ever built any exo-craft, as there is no incentive to set up a base on any planet. Therefore, I would give No Man's Sky A B-. For the most part I love the art styles in space, however the art styles on 90% of the planet seem too harsh and out of touch with the other art style of the game. I love the free roaming an exploration aspect of the game, however it does feel excessively grindy at times to get good ships. Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a free roaming space exploration title, however I would wait till it goes on sale because I do not think it is worth $60.00. To me I would happily pay $20 or 30 at the most for this title as that is what I think it is worth.

A semi-relaxing exploration/adventure game with a space theme. I really like this game and I had given it a positive review but it crashes far too often. I am NOT running any mods and my computer is well above recommended specs. Constant crashes and QOL issues need to fixed before I will change this review.

Pros:
Can play how you want
Open world(s)
Lots of exploration
Space!

Cons:
Program crashes frequently (usually after time spent collecting/mining [read an hour or two] resulting in the loss of everything since previous save point). If you find an S class ship/multi-tool and buy it IMMEDIATELY save the game. ALWAYS carry a save point and use it OFTEN. Game seriously needs to be optimized or at least have a hot key combo that lets you quicksave.
Mapping system is non-existent. Say you find a cool spot and want to return to it. Great, put down a save beacon and you can find it again, BUT there is no way to label the beacon, and you don't have a log to remember where you have been. Some planets are huge and you may lay down 4 or 5 beacons. Sure you can color code them, but then you have to remember exactly what coloring means (and it is easy just to put a beacon down and then forget to change the color from the default value). Add that to the fact that you might travel to 40 or 50 different systems in the mean time (or not play the game for a few days/weeks/months) and then you are supposed to remember what exactly you plopped down a beacon at a certain point for. Without any type of text label or log system it is really easy to forget. Sure you could build a base computer at every spot and label them, but that is a waste of resources (and IIRC there are a maximum number of bases that you can build)
UI design needs improvement. Example(s): There is no way to input a number when selecting quantities of items. You have to use on-screen arrow keys, split a stack in half, or start a new stack in multiples of ten. You spend 5 minutes trying to get 852 of an item in a stack when you start with 4579 of them. This also applies to selling an item. If you make stacks to sell then use a trade terminal/trade with an NPC ALL the items of each item are shown in the full quantity that you are carrying (and at this point you HAVE to use the onscreen arrow keys to sell less than the full amount). This DOESN'T apply when using/inputting quantities in a refiner though, which makes no sense whatsoever.
Can get boring/lack of variety/can turn into a grind fest
Base building is limited/poorly implemented. Most base items are purely cosmetic. Some items snap, some don't. Some items are impossible to place in logical positions (I am not rebuilding my base because a staircase refuses to be built in a certain orientation)
Easy to master. Once you figure out how to make boatloads of money and what items are useful you pretty much win the game.
Meh story/quest-lines/missions
Combat is a joke once you figure it out. I would say this isn't really a combat/fighting game though.
If you start a new game you can't skip the 'tutorial' (you can ignore it though, once you figure out what is important).

Overall Rating 52.5/100
Recommend you wait for further patches and/or then only get it on sale/deep discount

Note: I have not tried multiplayer so I have no opinion on that aspect of the game

I have played many, many more hours on PS4.

The game has a friendly community, the graphics are great and it's well optimised.

However, No Man's Sky is the definition of "miles wide, inches deep." NMS prides itself on its 'infinite, procedurally generated universe,' but the different planet types are, for the most part, functionally the same; they just have a different skin. There are minor variations: such as the amount of fauna on "dead" planets will not be as bounteous as it is on more Earth-like biomes; there might be more sentinels or storms on one planet than another, but that's it. It doesn't change the gameplay enough to be considered any more than billions of the same planets, but coloured in different. An entire universe to explore, and yet you've seen it all in a few jumps.

The story is intriguing, during which you uncover the fundamental nature of the universe, but the payoff is unsatisfying, and the missions just boil down to a bunch of shallow fetch quests. The base building is extremely limited compared to other open-world-survival-craft games, although some creative travellers have made spectacular constructs.

I've not played with friends that much, although it seems the core gameplay is the same and you can do rather basic missions together via the Nexus. Based on my experience, I can't suggest you buy this as a social game to play with friends.

Yes, it's true that Hello Games continues to add content, implement fixes and update the game, but they can't change the fundamentals. You can't build a house on sand. What a shame.

I originally tried NMS in 2016 at launch, and found the game to have a lot of potential, but definitely lacking in depth and things to do.  I recently re-installed the game and, after 4 years of further development, boy, have they fulfilled their potential!  There are so many things to do in the game that it can almost seem overwhelming.  Fortunately, the early series of missions that new characters go through do a fantastic job of guiding players through all the different activities that are available.

Talk about depth!  Crafting is fun and rewarding, encouraging players to research new combinations of resources to maximize their profits.  Exploration, always the core of NMS, is vast and fun.  There's always a better ship for a specific task, a more efficient multi-tool for whatever job you're on, and plenty of improvements to your exo-suit that will make it more survivable for the environment you enter.  

I challenge anyone to log in to the game with one specific task to accomplish, and find that they're able to complete that task without getting sidetracked by all sorts of other interesting and exciting things that pop up constantly.

Story: 8/10 -- relatively generic and while not bad, its nothing mind-blowing either.

Cost: Overpriced -- I personally got this game on sale for $30, and for the gameplay, I think it is definitely worth waiting for a sale.

Gameplay: 9/10 -- There is an insane amount of gameplay, every playthrough is different and there is such
a variety of paths to take and things to do. I'm also a big fan of the quest system and language learning system, they both add so much to the game.

Graphics: 9/10 -- Good graphics for such a big game, especially considering its procedurally generated and basically infinite.

Soundtrack: 6/10 -- Just an ok soundtrack, nothing special, but nothing bad either.

Combat: 6/10 -- This is a special category I specifically wanted to add because it is my biggest problem with the game--While fighting is not terrible in this game, it gets bland fast. While it's not necessarily at the core of this game, it still is a big issue and should be updated in the future. (The combat I'm speaking of IS NOT spaceship fighting, I am referring to combat with Sentinels especially!)

Other Pros:
-The grinding in this game for money I personally find very enjoyable
-The way the galactic trade market works is very simple and easy to use
-There are alot of upgrades and ships to buy
-It is VR compatible (and Iv'e tried it--super fun in VR too!)

Other Cons:
-Variety from planet to planet can sometimes be very miniscule -- some planets are almost hard copies of each other
-Quests can get repetitive after a while
-VR is a bit buggy, but nothing game breaking
-Multiplayer connection issues (It took me 2 whole hours to get my brother in-game with me!)
-Lifeforms from planet to planet look almost identical at times

Overall Score: 7.5/10-- Definitely a good game for sci-fi fans, but waiting for a sale would probably be better than buying it for full price.

I don't recommend this game at full price with the current content. The game is very pretty, but even with all their updates, once I got a few hours in and discovered some planets, it just got way too repetitive. The game is advertised with huge focus on exploration, but there's not enough there to justify exploring so much. The mapping system needs work. Not much sense of survival or danger once you pass the first few hours of play.

Pros
------
- Really pretty visuals. The amount of awesome screenshots I have.. is a lot
- Base building is cool. You can build land, orbital (requires a bit of glitching), and underwater bases.
- Great sense of wonder with the first ~10-20 hours or so of planet exploration

Cons
------
- QOL changes sorely needed with the mapping system
- Exploration feels shallow quickly, not enough variety
- Alien animals... minimal/barebones implementation. 

Discussing pros
--------
- Visuals- The visuals really are great, and the beauty in certain locations will really blow you away. Especially in multiplayer, I think this can create some memorable experiences. For example, one of the planets I discovered [spoiler]had weird onion bulb plants with giant vines, the size of buildings. building bases under these things felt pretty darn cool. They were non-interactable besides building near them, but they were really good eye candy. [/spoiler]

- Base building- Yea.. they pulled this off and its pretty decent.  Underwater bases are pretty sick. You can build really cool orbital bases with a little bit of glitching (you have to glitch to start building that high). What more can I say? They could add more cosmetic structures, but its pretty decent as it is, so I dont think they should add anything here until they improve the stuff that needs work.

Discussing cons
--------
- Exploration- That's the whole point of this game, but once you see a few planets you will feel like you've seen it all, and the initial sense of wonder will fade. Some things the developers could implement is diversifying caves, landscapes, planetary events, and maybe adding dungeon-like areas. Overhauling how animals interact with you, and their variety, could really help this area too. 
Since exploration gets old fast, late game for most people gets pretty much focused on maximizing your revenue sources and getting the best ships, freighters etc. That's all well and good if that's your thing. But for game advertised with a huge focus on pretty much endless exploration, it is a negative. 

- Mapping- Going off of how exploration is one of the biggest draws to the game, you would think their mapping system would be better, to keep track of cool areas you've discovered. The tutorial introduces you to beacons as a way to mark points of interest. Once you put a beacon down, you can't give it a name, see its coordinates, or see the distance units until you reach it. You would think you could see a list of beacons you've placed down through the menu/interface, but you can't. 
The developers have implemented the ability for you to see your current coordinates, but to utilize that for navigation will require you pulling down a notebook to keep track of your points of interest. And returning to those specific coordinates is a pain in the butt, unless you decide to place down a base computer and portal at every single interesting discovery. 
At the very least, coordinates should have been tied in with beacons, along with the ability to see a list of those beacons through the menu. 

- Animals: Really barebones implementation. You can mount animals, but directing them is so cumbersome, its not worth it. It feels like a minimally implemented feature so that the devs could say, "Hey, look we added this!". Its there but its so  barebones that its not worth using, and doesn't really add anything to the game. 
Animal aggression feels like a joke. They pose absolutely no threat to the player at all, you can just murder the entire population with your mining beam as soon as you land on your first planet. 
There's little things they could have added that would vastly improve the animal system. For example, maybe adding animal nesting or den areas, or rare mutated / giant animals.
Currently all they do is roam around mindlessly, and you can harvest them for a few resources.

I would say get it on sale if you really want to. Even with all my gripes, it can be a cool experience late at night, walking around a planet you have all to yourself- just enjoying the beauty of the game and the music. Also, I imagine that playing with friends in multiplayer mode  would add  a lot more enjoyment to your gameplay and keep you playing longer.

This game deserves more love.

I haven’t been following it since the launch but I know it had its fair share of criticism and I’ve always been reluctant to buy it.

But after getting bored of pretty much all the other games I’ve been playing (including Cyberpunk), I decided to go for it and I don’t regret it one bit. I’ve been playing it every free moment since New Years, 40+ hours on my first save and I barely scratched the surface. There’s just so much to do, so many planets and solar systems to explore, ships to find and collect, bases to build, gear to upgrade... I’ve only managed to explore 10 or so systems and haven’t even gotten into farming and taming animals yet!

The game does a pretty good job at guiding you through what to do without unnecessarily holding your hand. You start off on a planet with a series of quests meant to show you the ropes but there’s no boring, tedious unskipable tutorial; you’re already in the game, learning as you go. 

The amount of things you can do can be overwhelming and a bit distracting (lost count how many times I started working on one thing and got sidetracked by another) but that’s not necessarily a bad thing considering how much content has been added and how immense the universe is. 

You get to travel across planets, scanning the flora, fauna and minerals for all types of resources, stumble over secured facilities or outposts, fight sentinels, learn the languages of the alien species you encounter, collect and fly starships of different shapes and sizes, command your own fleet of exploration ships, repair them when they break down (discovered this only yesterday, it’s so darn cool), fight dangerous space pirates, be on the lookout for the most stunning planets you can find and set up a network of bases, roam around in different exocrafts... the list goes on. Probably my favourite things to do is building and flying around in my spaceship (I didn’t set up all my teleporters yet, flying is just too fun).

The game runs pretty decent on older specs, with lower settings. Don’t expect incredible graphics, the textures are pretty low quality on those settings but the game runs smoothly. The only issues I had were some visual glitches due to outdated drivers and a bit of lag here and there in the Anomaly because of my internet connection.

All in all, it’s a great game, with a lot of content and a huge universe to discover. If you like survival-type games where you can build your own little nest (or a web of them across the galaxy), fly around spaceships, explore beautiful planets with a plethora of various biomes, then I wholeheartedly recommend it, it’s well worth the price.

So I've been enchanted by this game for the past week or so, picking it up during the Winter Sale, and I feel it is finally time for me to give a review of what this game has to offer. Note that I use the spoiler tags that I have put up here intentionally: This game is [i]much[/i] better enjoyed spoiler-free.

So let's start off with this. The game as you may probably know released several years ago, and it probably received the biggest bashing in the history of the Internet. For you folks that did not pick it up back then, I would say you probably did a good job resisting the hype. After having watched Internet Historian's take on the game, I was wooed into the idea that I should pick up this game at some point in the future, and so I did. 

So, what have I gotten out of it so far, for the 27.5€ that I paid for it? Well, since I played this game completely spoiler-free, I must say that I have definitely enjoyed it. However, it has not been all pleasant at all times, either. I have basked in the rather large amount of content that this game has to offer. Space battles, defeating 5 star Sentinels [spoiler] both planetarily and interstellarly[/spoiler], completed a good chunk of the main story as well as several side quests, bought myself a [spoiler]freighter[/spoiler], built up a collection of multitools as well as multiple starships, and built massive planetary bases. There is still more that I haven't done in this game thus far, and I'm still progressing along the grind for the resources required for future tasks. This game has been played in survival mode, which can be approximated to Terraria's mediumcore mode for a character. I have yet to engage in the multiplayer experience, something I hope to do in the future.

Now, has the content I have engaged with been good? Well, yes, I would argue that it has. I have thoroughly enjoyed my explorations of the 7 or so solar systems that I have gone through. For the price I paid I'd say that so far I have gotten my money's worth, and I intend on continue playing. The problems that I have had can be summed up into three main points:

1. The game can be quite unstable at times and/or has some rather bad bugs. The problems that occur can vary from something as simple as clipping through terrain while digging tunnels on planets, enemies getting stuck in place providing shooting galleries for me while I finish them off, periodically taking cover behind a wall, all the way to crashes and glitches during quests that once set me back an entire hour worth of gameplay. This happened during the main quest when [spoiler] I ended up in space and managed to suffocate to death, which overwrote my autosave and wiped my entire inventory while at it, while also crashing my spaceship.[/spoiler]

2. The game's progression curve can be rather unfortunate at times, since the game from a progression standpoint expects you to do certain things in a certain order, however the game will be perfectly fine allowing you to break this progression in multiple ways. For example, I managed to [spoiler]obtain the Large Refiner long before I obtained the Medium Refiner [/spoiler] because I did certain quests out of order, and because of a system that allows you to farm blueprints, you can easily [spoiler]buy certain blueprints long before they become available through their corresponding quests[/spoiler]. This is likely something intentionally done by Hello Games, but when I then went back to do these quests at a later time, I felt disappointed that I wasted my time on this particular task.

3. A fair chunk of things are very badly explained in the game. For example, the fact that you can own multiple starships, or multitools, is badly explained. There is clearly a button that states that you can add them to your collection, but the game does not at all explain to you how to switch between them. If you buy this game as a result of this review, you can access them by pressing X in-game.

In all, the game has some bad sides, but I have thoroughly enjoyed the game and its content despite these. I would recommend the game, definitely, but I would not go into the game expecting a perfect experience. As such, if you see it on sale, I'd highly recommend buying it!

This is a great game riddled with a lot of bad sci fi. It represented good value for money after about the second free major update, and they're on about their sixth now, so the things I'm about to write about are not really serious enough to put anyone off buying. And if you play the game in 'explorer mode', covering vast distances and never returning to the same planets, then hopefully you'll hardly notice these little gripes at all. They crop up more if you do a lot of stuff in a small area - a dozen or two systems - but that happens to be the way I'm playing at the moment, because I'm base-building.

Let's also be clear that these are only grumbles rather than serious complaints, and Hello Games are continuing to work on improving things. I suspect in some cases the issues are simplified placeholder content, which works okay for what it is, but which doesn't stand up to any scrutiny. But I've played for long enough that these issues do sometimes become obtrusive.

The basic issue is what you might call the 'rule of one'. Everything triggers just once. You go to an alien, and they will teach you one word, and one word only. You wanna learn another word, you have to visit another alien. Or another knowledge stone, or another ancient monolith. There are 'encyclopedias' you can interact with. They too will teach you one word, and then they're used up. Hello, Hello Games, that's almost the opposite of an encyclopedia! I had one teach me the Gek indefinite article, and then the next teach me the Gek for 'and'. And how do you do that anyway? How do you teach somebody just one word of a language in isolation and nothing more? There are storage containers littered over every planet. Every single one contains one item. There are drop pods on every planet. All of them are broken. All of them are broken in exactly the same way. There are 'malfunctioning machines' scattered everywhere. Not a single one of them is operational - until a PC comes by and repairs them. What are they for? Why are they there? In game terms they provide resources. In-universe, who the hell knows? I don't think there is an in-universe explanation. Writing stuff that makes in-universe sense isn't really on Hello's to-do list. Everything's game-focused. And that's why the game is riddled with bad sci fi. 'Rule of cool' always trumps 'what would make sense'. And that's a very hit-and-miss approach, because it isn't always that cool, and it may make so little sense it spoils the effect altogether. See below.

This is a huge universe, but it's a toy universe. Almost everything in it is superficial. In probably about 60% of cases, that's because Hello Game just haven't had the time to fill in the detail yet, and what's there now is simple placeholder content. As such, it's adequate, and I'm willing to forgive the lack of detail, and wait till Hello get a chance to flesh out those parts of the game. But for some of it, I get the feeling it's because it genuinely hasn't crossed their minds to do anything more original. When computer games were much simpler, it was fair enough that a storage chest only contained a single item, and that you couldn't put stuff back in it, or even look in it to see what was there, before deciding if you would take it. NMS still behaves as if that's how things should be, and faithfully restricts itself in the same way. For a game with such an enormous scope - a sci-fi universe simulator - to intentionally limit itself like this feels odd.

It's a bit like buying an electric car and finding that its range is 100 feet because that's the length of its power cable.

To expand more on the 'bad sci fi' complaint - well, for example, there are 'beacons' dotted about the place. Interact with a beacon, and it will tell you the location of a nearby settlement. But in order to interact with a beacon, you have to find a beacon (and they're quite hard to spot, so they've already failed at the basic JOB of a beacon), land, get out of your ship, walk over to the beacon and click-hold on it. That's not a 'beacon'! Imagine if you wanted to read a road sign and you had to stop your car, park, get out, go up to the sign and read it, then get back in your car and drive off. And you could only track one beacon and consequently one settlement at a time, and once you've used a beacon once that's your lot - you can't use it a second time, oh no! It's preposterous. Almost all NMS entities behave in this way. It's a bizarro universe, and once you start noticing it it just gets stranger and stranger on you. In every case where there's a game-ified way to do something and a real-world way to do it, NMS goes with the game-ified way. For something like Borderlands, you can get away with that (probably), but for something which aspires to be a universe simulator, this is a very odd way to do things.

Distress signals: distress signals often go unanswered for decades(?) at a time in the NMS universe. This is because the typical way to find a distress signal is to obtain some random navigation data by visiting an outpost of some kind, take it to a cartographer who will convert it into emergency coordinates for you, and then follow those coordinates to the crash site. There's no way to tell what's there beforehand, how long ago the message was sent, or even the coordinates of the signal. without actually physically travelling to the site. Wait, what? This is an EMERGENCY. Somebody's DYING, maybe, and you gotta jump through all these bureaucratic hoops if you want to help them? No wonder no-one other than the player character ever bothers to go help. And Hello Games coded it like this, and it never once crossed their minds that this whole rigmarole was utterly preposterous? Or else it DID cross their minds, and they went 'Meh,' and carried on coding it that way anyway.

As I said, riddled with bad sci fi. 'Gameplay' always trumps 'realism' here, and for loose values of either.

NPC interaction is also rather limited, but I reckon that's placeholder material, so I'll make allowances for that. 

Some of the glitches are quite funny. I helped a guy, he rummaged about on his desk for a reward, and the game generated a random item of trade goods for him to give me, and picked... Dirt. SEVERAL TONNES of dirt. I mean, yeah, okay, my desk's quite dusty too, but it's not THAT bad! This isn't just a one-off glitch either. I've been rewarded with tonnes of valuable dirt more than once.

Item pricing is all over the place. A large capital ship is cheaper than a high-end one man starship. OTOH one spacer with an upgraded backpack can carry more than the freighter can, so the best way to carry stuff in vast bulk between the stars would actually be to get a buncha guys with upgraded space suits, and a personnel shuttle, and carry the goods that way.

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim is an open world action role-playing video game developed by Bethesda Game Studios and published by Bethesda Softworks. It is the fifth main installment in The Elder Scrolls series, following The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, and was released worldwide for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360 on November 11, 2011.

The game's main story revolves around the player's character, the Dragonborn, on their quest to defeat Alduin the World-Eater, a dragon who is prophesied to destroy the world. The game is set 200 years after the events of Oblivion and takes place in Skyrim, the northernmost province of Tamriel. Over the course of the game, the player completes quests and develops the character by improving skills. The game continues the open-world tradition of its predecessors by allowing the player to travel anywhere in the game world at any time, and to ignore or postpone the main storyline indefinitely.

Skyrim was developed using the Creation Engine, rebuilt specifically for the game. The team opted for a unique and more diverse open world than Oblivion's Imperial Province of Cyrodiil, which game director and executive producer Todd Howard considered less interesting by comparison. The game was released to critical acclaim, with reviewers particularly mentioning the character advancement and setting, and is considered to be one of the greatest video games of all time. Nonetheless it received some criticism, predominantly for its melee combat and numerous technical issues present at launch. The game shipped over seven million copies to retailers within the first week of its release, and over 30 million copies on all platforms as of November 2016, making it one of the best selling video games in history.

Three downloadable content (DLC) add-ons were released—Dawnguard, Hearthfire, and Dragonborn—which were repackaged into The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim – Legendary Edition and released in June 2013. The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim – Special Edition is a remastered version of the game released for Windows, Xbox One, and PlayStation 4 in October 2016. It includes all three DLC expansions and a graphical upgrade, along with additional features such as modding capabilities on consoles. Versions were released in November 2017 for the Nintendo Switch and PlayStation VR, and a stand-alone virtual reality (VR) version for Windows was released in April 2018. These versions were based on the remastered release, but the Switch version's graphics upgrade was relative to its hardware capabilities, and it did not include the modding features.

Gameplay
See also: Gameplay of The Elder Scrolls series
The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim is an action role-playing game, playable from either a first or third-person perspective. The player may freely roam over the land of Skyrim which is an open world environment consisting of wilderness expanses, dungeons, caves, cities, towns, fortresses, and villages.[1] Players may navigate the game world more quickly by riding horses, paying for a ride from a city's stable or by utilizing a fast-travel system which allows them to warp to previously discovered locations.[2] The game's main quest can be completed or ignored at the player's preference after the first stage of the quest is finished. However, some quests rely on the main storyline being at least partially completed.

Non-player characters (NPCs) populate the world and can be interacted with in a number of ways: the player may engage them in conversation, marry certain NPCs (irrespective of gender), kill them or engage them in a nonlethal "brawl". As in previous The Elder Scrolls games, killing certain NPCs can make some quests or items unobtainable. Some NPCs cannot be killed due to their importance in later storylines. If witnessed, crimes like murder and theft accrue the player a bounty which is tracked independently in each of Skyrim's nine holds. Should the player be stopped by a guard, they may wipe their bounty with gold or jail time or may resist arrest which will trigger an aggressive pursuit. It is also possible to bribe a guard, or convince him to forget the crime, if it is a minor offense. NPCs may offer the player additional side-quests and some side-quests have parameters adjusted based on nearby dungeons which the player has yet to explore.[3][4] Some NPCs who are befriended or hired by the player may act as companions who will accompany the player and aid them in combat.[5] The player may choose to join factions which are organized groups of NPCs — for example, the Dark Brotherhood, a band of assassins.[6] Each of the factions has an associated quest path to progress through. Each city and town in the game world has jobs that the player can engage in, such as farming.[7]


The player's character engages in combat with monsters while exploring a dungeon. The player may dual-wield weapons and magic at the same time in order to be more effective against enemies.
Players have the option to develop their character. At the beginning of the game, players create their character by selecting their sex and choosing between one of several races including humans, orcs, elves, and anthropomorphic cat or lizard-like creatures and then customizing their character's appearance.[8] Over the course of the game, players improve their character's skills which are numerical representations of their ability in certain areas. There are eighteen skills divided evenly among the three schools of combat, magic, and stealth. When players have trained skills enough to meet the required experience, their character levels up. Each time their character levels, the players may choose to select a skill-specific ability called a perk or store perk points for later use. After about 2 years I have now revisited this game and I am having an incredible amount of fun. With the shier deapth the game offers now it is almost inconceivable that this game was ever launched in the state it was in. I give as an example base building. Instead of being immediately thrown into the story and skipping star systems to get to the center or following the path of the atlas (if I am remembering correctly), you are first and foremost, after repairing your ship, asked to start off with the whole basebuilding aspect. Which is a very good decision on Hello Games's in my opinion, because it introduces you to the mechanics of the teleportation system. This way you don't get lost trying to find your way back to your base and after hours of searching notice that there is a teleporter system.

Another thing to note is the tutorial / hint system. Though a bit confusing in the very beginning, it does help allot with getting to know the different mechanics of the game. With it, I only needed one or two quick google searches, primarily because there is no indication on how to switch camera perspective from 3rd to 1st person, which I prefer in this game (by the way you need to press "x" or "d-pad down" then in the popup menu navigate to the settings icon and from there you can switch perspective). This should be better explained as it is probably the first thing people might want to change.

This kind of brings me to my next point. The popup menu is a great tool, once you know it exists. It is incredibly user friendly, to the point and has all necessary information right in front of you on the HUD. It is very easy to navigate this menu once you've familiarized yourself with the controls for it, which are helpfully prominently displayed at the bottom. Once you've taken a look at them, finding the right thing is a matter of seconds.

Which brings me to basebuilding. It is a very good decision to have all the building take place in this little menu. As stated, it is extremely easy to navigate and find things. This is a good system in comparison to, for example, ARK: Survival Evolved where you need to open your inventory, pull the building items into your hotbar, close the inventory, select the item and then be able to place it. In No Man's Sky you need only navigate the menu to the correct item and then place it. No need to craft them as they are crafted when placed down. The resource requirements for placing (/crafting) an item, say a wood floor, are shown on the right side of your HUD. This system completely eliminates useless inventory skipping that makes many other games building mechanics so tedious.

Exploration is a big part of this game. And even if you don't feel like doing it, you will have to at some point. To advance more crafting blueprints for basebuilding you must find certain buried items. They do spawn frequently on planets, however you will need to go at least a little while to reach them. Not only can you then unlock certain blueprints for items used in building, which is not my main point, it also encourages you to wander the planet a little, even though you only wanted to get a blueprint. This part is the most important of the game and I am so happy that Hello Games have managed to get it right. Exploration is exciting, as you fight off sentinals, when you get caught mining or are constantly trying to find resources to refill your oxygen supply and / or hazard protection systems. Inventory management is also a constant fight, similar to Minecraft in a way. With a limited amount of slots in your exosuit and, in the beginning, your ship and very rare exosuit upgrades you can find that unlock one new inventory space you are always trying to manage your inventory in the most efficient way.
Planets are basically littered with abandoned outposts that you can save your game at. Should you die, you respawn there and don't need to walk for miles trying to find your lost loot. And every now and then you'll come by and inhabited facility with a launchpad where, should your ship be repaired and have fuel, you can call it to your location, thus effectively eliminating useless travel time. Keep in mind you do need one "navigation data" to call your ship, still an effective tool though. And though I do not know if exploration becomes tedious as one progresses, I do have a feeling that it will still at least be a decent system for players to engage with. And I hope this game will remain as fun as I progress my savegame.

This game has come a very long way from what it was when it released, but even now there is still so much more potential for it too. Given the way the devs have continued working on this way after launch, its clear that it will only get better as more updates come out. I actually remember playing this game when it first came out and being rather disappointed, and it definitely suffered from over hype, however, with the recent updates this game has become everything that it was originally hyped to be. I understand this is certainly not a game for everyone, but it is worth a look for sure. 

Down to brass tax

Pros:
- mechanics and crafting system is extensive with all sorts of things to create
- The styling of the worlds and variety is endless
- operating your own fleet with frigates and capital ship
- exploring derelict freighters
- a variety of unusual and exciting encounters while travelling
- the missions are enjoyable

Cons:
- more interesting/exciting space battles. 
At the moment you only have small fighter to fighter battles with pirates and enemy craft, but I really want there to be much larger scale battles between fleets. I want to see my capital ship and frigates in action or have missions that you had to take another capital ship or battle random frigates.

- Lack of other enemy types on planets or on foot.
right now the only real enemies are the sentinels, you do have the occasional pirate encounter in space, but you never really fight other species on planets. Maybe having outposts to attack, other bases, or just random encounters. I feel like this would add even more to the experience if there were enemies that were other intelligent life rather than just the sentinels. While they are enjoyable and challenging to fight at times, I would definitely like to see more variety. 

- No new starship vendors or shops for space ships.
I really, really, wish there was a way to customize or buy ships from a vendor instead of from random encounters on space stations or trading posts. It would be great if there was a way to buy ships by class system or stylistic category that you could buy and then be able to customize later. Additionally, I would love to see the same system for freighters/capitol ships.
 
- I wish you had more customization control over your ship/multi tool colors and look.
If you get a ship, you are stuck with the colors and the aesthetic look of it. It would be great to see some sort of hanger bay starship customization where you can change colors or certain looks to your ship/multi tool. Perhaps it takes certain materials that you have to gather to change aesthetic items  or they have class designations that you have to unlock. maybe even those items have minor stat improvements for your ship.

- Some of the random encounters in space seem pointless because you either run into an enemy you can't destroy in space or you show something that you can't interact with in anyway. 

- Back locked rooms in buildings at times feel very pointless or lacking in loot/interactive items. you need key cards for many of the back room doors to buildings and many of them feel like they need more importance or have some sort of objects to interact with such as worthwhile loot or mapping information.

Overall, I would say that this is a great game with a lot to do and places to explore. I think it would be an absolutely incredible game if the devs included changes to cover some of the cons I mentioned, but I think that it is still worth the buy.

I've owned NMS since the beginning. Played it off and on, and I've enjoyed my time with this game. If you're looking for a relaxing space exploration/survival sim to play with friends, this is it. It was a rocky launch, won't lie. But Hello has genuinely made a huge comeback on all of their promises for this game. I don't play it so much anymore, but that's only because I wanted to give the rest of my library a shot for a change. This is a great game to play with friends but I would definitely suggest doing most of your initial grinding alone and quickly, and I would also look up a guide on ways to make units and nanites quickly. they're easy to get if you take the right steps. Personally, I crashed the tech market in about 90 different systems and made almost a billion units doing it too. I still haven't had to look for more credits purposefully in almost 2 actual years. But you can play this game literally any way that you want to. It's always worth the buy and has a lot of enjoyment to offer anyone willing to invest the time to get started.

Reviews.115702: I'd recommend this game to anyone who wants a relaxing experience where they can explore planets and moons, find alien species, and sink time into upgrading a ship into something that grows alongside the player. I've played on one save file for close to seventy hours now and haven't had a single time where my shield bar went all the way down, much less where my HP started taking damage. But to me, that's not a bad thing. The threat of death is present, but with proper preparations, isn't something the average player will need to worry about. The story was a fun experience to go through, and I was genuinely attached to some of the characters, which isn't something that a lot of games have done in my experience. Overall, they've done a great job recovering from the lackluster launch, and if you have some friends to go explore around with in space, I would totally recommend this game.

(Playing on Kubuntu 20.10 with Proton-5.21-GE-1, game works great.)

NOTE! Some small spoilers below. Nothing major but if you don't want to know what locations/encounters etc exist in this game then skip the following paragraph.


Wow this game is great! Mind you I haven't seen the whole game yet (lol). Been to a few systems, scanned a few planets, done a bit of missions, boogied with some pirates, looted some crashed ships, pulled off a few heists on planet side buildings and built a bit on my own base among other things.


I really like the design, gameplay, graphics and the epicness of this game. Sound could use some work maybe, it needs more epicness in it. The exploration aspect is terrific.

Let me tell you, if you just turn off youtube or the wiki or whatever you're using to spoil yourself and just figure stuff out at your own pace you will have fun for hours and hours. I'm the type who enjoy the first steps into new games the most tho. Not knowing what is out there is so exiting and the greatest feeling when it's a game as good as this.

And the game does a great job guiding you through how to play it. Also I really like that they offer survival and permadeath game modes as well as the sight seeing mode. Having so much fun right now on permadeath.

I started on normal mode until I got the hang of surviving the first day. Switched to survival and noticed it changes a few things around. From what I noticed it changed the inventory slot sizes and the exosuit scanner has a longer cooldown and probably loads of other things.

Played a bit on survival and thought it was a really fun game mode. Figured I'd stay on this mode but permadeath was tempting me. So I started up a permadeath save and been playing that the last few days. 

We'll see how it goes, all good so far, unless you're counting deaths =D. Turns the game into a bit of a roguelike lol

I feel like I've gotten my money's worth already since I bought the game during the winter sale for 50% off. I do hope they continue patching in new great content and fixing bugs, not that I've encountered any so far *knocks on wood*. 

The developer is really good with putting out patches so I'm not worried, they seem to want more epicness from the game too!

This game is already way more polished and dare I say "done" with tons more content then some of the games I've bought lately. Basically you could ship it and just do bugfixes for a while and be done with it and onto the next thing.

I'm hoping for more content updates tho cause this is such a good place to tell stories, explore and adventure in. So I decided to order some fluff from their merch store to make up for buying the game on sale a bit. Wonder if the developer even gets 10% of that lol.

I tried playing for about an hour and a half. Maybe if I played a bit longer I could get into it, but my experience of what I played was not enjoyable.

Gather, craft, build/repair is what I expected, but you run so slowly that it hurts and your sprint energy runs out very fast. It could be if I gave it more time I would get past this early tedious and frustrating grind and battle with the UI, but if I can't enjoy a game in the first 90 minutes, my spare time is too valuable to me to spend it doing busy work for the possibility that I might enjoy it several hours down the line.

Reviews.115856:
Bought the game while on sale. It was worth the money, bt I wouldn't say the same if I had bought it on full price. 
TL;DR:
Personally had the most fun while playing multiplayer. However, there are a load of bugs and annoying game designe descisions which shouldn't be there after two years of adding content. Some things I noticed. 

[b]Base Bulilding[/b]

Can be fun if you have enough data to unlock all structures. However, more than 300 data is needed for every structure. 
Base Building is buggy if you want to build inside a hill/mountain or do some terraforming. 
Some building will just merge without preblems while others just on't merge at all. There is absolutely no reason why a large room shouldn't get attached to another large room. 
I haven't tried buliding subnautic bases.
The bulding menu is huge. Keeping in mind where to find which bulding and navtgating through all the pssibilitiescan take up some time. 

[b]Quests[/b]

Quests are buggy and sometimes even prevent you from talking to important NPCs. This was also a ticket in the past in the bug tracker, and got closed that this is an "intended feature". 
Quests also take forever to update. You already hacve 5 of x? Please wait another 15 seconds until the game realizes that. 
Some kill quests are stackable. If you need to kill 15 of X and 15 of Y, it seems OK just to kill 15 of X or Y and both quests are done. 
If you don't want to spend horus of grinding factories, and/or want to have access to all building options there is no way around the main quest. I have seen some comments that the main quest is optional. This is not true at the current state of the game. 
The main "quest" to get to the center of the galaxy is a bit buggy, too. While it suggests some path, it's better to find your own as the maximum jump distance the path suggests seems to be 900 LY. 

[b]Multiplayer[/b]

Multiplayer is more of a "see what bases others built" thing. You don't share progress of quests or anything else. You can just trade with each other. (Which is, if you figure out how to trade with each other.)
At some times players within one session just get teleportet around randomly. 
While it's not possible to summon your freight ship if another players ship is already there, your freight ship will teleport with you in any system no matter if there is another players present. 
It 's not possible to locate your friends/group members if they are more than 1000 LYs away from your current location. 

[b]Keymapping[/b]

There are a some decisions which just don't make sense. Why is the button for switching between storage tabs the same as for creating more of an item (E)? Why is there only a very limited editing of settings and keybindings? 
I got the feeling that in some menus the scrolling direction is inverted. However, it can not be changed. 

[b]Portable Production Units[/b]

Every single portable production unit will be completely empty if you exit the system they are in. Sometimes they are even empty if you leave the area. It seems like the game saves that the units are placed correctly but without any context of fuel or extracted items. This means you will have to babysit them which is really annoying. 
Other production units can only be built within a base for whatever reason. If you really want to use them you have to have multiple bases on one planet which can be confusing and frustrationg when trying to fly to your main base. 

[b]Other[/b]

While it is possible to "talk" to NPCs it is a very numbing process. EVERY TIME a dialogue is initiated, you get the same greetings. 
So if you want to train your language (highly recommended in early game) you have to click through the same menus over and over. 
Certain items can only be bought from terminals. However, there is a chance that those items aren't sold on the terminals. If you really want them, you have to jump through the systems and outposts and hope for the best.

Reviews.115972:
Superb Game: 9 out of 10 

This in my honest opinion is a very interesting and engaging game. 
Like most gamers, hearing the negative reviews years ago turned me away from the game, and I never played it until just a couple days ago, and I love it. I'm not too sure where the angst was for the game (other than what was mentioned about bugs, glitches, etc.) 
But playing in a good novice hours later and I've yet to experience any of these bug or issues.

Good Pros:

Engaging Worldspace
No Man's Sky's insane amount in level to detail of what you can explore both in outer space, and on different planets is amazing. I've yet to see any game go that much in depth with game exploration to date. To be able to jump in your spaceship and zoom in and out of space whenever really grants me as a player a sense of adventure, and suddenly the entire game seems just as expansive as space itself.

Not only can the player discover both many wonders (such as interesting sights, new foes (haven't gotten that far yet) structures, and creatures and plants, etc., but you can name each and every object you find.

If you discover a planet, you can change it's name and call it what you like (I called one planet FrostFall-101, because of it's icy weathers and temperatures.
Animals, plants, all can be custom named to whatever, and whenever you see them on your scanner, it will even refer to the creature as the name it was given.

This opens the world to seem like planets that humanity never discovered, which makes me feel like a trippy epic scholar that has brought something to humanity (this planet, I named it, this never before seen creature, I named it). It's very interactive in that regard.

Scifi Elements:

NMS does a heavy job in giving off a hard scifi feel; using our real world Periodic Chart, playing the game tells you both the initials, and the name of each element, and by the time you get through with the game, I promise you'll be more than likely to know that entire chart by heart, as you scan the game looking for items with the same properties :) Which is pretty impressive.

CONS:

Slow Start:

The game though is very good on helping the player where to go and what to do, and how to do it next, it will start you off pretty slow. Your ship won't be given to you, you'll have to go through the short tutorial that make take up a good bit of hours. Though you can choose to handle each quest and side quest at your leisure, classic mode will push for you to take things a step at a time.


No Intense Combat off the Bat:

I like to compare NMS as a sort of Minecraft-styled game (without the squares). What I mean by that, is that if you're looking for this "intense in yo face Call of Duty battle Royal (like sprinting from things as you take them down with your AK-47 Rifle. Naw man. That ain't gunna be this game.
No Man's Sky suits players who want to explore and go on grand adventures, leaving the blood lust behind. Roaming the galaxies in an ultimate sandbox.

Slightly Hindering Grinding:

By grinding I mean you'll find yourself scavenging a lot to get what you need. It's easy for the most part, but time consuming. 

The last thing thus far---Still playing the game---Is the save system takes a minute to get used to. You won't be able to save exactly how you feel unless you return to a save point. Not gunna bash that too much, because once you get going, saving is as easy as just return to your ship, enter, then exit and your game is saved. It's a simple peeve.

All in all, despite the cons, the pros outweigh them, as the vast exploration, customization, exploration, and many more details are just too good to pass up. If you're looking for a game that is relaxing to play, is scifi themed, friendly, tame on the gore, and reminds you of Minecraft then this game is for you. 
Just keep in mind though, the modding for No Man's Sky isn't really exactly as elaborate as Skyrim or Fallout (No bit boobs bouncing, sex, shooting Call of Duty Missile stuffs, or anything etc.) 
Mods are a bit more challenging to implement, (some'll work, some might not) but there is a community for it. 

Have fun Space Cowboys ^~^

Reviews.115989:
No Man's Sky has become a game that does the near impossible: every gameplay milestone you reach, it evolves radically to encompass different features. You go from surviving a hazardous planet trying to get the resources to leave it, to occupying planets and systems, to travelling entire lengths of the galaxy. Even the smaller activities, like missions and derelict exploration, have a unique charm to them that can even transform the game into, say, survival horror, while still maintaining the original feel of the game.

While this might sound intimidating at first, that you'll have to 'keep up' with all the new things it teaches you, you'll also feel yourself getting better as the game progresses. In time, the entire galaxy becomes another playground to discover strange things in and brave horrifyingly precarious planets. One planet I'd ventured to had radioactive winters at night, and firestorms in the day whenever the planet felt like.

At this point, 100 hours in, I'm still discovering anomalous entities and planets. That's not even a subjective, 'take-our-word-for-it' thing either. One planet I'd been to had Will-o'-Wisps as the only animal present, while another looked like a hellish datascape.

Say what you like about the game's initial release, but this has easily become a GotY contender for me. It has scratched so many itches that I had with gaming as of late (character customization being one), and I sincerely hope the developers continue working on this. It's an amazing game.

This review comes from a general gamer's point of view.

The game is fun, I would say. The graphics are stunning and each planet is different to itself which makes exploration very exciting. What I don't like too much about the game is the "grindy" aspect.
You can run out of fuel fast in this game if you only put in one fuel pack thing. One fuel pack can last you two trips. When you run out of fuel, you have to look for materials and build a new fuel pack. Which I think is not fun for me. 
What also runs out is your life support and stuff. You're going to have to constantly refuel your stuff, so that you stay alive.

There's going to be a lot of traveling in the game. Since the planets are pretty big, you have to walk a lot, looking for materials that you need. While looking for materials, you're going to run into bots. They can get pretty annoying since if they catch you mining, they're going to start attacking. Since you dont start with a weapon you're going to have to use your mining tool to kill the bots.

What I do like is that you can build and break anything on the planets. You're able to create castles and huge homes for you to live in. Minecraft would be the closest thing to compare it to, but No Mans Sky is nothing like Minecraft.

I played this game in VR and on flat screen. When playing in VR I got very motion sick. I've played many vr games before this, but I don't play for many long periods of time. I usually take a break every 45 mins since I get motion sick easily. Another problem in vr was the weird ship controls. At first I didn't know that rotation your hand would rotate the ship, I thought you had to move your hand. Because of this, I was just spinning around in circles while in VR. Which if you didn't know, doesn't feel good. So now, I only stick to flat screen :D

besides all the downsides, I quite like the game.

Graphics: 9/10
Music: 6/10 (not really that important)
Gameplay: 7/10
Combat: 6/10

Overall Review: 7/10 (Average)

Pretty much a meh title.  I tried to like this game, really did, bought it late, tempered expectations, etc.

Problem is, the developer really went out of their way to make every interaction painful.  Everything you want to click needs you to hold down the mouse for 2-3 seconds.  Every time you get a milestone, it brings an overlay into view for 10 seconds.  Every time you jump to a system its a 10 second animation (ok, maybe loading screen, right?), but then every time you access the galactic map (which you'll be doing endlessly), it swivels and scrolls around a very plain starmap for 5-10 seconds before you can interject and take control.  Want some dialogue?  Enjoy 2-3 seconds between each 2 lines of alien chatter.

Basically, the game has heavily invested in making you watch a *ton* of micro-cutscenes/actions from 1-10 seconds, thousands of times over.  I get for presentation, the first few times it's really nice to have those overlays, providing story, vibe, etc.  But after the 100th time?  Geez, just make it stop.

The devs have gotten a good bit of feedback on this, but apparently it's just fine, you can edit files to make some actions immediate, but not others (when people have to hack your ini files to make mouse interactions move at a normal pace, that's not normal).

Bottom line, it's a new kind of "grind".  It feels great for the first hour, and gets progressively more frustrating at that.  Add to it the sheer pointlessness of the game (grind central), resources only to upgrade ships/suit/scanner, none of these things matter, because survival, combat, etc. are all entirely trivial.  It's just a perpetual grind for no real purpose.
