Played for about 5 hours. Waiting for it to get fun, but never happened.  

The game just feels like a weird combination of different systems that don't work well together while also being really grindy. I like resource management games. I totally get the appeal of them, but the dev here just didn't make this fun. 

First off, we have mining. You pretty much zap materials and they accumulate in your inventory. Pretty straight forward. You can upgrade it later to tackle more difficult mining structures. You can zap plants, rocks and even animals. It's frustrating because yous tart off wanting to zap all you can to see what you can do with it and your starting inventory is so abysmally small you have to start throwing things away just to craft. Slight annoyance ok, I toss whatever is useless or try to hoard til I get back to a space station and/or build a shop terminal. One of the early missions I had to find Copper. My scanner didn't pick up any deposits nearby. So I walked in a direction for 10 minutes before I finally found one. It only had half of what I needed. Cool. Did the same thing. I'm sure there's an upgrade or travel mechanism down teh line that will help with this but at the beginning of the game it's just not enticing me to play more. Especially because...

The worlds feel so dead. The worlds are just NOT pretty to look at. I've been on 3 planets so far(frozen, toxic, heat) and *none* of them actually looked good. I'm playing in 4k on a 3080 and the game could stand to look a lot better. Especially when it comes to rock and mountain textures where textures look super weird and sometimes fail to load(most commonly when you're using terrain gun to make holes inside). 

One thing I did start to enjoy was using the terrain gun to go underground and through mountains..... except that it's just as shallow. For larger mountains you can't actually go through them. You'll soon encounter an rock wall you can't go through shortly after entering. From what I understand the Terrain Manipulator has no upgrades so this is the same throughout the whole game. 

The crafting system is ok... just too much junk and materials with such a limited inventory to start off with which discourages you from mining or picking up something you don't immediately need.

I am new to this game.  I held off buying it due to the mixed reviews and high price tag.  But the reviews got better and it went on sale.....so here I am.  

There are lots of different parts to this game.  You will find yourself going off on so many tangents.  But for me the one part of the game that still needs work is balancing it and pulling it all together.  

There is a story line that you have to follow to unlock critical elements of the game.  So it does help in showing you certain fundamentals.  But as you follow the story you come across so many other elements that you just start down a different path....and that's ok.

The one thing this game does so well, and for me makes it worth the price, is creating a sense of adventure.  The game continues to surprise me, and impress me.  I am still with the game, not because of the story, but because you literally don't know what will be around the next corner or on the next planet.  The time and effort that is put in to give each planet a unique feel and look is well worth it.  

The game does pay homage (or rip off depending on how you feel) from many other sci-fi franchises.  So part of the fun is finding and recognizing them.

So the biggest issue I have with the game is the lack of balance from all the different elements.  Its not a deal breaker because the game does a good job teaching you the basics.  It gives you enough information to stay alive and get around (that being said you will probably die in the first five minutes after you start a new game,  just let it happen and move on).  Its when you try to move beyond the basics, or start to explore areas of the game that haven't been covered by the story yet where it gets a little iffy.  There is an in game information center.  Just hit escape and you are brought to an information menu that can answer a lot of questions.  So the game does a good job of explaining different elements but it really up to the player to understand how to bring the elements together to accomplish a particular goal.  

So there you have it.  If this review seems a bit confusing but gets you interested enough to buy the game then I have succeeded in communicating how I have been experiencing the game.  The developers continue to make changes and improvements (which can throw a monkey wrench in when you are learning a part they decide to change) so be prepared for that.  

So if you are looking for a game that can bring a first person experience of what it would be like to explore  alien worlds, fly around in space ships, walk through teleporters and mine rocks with a laser beam, then this is the game for you.  There are so many planets to travel to you will not have enough time to visit them all.  There are many games that say "open world" but this game really delivers on that promise.  The universe really is at your finger tips and that for me is worth the price of admission.

What a difference a few months make.  I'm glad I got the game now and not earlier.  This game is very engaging and thoroughly enjoyable on so many levels.  The devs are still cranking out free content and improvements, so I'm really looking at sticking with this for a long while.
For those not loving the motherhood statements here's some more details to ponder.  My opinion and thoughts only and I'll compare to some more established titles with no real over all bias (intended or sponsored I'm just an average-Joe-gamer).

Pros
Very detailed and complex crafting, building and manufacturing.  
The tutorial is more like an evolving campaign, well actually the campaign is basically the tutorial expanded of course.  One could follow that and nothing else for what most consider a complete game.  I'm 40+ hours into this and only the second crack (first was a handful of hours to get used to the controls and the major aspects of the game) I have the feeling the complete play through campaign is a long one compared to most.  
The galaxy is so vast it would hard to imagine it being exhausted quickly even if the player base gets large.  For a procedural galaxy the diversity is good (not beyond becoming repetitive but still very, well ... diverse).
The single v multi seems balanced.  I'm not big on multi player games and those players I do see I simply nod and wave and it makes no difference to either of us.  I'm playing solo but I feel like I'm perfectly in control to reach out or not which I like and haven't felt in most online games.  I actually feel like it's a shame I work too much and can't join in the fun but RL has bills to pay.

Cons
The complexity does take some getting used to, hence the restart.  I hate mess.
The logic used to control the players is a bit Mehhh at times.  E.g. I can build a computer but not a box to store my ore in. (wtf?) I acquired a Capital class ship or could have purchased a better space ships fairly early but the storage is still very limiting.  When I finally do get storage in my base it has to be powered and I can only build a limited number of them.  Why? (well - To limit the players of course and prevent crowding attacks and clogging the servers etc.).  
The grind of it also can be burdensome. For those wanting a quick no thinking game, sorry your out of luck here.  If standing blasting rocks and trees for quite some time (every now-and-then) is not your cup of tea again this ain't for you.  Probably more grindy than Ark or Empyrion GS but not as much as Wurm.  Hopefully the later game automation reduces that a bit.  I haven't even looked at farming plots and auto extractors yet.  Probably again used to limited over crowding and make groups more profitable.

For those thinking of playing some words of warning and advice (besides looking for some good videos).  Don't forget technology upgrades are not transferable so consider hard if you spend money on your gear and ships, it's usually a lot easier and cheaper to buy a new one,  Save your Nanites for much later as you get a lot of the basic blue prints and stuff for nothing.  Finally don't bother too much about base building unless that is your passion as the space ships rule.  You can always build a base on your freighter and have the best of both worlds.

Never wrote a review, however with No Man's Sky I felt the need I had to. Different people have different taste in everything, and that includes which game someone likes, and which they don't. No Man's Sky offers different types of play one can choose from, or play them all. What I write is my experience, which could be very different from other opinions.
 
The sheer size of the game is amazing imho. So many things to discover, it's amazing. It offers you different play styles.
- Hit on NPC's freighters, or other players (if you encounter any, cause the size of the game is 
  so huge, you probably won't).
- Focus on the building aspect, which is one of the things I like. You can build amazing bases, 
  even under water. This doesn't just stop by just placing a building and be done. You can also 
  create your own home internally by adding just    cosmetic items (like beds, plants, etc, etc.).
- Follow the quest line. There are main quests, and secondary quests. Following the quest 
  lines allows you to discover 
   blue prints for free, in order to build new items, or technologies for either your ship, base, 
   exosuite, or exocraft. Following
   the quest line is not a must, however it will allow you to learn how to do/build certain things. 
   Most things you can also
   buy at a certain place, with items you find on planets.
- Just explore. The sheer size of amount of galaxies and planets is overwhelming.

Your actions in game will determine how you are perceived by other races, so make your choices carefully.  
 
I've been playing the game for a bit now, and I have to say, I love it. I've been focusing on base building and following the quest line, and generating income. The game has a steep learning curve, however you will learn things fast enough, especially if you start to follow the questline in the beginning, after which things start to make more sense. At some point, you will also get the option to get your own big ass freighter in game. I had placed ii above the planet with my main base, and when you look up, the view towards that big ass ship is amazing (if you google, you'll see others having made a screenshots of it). With this freighter, you can buy/hire frigates, which you can send out on missions for you and gather
the riches of other worlds, or resources you can re-use. 
 
In the beginning, I felt not comfortable leaving my base too far, as I was afraid not being able to find it again, however, where ever you are, the game will always allow you a way back. Every galaxy has their own space station, which will allow you to teleport to locations you know/have discovered. You will be able to "summon" your vehicles where ever you are. 
Every planet offers the basic materials you need to craft the most commonly used items.
 
If you like to play with friends, this game offers you to play solo, and being able to join a friends game, with your own saved game. That said, you will end up in the same galaxy as they are, if you join their game, and if they join yours, they will end up in yours. Not to worry, as said, there is a space station in every galaxy, which will allow you to teleport to locations you know/have discovered/own bases. It also offers the ability to do missions together. You can enter each others bases, and make use of each others technologies.
 
I've read a few things in some of the negative reviews, which one can easily overcome by adding a mod. Not needed by myself, but if you google, there's a few mods one can use to overcome some of the things mentioned.
 
Before this turns out into a novel (I can continue a long way after this), my personal opinion is that I like the game very, very much. I love building bases, seeing what I can to to earn as much cash as I can. It's an open world, in which nothing will hold you back from exploring, base building, generate income, get into space fights, or do what ever you like. For people like myself, I highly recommend this game, as it offers so much one can do, in such a incredible huge world. 11 out of 10 from me.

No Man's Sky was... an interesting case.

I'd like to say that NMS is a riveting experience from the start. Having heard a lot of negative feedback from people concerning the core gameplay loop, I was definitely sceptical. My first couple of hours involved me running around completing quests and wandering how the hell everything slotted together. Why did one resource need to be found? What happened with this quest and why is it useful?

After fixing up my ship and struggling to figure out what to do, I decided to sit back and take some time with the game itself. I still didn't have much of an idea on why I needed to undergo certain quests or what materials I needed for certain devices, so I flew to another planet and underwent some base building. And you know what? It really helped.

After my break from the quests to teach myself the basics, I found myself understanding everything a lot more easily, and everything started to slot into place. That's when I found myself appreciating the game a lot more. Sure, it's a little buggy in places, but what can't I say about it? The environments, the space exploration, and even the base building felt amazing after a while. Getting back into the quests after that felt much less daunting, and I finally had a grasp on what I needed to go forward with the tasks that were set.

Would I recommend this game? By far I would. The early game can be somewhat confusing for simpletons like myself, but once you fix up the ship it's not all mandatory - you can go off and explore or battle to your heart's content if you desire. And at its sale price of £20, I have to say it's well worth it.

No Man's Sky is a survival game focused on space, solar systems, and strange planets. You start with nothing (par for the course) except your basic tools. You eventually build yourself up, work on getting your space ship up-and-ready, and you explore the cosmos.

You can build extravagant bases, research new technologies, recruit giant space fleets, terrorize life on all planets, become a space billionaire, etc. There's a lot of stuff in this game to really sink some time into, especially if you're the building/creative type.

There are some things that I wish I saw more of in the future, of course. This game has pretty limited multiplayer, but it works great with friends. I would like to see 'hub systems' or something where players can group up in larger groups to play, explore, and build together. There's also a few bugs that might get annoying, but nothing game breaking. A restart will work with most bugs that don't have a more simple fix. 

If you gave NMS a shot when it came out and instantly uninstalled as I did, now may be a good time to come back and see the massive changes that were made to this game.

Please note that this review only applies if you are planning to play this game in VR. Before you say that "You only have 2 hours of playtime! You can't leave a bad review," I couldn't bear the game long enough to get past the two hour mark. I don't care if it gets better, because first impressions are the most important aspect of your game. And nothing will take away anyone's right to criticize anything, for love or money. And remember: this review is ONLY for the VR aspect.

When I was about to buy this to play it with my friend, the fact that the game could be played in VR really caught my eye. Immediately, I said "Oh-ho-ho-ho-ho!" I personally own a Valve Index, which is why that aspect excited me.

While it was cool that my friend who was not playing in VR could see the exact position of my hands (when I met him, I t-posed and asked if I was t-posing. He confirmed that I was, in fact, t-posing on his screen), this was one minor good thing in a sea of negatives.

The first red flag I came across (but brushed off) was that the game doesn't take advantage of the Index's ability to track individual fingers. You can clench your fist as hard as you like, but all five fingers will remain extended until the game says they can retract into the palm of your hand.

Also, you can't crouch in this game in VR. I don't know if you can do it in non-VR. I don't care. If you bring your head too low, you exit the game boundaries. Having the boundaries be vertical as well as horizontal is pretty dumb if you ask me.

Then there was the issue that the HUD that tells you your health and your life support levels and et cetera doesn't even remotely follow your face. The only way to get it where you need it to be is to use the right joystick to perform a sharp rotation. Sure, you need to be able to look at the stuff, but maybe have it slide over if you move your head until two thirds of the display are off screen? Or maybe do something like Half-Life: Alyx did, where it had the HUD details be on your hands? Have looking at your health and life support be like checking the time on a watch?

Another thing that made no sense was that when you grabbed your omni-tool from over your shoulder, it would fire (right trigger was needed to grab it and to fire it). This could easily be fixed by giving the omni-tool a second or two after being grabbed where it can't fire, or by programming the tool so that it can't be fired in the same instance of pressing the right trigger as it was grabbed in. Also, you can't put the tool away by bringing your hand over your shoulder and pressing right trigger. Only way to get rid of it without it re-materializing in your hand was to open the inventory.

I was also having some trouble with the menus. The right trigger was the "select" button, but it kept sending me back to the previous menu with no clear pattern as to why. Eventually, towards the end of my experience, I discovered that it was because the fingers on my right hand were pressing a little too hard on the sensor, which re-purposes the right trigger into a back button. This is incredibly stupid because A: naturally, I'm going to have my fingers there because I'll want my hand to be in the pointer position, just like the hand in the game when I'm going through a menu, B: the left trigger already fills that niche, and C: nothing in the game during the first two hours tells you that! I had to combat this annoying feature several times before I realized what was going on, sometimes resorting to physically moving my hand towards the option to tap on it. By the time I figured out what was wrong, it was too late. I already discovered too many other frustrating aspects.

The next issue that took me too long to work out was movement. I used smooth movement, where you can go from point A to point B without needing to teleport. Occasionally, I would have trouble moving forwards. I thought at first that it was with the terrain, and what reinforced this was that using the jet pack seemed to make going forward easy. I later figured out that movement was done based on hand orientation, and there was no way to make it based on head orientation. Movement was difficult when my left hand was pointed right at the ground. The jet pack seemed to bypass the issue because every time I used it, I also just so happened to re-adjust my left hand. There was one moment before I worked this out where the jet pack didn't work for this purpose and- you guessed it! I didn't know why.

Often when I grabbed stuff (with my left hand because the right hand was always occupied by the omni-tool that I couldn't conventionally put way), the inventory would pop up. I found this perplexing, and of course, I didn't know why. Later, I found out that it was because I was squeezing the left controller. It may seem cool on paper, but when you need to squeeze a hand to grab something, it gets annoying. Besides, there is already another way to open the inventory more intentionally. Bring your right hand to your left. A little quick menu shows up. One of the options is inventory. Select that. Bam. Why do we need the left-hand-squeeze-to-open-inventory again?

Lastly, we have the spaceship. Oh goodness, the spaceship. While it is cool that there are two things that you need to interact with in order to control the ship throttle and rotation, for some reason, my hands kept letting go, and getting into orbit was a struggle because few things, if anything, made sense. Either I wasn't squeezing hard enough (which is unlikely because I was squeezing with all I had), or there is a threshold for how far away your hand can go from the control before automatically letting go, and that threshold isn't clear. It's most likely the latter, which is another design flaw because the hand should always hold on as long as the controller is squeezed. It is especially an issue in combat, where I ended up getting on the wrong side of the Gek because I wouldn't make a donation. In the heat of the moment, it is very likely that your hand can accidentally stray way too far from the throttle or joystick. I ended up having to bail out.

Here is my final reminder that this review ONLY applies to the VR aspect. I'm not criticizing the entire game, just the VR version of the game. And my small play time does NOT strip me or anyone else of their right to leave a negative review. Neither would a huge playtime total. But you know what? Fine. You have the right to complain about playtime too. Just remember that others also have the right to explain why your logic is flawed.

There is no exploration in No Man's Sky. The game is just a sightseeing tour with a couple chores along the way. I can see a cool mountain planet, some interesting rock formations, maybe even a few settlements and even a crashed, derelict freighter. But that's all I'm doing, seeing them. Every settlement has one basic interaction with the one NPC that spawns and maybe a little loot. There might be a couple minerals on those rock formations, but they're the same I can find anywhere else on the planet. I can't even really enter the crashed freighters, I'm told to just dig around to find a few loot crates with potentially useful loot, and once they're all open, the Point of Interest quest clears and now I'm done. Except I never really was in a point of interest in the first place, because even that loot is nothing but some raw materials that I could have also picked up from the planet or bought in a space station. Some people are going to bring up the 200 quintillion or however many planets there are, but frankly, it doesn't matter how many planets there are if they can't make them interesting. People have pointed out to me that, yeah, there is a story, but there are two key points in that. 1, the story, really doesn't have any connection whatsoever to the world I play in. Now this freighter has one captain's log that's ridiculously cryptic and pretentious, good thing I'll never find another freighter with any background info surrounding it. 2, this game is being sold on it's world, not on it's story. If I'm buying steel and you give me rope, it doesn't matter how much rope, how high quality, any of that, I was buying steel. I bought your world, you gave me nothing, and said "but at least there's a story."
And I will not even get into the general bugginess of this game. I haven't encountered anything game breaking, but there have been multiple times where I've clipped through walls, fallen through the floor, or watch as the animals around me desperately attempt to escape their stone prison. I buy a game, I expect polish. This is not early access, this is a finished game on the market for $60. Bugs should be few and far between, it doesn't matter how much content surrounds it.
If you want to buy this game, know that the exploration is incredibly stale, and especially don't go looking for the echoes, as they are easily the most disappointing part of the exploration. If you still want to buy this game, do not, under any circumstances, buy it for $60, as it is simply not worth that much in the slightest.

Out of the thousands of titles I've played, THAT was the singlemost bullshit intro to a game that I've ever seen.

The universe is created and initialized. You're placed on a toxic planet, with a broken suit and broken equipment. You're given instructions on how to fix the equipment, which is easy enough because it uses materials which are right in front of you. Then you're given instructions to use your scanner and find a particular element (in my case it was sodium) to keep your suit running and protect you from the toxic atmosphere.

Problem is, plants containing that element are generated by RNG. A lot of players have those plants within a respectable distance and this isn't an issue. I was not one of those players.

My first guy died. He had so little of a chance that I assumed you were supposed to die, like one of those games where you get your ass beat at the outset, then you're revived and introduced to the real gameplay. Nope. My second guy popped up in the same spot as the first, with the same quest requirement. He died soon after.

So I came to the forum, thinking this can't possibly be how the game is. What did I miss? Then I read that there were some people who'd played for hours like this, dying, getting revived, dying, getting revived, until they finally found the types of plants they needed for their suit so they could then work on getting off the first planet.

If I was 12, and I got this game for Christmas so refunding wasn't so easy, and it was something I'd wanted forever? Maybe I'd spend a few hours dying over and over again while wandering around this same landscape. But I'm not 12. I'm not going to waste my time on something that pointless. If you've got a good game here, then let new players get to it.

Maybe the game gets better, but on top of my own play experience the stuff I've read about NMS even now seems pretty mixed and the community looks toxic as hell. My view is, if a developer believes that this is the best way to intro to his title, then that's a developer who probably hasn't written a game I'd like.

To be honest I didn't think I'd like this game, not 100% my style. However it started getting good reviews and I couldn't resist having a go. After a couple of hours gameplay I thought it was OK but still unsure, it all seemed a bit slow and lacked direction. However I'm glad I stuck with it because 70 hours+ later I've really grown to love this game.

After the sheer depth of the game became apparent I realised that there's a lot more to the game than I first thought. Base building, gaining knowledge, flying/warping to different systems, buying/selling products, fighting aliens and discovering new technology/fauna all have their own challenges but are completely engrossing. You'd think with all the above it'd be a complex game to get used to but that's where the initial slow start to the game is actually important, it gets you used to the controls and interface without masses of in-your-face instructions.

To cut a long story short, give it time if you're not sure, it gets better and better. The graphics are stunning and the seamless gameplay is very well programmed. I play it in VR and I'm a bit of grumpy old B when VR controls are poor, no worries in this game they're very well thought out. I tried the desktop version (which you can switch to seamlessly) but sorry non-VR players, VR despite the graphics not being as sharp just kills the desktop version for atmosphere and immersion.

I thought I'd have to wait a long time before playing another VR game as good as Half Life Alyx, but it's like the buses, you wait forever and then 2 come along at the same time. Congrats to the developers, keep the updates coming.

[h1]Why I think this game deserves the 2020 'Product of Love' award.[/h1]
When we first heard of this game, it was very little but a boisterous promise. A promise that enticed many gamers because it promised exactly that which many people dream of: infinite possibilities and infinite freedom. We knew it was a bold promise and I also think we were aware of the difficulties a small team would face if they wanted to deliver on that promise. But more than anything, we wanted them to deliver. We wanted this so bad, that there was what you would call a hype. A gravitational pull towards everything the people making this game promised. Because you know what? They wanted to deliver on their promise as well. They were so enthousiastic about it, so much in love with their dream of infinite possibility and infinite freedom. They took us with them on that dream.
Dreams are tough, when you're in the real world. And whenever there is money to be made because there is a large group of people willing to spend money, dreams are even harder to keep.
The group of people making this game have kept their dream, throughout the enormous pressure building on them from a demanding community and a demanding market. Over the course of seven years, No Man's Sky has seen many improvements, all of them given freely for those that bought the game. For those who were willing to wait for dreams to come true, everything that was promised seven years ago is here now, and even more. This game is a triumph of persistance and a labour of love from a small company that does not care what the big dollars say, but follows a singular vision that they truly believe in.

I recommend that everyone who has been along for the ride to vote with me, in appreciation of creativity over commerce, as encouragement for everyone who wants to use game-development as a way to make dreams come true. [url=https://store.steampowered.com/steamawards/#LaborOfLove]Cast your vote here.[/url]

Years and years ago I Alpha tested star wars galaxies. That is the only game I have ever played in 30+ years that had more bugs than this one does. The ground will revert on you undoing all the work you put in to modifying terrain, you should not even use that tool. If you build on the ground, 100% of the time the ground came back and filled in the base I built there after, so you have to build in air. The autonomous miners will disappear after you fill them with fuel and when they eventually reappear they are empty, i have to click them 2x to interact every time because first try auto closes. You will freeze and have to reload on almost a daily basis and if you are on an Xbox like my daughter you will have to do it multiple times every session. I have had my freighter revert and empty itself of things i built on there for no reason, fell through wire frame of world to death (happens to daughter on xbox a lot where bases just dont fully download design for her)  and on and on. 

That said, if you can tolerate an endless list of bugs, this game is awesome. It has so much potential and so many choices of what to do. You have a number of play modes from story where you dont die up to permadeath. You can play completely single player by turning off network, but if you play just normal you will have an experience that feels like there are other people out there, though you wont run into each other much unless you try. There is full multi to join friends directly but careful building that way, have had a fwee bugs make people I play with stop. Despite the bugs I have still enjoyed playing it and am giving it a thumbs up. 

If you do buy it, first thing you should do is change your multiplayer network settings. They have it set so anyone can kill you, take apart your base and just grief the hell out of you by default. Why its like that by default I have no idea. When reading about game before buying I found a quite a few people who were griefed right out of game before realising those settings could even be changed. That isnt that frequent though, I left pvp on for quite a while and only person ever attacked me. First two people that landed as i built my first base transferred items to me without saying anything, 3rd guy shot me dead while I was in 3rd person build mode far from body lol.

No Man's Sky is more than what it promised to be when ti came out - and though there are a few things I would complain about, I think it's more than worth the cost.
It's a really calming game interspersed with little moments of both brevity and there's always a feeling like there's more to see - though sadly, not really with the planets.

What this game really needs now is more 'events' but as applied to the planet surface. currently I feel there's more to experience while flying around than on the planet surface (except for the base building, which is really nice. Sort of Subnautica-esque, for sure, but back when we had the terraformer - which, wouldn't you know it, is a tool that is used to it's maximum effect here)

The other thing the game could use is a bit more depth - and I mean that geographically. planet surfaces are, sadly, *really* shallow so far. maybe the ocean planets go deeper in, but I've never  felt like I could make a cave system if I really wanted to - not enough space for it.

Otherwise, great game - never expected it to be. Congratulations, Hello Games, you're an inspiration to all who start poor and end great.

I don't even know where to begin. Forget everything you've ever heard that's bad about No Man's Sky. I came into this expecting really bad graphics and gameplay and wasn't only mildly surprised but overwhelmed by how incredibly good it is!

So far I've played twice - I couldn't get over how unique every single world I'd been to was. Now I've been on at least 20 different worlds and every one of them is so individual, so different in every aspect that I just want to play more and more and more and more....

It's hard work - there's a lot to do and it will keep you very busy trying to make progress, but even when it's slow it's fun. I expect to get many hundreds of hours out of this.

Oh, and the monoliths - look out for the monoliths, Dave. 

Just buy it - no question!

EDIT 7/1/21 Ok I have now played NMS for 300 hours! I am still finding new things and can't see an end in sight. There is SO MUCH to do in this game - and that's just single player. I haven't even tried multiplayer yet.

Things are starting to get a little repetitive, but only a little. Today I've discovered at least 3 new things that I had never even seen before. 

There are some bugs still - the freighter missions could do with some work (very unpolished although still playable), the emergency beacons have a few bugs and a statistics page would be very useful. Other than that, I stand by my initial review - NMS is a fantastic game and well worth the purchase. If you can get it at a discount you will get a great deal - I would still have paid twice as much as I did (£20) and been happy. Hello Games have been working on this for seven years and it shows. I hope they continue to make the game even better than it is. Thank you devs!

EDIT 21/1/21 Up to 450+ hours! Eventually, I feel as though I've explored pretty much all there is to explore with NMS. I paid £20! I do still have two achievements left to get, which are probably going to take many more hours, but as for the main content I think I've done all there is to do. The devs are apparently still working on the game and releasing new content periodically - they actually read the steam community discussions and work with the community to make NMS even better. What more could you ask for?

Btw I only played single player mode.

It's been a fun ride and worth every penny.

Alrighty, hope you got time and are willing to read a book, cause I mf wrote one for this gem of a game lmao. Although Steam says I have just broken 100 hours into this game, I originally had this on PS4. At the time, my computer was fubbernucked, and I REALLY wanted to pick this game up. So I got it on PS4 instead of PC, which was the platform I wanted it on. Once my PC was fixed, I bought the game, and 100.1 hours later, here I am lol. I clocked in about 93 hours on the PS4 version. So whatever Steam says I have on this, add about 93 hours to that lol.

Although this games early history is rough, it picked itself up from the ashes of it's harsh criticisms and made itself into a true GEM of a game. If you're into the survival exploration genre, I cannot recommend this game enough.

It's come out with constant new updates, that just constantly add onto the universe of No Man's Sky. From the "Foundation" update, to the latest "Next Gen" update, all of these new additions to the game is ENTIRELY free. You buy the game once, and then everything it has to offer is all yours. This even includes VR! Yep, you don't have to buy a whole separate copy of the game to play it in VR like..... other games. You buy the game, and once you boot it up, it will simply ask you if you'd like to play the base game or the VR version.

And VR plays REALLY well in this game! Impressively well for a game that was never initially intended to be played in VR. I wouldn't say that it's the greatest VR game on the market. As I said, it was never intended to be played in VR during it's initial development. I am saying however that, in it's own right, it plays impressively well! They took great care of it's VR counter part. Your save even carries over from the base game, so you don't have to start over from scratch. You can hop in & out of VR at any time. As well as play with friends who're in or out of VR. Yep! You can walk around, wave, floss, whatever with your friends who're not in VR, and they will actually see every action you make in VR!

Back to my actual thoughts on this game (I didn't mean to splurge on about the VR like that, I just think it's so cool XD), I think there's a little something for everyone here. If it's not your taste, or it doesn't scratch your itches just right, that's okay. This game has probably the LARGEST sandbox in gaming history. Spanning up to 255 galaxies to explore, and each galaxy having literally... and I mean LITERALLY... read what I am about to type slowly, because I am not being satirical when I say this:

B I L L I O N S

of star systems to explore and discover. To be break it down a little more, each galaxy has different regions. Each containing roughly 122 to 550 star systems. There are 3 to 4 BILLIONS of regions in a single galaxy. And with there being 255 galaxies.... Yeah, you do the math.
Humanity IRL will probably ACTUALLY be exploring the stars ourselves by the time every square in of NMS were truly explored by the entirety of the player base.

But trust me, this universe is not empty. You can:

Discover wildlife
Discover Plants
Build Bases
Construct Vehicles
Own a large Freighter ship that is basically a mobile base from star-system to star-system
Command a fleet
Explore Derelict Freighters (where the games ambiance basically becomes Dead Space, I am not kidding)
Collect multiple ships to fly
Hunt down pirates
Take up bounties
Join the Mercenary, Merchants, Exploration, or Research guilds
Explore crashed Freighters
When boarded the Nexus in the Anomaly (hub world), you can take up missions with your friends
Play VR (of course ;3)
Learn the languages of the different races in the game
Build relations with the races that can affect trade

and so much more that I'm sure I'll kick myself later for not including lol.

No Man's Sky is a PHENOMENAL game that just gets bigger every year. They have average updates to the game that add to it throughout the year, and then they have one annual BIG update to the game. Such as "Beyond," "Next" or "Visions." This year, they added "Origins." A MASSIVE updated overhaul that added Super worlds with GARGANTUAN mountains, new unique storms, and even binary or even trinary star systems. As well as new creatures, and even GIANT sandworms the size of skyscrapers that explode out of the ground in more sandy worlds. They have updates like this in different variety every year. This year, the overhauled the types of planets in the universe. Next year, who knows? The next big update may give us an all new combat system, or a new enemy to face, or a new dungeon type location to explore (such as the Derelict Freighters).

Did I ever mention all of this was free? You purchase the game ONCE... And all this is yours, as well as future updates. This game has gone from the biggest let down, to the greatest comeback story in 4-5 years.

If you're still not sold, this game now features cross-play. So if you have a copy on PC, and your friends are on PS or Xbox, no worries. You can still play it with your friends.

I think I've rabbled on long enough lol. This game is a true gem, and it's community is incredibly welcoming. They're so sweet, and organized. Hell, they even found a designated planet to call a community hub, and built upon it. It's called the "Galactic Hub," and it's where players can meet up and work together, and build bases. The COMMUNITY made that happen. Not Hello Games, not Sean Murray (director). Take that as a testament to this communities welcoming nature. Check out the subreddit if you want to know more.

Edit: THERE'S EVEN A FRIGGAN COMMUNITY TAXI SERVICE, IF YOU DON'T HAVE THE MEANS TO TRAVEL TO A SPECIFIC STAR-SYSTEM OR GALAXY. I just figured this out and came to edit my review to add that lmao. This communities too good bruh XD

10/10 game
Recommend to anyone with a powerful enough platform that can support this game.

My overall impression at 3 hours in is very positive. It's beautifully made, the dynamics all feel fluid, the science aspect is well-thought-out, fun and immersive, and the base-building looks good! There's a lot to learn and the learning curve felt steep for the first couple of hours, and 3 hours in I'm still learning new things about how the game functions. There's a LOT to know. However, the nice thing is that virtually all the needed information is available in-game (it cues you which buttons to press, and refers to your remapped buttons rather than the defaults, which is nice.) The available information is presented immersively, which is a nice plus.

There's a few things that I like to know about a game before I buy that are rarely covered in reviews, so here they are: 

SAVING

-You cannot save anytime, only at a save point. Your first way to save will be by exiting your ship. Later, there are more opportunities to save.

CONTROLS (For reference, I use a laptop and trackpad and use arrow keys for navigation.).

-Controls are almost all remappable, including movement (Default is WASD). 

-The game assumes you have a 3-button mouse. The middle-button controls are NOT all remappable. Specifically, the middle-mouse button control for discarding inventory items is NOT remappable. This means if you don't have a middle mouse button, you will not be able to discard items and your inventory will become full. You can get rid of items at traders, but they aren't always available. Your best option may be to use a mouse emulator or AutoHotKey. This should not be necessary, and is not cool.

-If playing on a laptop, you may encounter that common issue with PC games where you are unable to use a feature using the default keys because your use of the mouse is frozen when a letter key is being held down. You must remap that key to a key that does allow mouse movement, such as L-CTRL. In No Man's Sky, this will allow use of the Scanner, which is necessary for game play.

I definitely wish that game designers paid more attention to the laptop gaming experience and to differences in hardware that players may have. 3 button mouses are not all that common. And remapping should be possible for every key/mouse button, because someone will inevitably need to remap it for some reason.

Beyond that, I expect that this game will continue to be awesome as I discover more.

I've put in over 2000 hours with NMS on the PS4, almost from day 1, and it's been an interesting journey. The game's environment is massive, and there is a lot to do, at least in the early to mid stretches. Hello Games has come a long ways since the initial release, and the current game is visually gorgeous and offers many different paths for the player to take.

On the other hand, if you're looking for an immersive experience based on real world physics, NMS is not that game (that game would be Elite Dangerous, Eve, or Star Citizen). After all this time NMS still doesn't have beds that can be used, chairs you can build and actually sit in (although you can put in a sofa and sit on that), or a food system that is actually useful. From my perspective much of the add-ons to the game have been more in the category of "bells and whistles" rather than substantive improvements. That doesn't make them any less appealing visually, but they just don't add anything to the overall experience for a player with a lot of experience with hard-core simulators and games like E:D.

That being said, NMS is still a lot of fun, and each update has moved it to what players expected initially, and beyond. As future updates hopefully fix issues like the NPC dialog, add more backstory, and introduce new challenges, the game will likely continue on for a long time.

I would give NMS a 4.5 out of 5 for visual aesthetics, a 4 for the play experience, and a 3.5 for immersion. I would recommend it.

Ok I'm gonna get the bad stuff out of the way first. Essentially, I really wish there was more variety. Things like multiple biomes on a planet, even just ice caps like there would be in real life, more different kinds of plants and creatures, and definitely more types of buildings and little civilizations on planets (I really find it hard to believe that with all these beings around there would be no distinctive towns, cities, roads, etc.). Different space stations would be nice too. I don't think every one needs to look the same.

Having said that, it's beautiful. I wasn't there at launch so I don't know how far its come since then but I love it so much. So many unique places and so much beautiful scenery! The story is really profound and the characters are designed well. Crafting and materials can be challenging, but is simple to understand. I love the feeling of landing on a planet and knowing I'm the first person to ever see this, the infinite-ness is incredible. Using they/them pronouns for everyone is something you don't see often and it's kind of a nice change of pace. All in all, cool stuff, love the alien feel to everything, and I'm really excited to see how this will keep getting better.
Reviews.116913:
I followed No Man's Sky from the very beginning. The first announcements and trailers had me completely stoked. When the game came out, it was a disappointment to see it's poor condition. Even with all of the bad press and backlash, I continued to take interest in the game and the small community around it. I watched and waited to see what would happen with the future of the game, hoping that something would come of it. I even participated in the Waking Titan ARG surrounding it, getting one of the fancy Level 4 Atlas Passes they sent out for people who contributed.

Four years after the launch of this game, I have never been so happy to have stuck by a studio and game. Watching the game grow into something beautiful, and watching the community grow as people outside of the community began to change their minds about this game. It's been an amazing ride, and Hello Games should take pride in what they have done to fix their past mistakes.

All in all, No Man's Sky has improved greatly over the past four years, and I am happy to be able to recommend this game to anyone interested in space and sci-fi, as well as people who are just interested in the story of this game and how far it has come over the years.

This game is an impressive use of procedural generation to produce a vastness... but that means there's every chance that this vastness is experienced in a way which feels a lot like uninteresting randomness. It's just how the randomness of the procedure works.

On top of this issue is the very plain and 'flow-chart' style of interaction with everything. Mine things, shoot things, dig things, go into a horrible menu (at least on controller, don't see why it would be better on M+KB though) and build things. Very few options to deal with everything. This is clear when talking to aliens: the wonderment of meeting wholly different species with some genuinely flavoursome writing to describe them, but you always have the same three options to exhaust and it turns the alien into the mundane almost immediately.

I suspect I'll keep putting time into this here and there, mainly to find cool pictures, but perhaps also to see if I can scratch a surface and find anything beneath it. Yet, as a game to play, there's something that might be fatally lacking here: in the end, everything is the same, and there's not much you can do with it. It's cleverly constructed to keep you busy with literal busy-work, but frankly that's not something I find very fulfilling. 

A universe where aliens are just waiting to tell you a word, to listen to and react to a word, or to be given a gift... it's not really very alive.

I really want to like this game, because it does feel like there are some interesting things about it and they've added a ton of stuff over the years to make it more the game it was originally supposed to be, but I just struggle to find the fun in it.

The new player experience quite honestly [i]sucks[/i]. You can't change any of the settings until you're in-game (which is terrible), and the game doesn't pause while the menu is open (which would be fine on its own...), so by the time I'd managed to do stuff like disable motion blur I'd literally caught on fire and died. In the tutorial. Judging by what other people I've talked to have said I just have [i]incredibly[/i] bad luck with the RNG when starting new saves, because all three times I did my starting and second planets were miserable disasters that made it much harder and much less fun to get started on. I could maybe forgive that, but the UI is pretty unpleasant too, with menus moving around in the opposite direction from my mouse and weird click-and-hold to select things and stuff like that. Between this and going back to Mass Effect 2 for a bit recently I swear game devs are completely oblivious to the past like three decades of UI design improvements...

And like, exploring is actually kind of fun, and some of the weird stuff you find is kind of neat, and there's decent progression to finding new stuff, unlocking new things, getting new things you can do, etc. But even after all the updates a lot of planets don't look nearly as cool as the ones they highlight in trailers or that people post screenshots of, even running on ultra, and a lot of the procedurally generated stuff gets kinda samey after you've seen a few planets, so even the good bits just aren't quite good enough to get me to keep fighting through the frustrating stuff.

Oh well, not for me, but it's definitely for some people. I have friends with dozens or hundreds of hours in it, so if you're more into survival games than I am maybe you'll get more out of it than I did. Also it runs flawlessly for me on Linux through Proton; I just installed and clicked play.

Reviews.117046:
Overall Impression: Having previously seen such negative press on NMS some time ago and knowing that it still had mixed reviews, I was pretty skeptical to try it out. Ultimately, I'm glad that I did. After 50 hours, I feel like it was money well spent. The game is, however, a shadow of what it could have been and so I walk away a little disappointed.

Some of the good:

- The procedural generation of worlds, fauna and flora was surprisingly good. I was often impressed at the variety of discoveries in terms of living things and landscape. 

- The story-line and dialogue are unique and engaging, often dipping into some fascinating philosophical concepts. Not only were the characters and story interesting, there was also a depth of emotion to it I don't usually expect from a game. I felt welcome as the "traveler-friend".

Some of the bad: 
*Note that most of the bad aspects seemed to creep up while I was playing multiplayer with my wife.

- LOTS of very annoying glitches. At so many point we tumbled into very irritating pitfalls in the game mechanics, that would then send us searching through forums to determine how we might repair the problem. For example "oh yes, you can no longer build your base because you had two almost identical quests, and you completed one while having the other one selected, now you have to start over" 

My wife's character and spacecraft were constantly lagging and glitching from my perspective, even though  my PC and internet are far beyond basic requirements. This doesn't happen with any other game. Also, if we rename our ships or planets, that new name is not visible to the other.... eliminating one of the core aspects of the game (the element of sharing discovery) 

- Base building is dismally shallow. For a game that has so much variability in the worlds, the number of available components for base building is brutally small. It feels very much like a halfhearted afterthought, and frankly doesn't compare to other base builders. 

- Galaxy navigation is infuriatingly awkward. I'm used to 4X navigation in games like Sins of a Solar Empire or Stellaris. In NMS it is absolutely painful. 

- The playability drops of steeply at around the 40 hour mark, which I found extremely disappointing. I spent the first 20 hours in wonder thinking "oh man... this game has so much depth, I can't wait to see where it takes me". Another 20 hours later and I bottomed out on most tech trees, and quests went from unique and creative to abysmally repetitive. 

Try it, it's fun. Just know that the promised complexity and depth bottoms out pretty fast. 

Ultimately, this is like the foundations of a much better game they could have made.

The things that ruined the game for me:

1. The writing. Whatever story is going on is so very cryptic I don't feel any involvement in it. Everyone talks in riddles, and I have no desire to wrap my head around it.

2. The progression. There are quests related to specialists you hire for your base, but by the time I got the specialists I already bought the blueprints the quests rewarded from the Anomaly. I assume the Anomaly was introduced to the game later than other content, and it renders that content irrelevant.

3. The lack of variety. Sure, everything looks different with procedural generation, but behaves pretty much the same. You can visit a million different planets, but if you stop at ten you won't really miss anything.

The most fun I had with the game was building a base. It's very satisfying how the structures connect and how fast one can erect an impressive looking dwelling. However, different categories of structures don't play well with each other, so you have to find tweaks and workarounds for simple things like having paving around the base or stairs leading to the entrance.

I have not played this game before, I never got on the OG train. 
At time of review, Dec. 14th 2020, this game is barely ok. I don't like recommending games that are barely ok. 
NMS is a good example of how far we still have to go in making complex procedural generation work for us. 
I can tell there's a lot of work that's been put into this game, but NMS still faces a monolithic problem. 
The first time you load into the game and walk around the planet is and will be your experience with the game in almost its entirety. 
Play the game for 10 minutes, then ask yourself if this is what you want most of your experience with the game to be. If not, spend your money elsewhere. There is no plot (no, there isn't), there are no characters, and all other features feel fundamentally shallow. 
I don't want to suggest grand ideas for expansions to make the game into something worth remembering (aside from hello game's already notable turnaround); kudos to hello games if they figure out how to turn this game into something remarkable. 
Instead, I'm going to list what I want to see changed in terms of QoL improvements. What follows are a list of general gripes, minor gripes, and nitpicks that are largely responsible for turning my experience from a hesitant thumbs up to a frustrated thumbs down. 
-Let me see freighter class without having to speak to the captain
-Let me at least build technology that auto-refills my gear
-The less time I spend in my inventory the better and I spent way too much time in there
-Add ship customization and/or let me put in the work to find higher class ships rather than hoping they show up (the same for freighters)
-I never saw a multi-tool in the space station greater than B, I only got a hold of an A class out on a planet. Never even saw a S class
-You guys made cool anomalies for me to "stumble" across in space, but half of them I can't even interact with...why?
-The derelict freighter was interesting for the first 15 seconds inside because of the forced change of pace, but was otherwise unremarkable and not worth either the time nor 5mil you asked from me
-The technology upgrade system feels plastic and gimmicky. I get an upgrade and it shows me percentage ticks on numbers that ultimately don't mean all that much. The upgrade system is about as interesting as upgrades are hard to come by. I.E. not very.
-Make a separate tab for repeatable quests
-Let me teleport to my freighter
-Let me save my base schemas so I can transfer my freighter base layout
-Why my are my freighter scouts incompetent? You're telling me they own a giant space ship but have no idea how to repair it and need me to come fix it for them? Instead turn it into a "help fix scenario" where without my support it'll take X minutes before the ship is available again but if I come fix it immediately then I can use the ship immediately
-Let me teleport to my freighter scouts
-Instead of scouts automatically upgrading after going on expeditions, let them upgrade slowly or not at all. Then, allow me to fly/teleport to those ships to speak with the captain to customize crew and install upgrade modules and upgrade the ship class 
-Fix the "find all plants/animal/wildlife" quest, I had it since the start and was never able to finish it. Let me build gear that will help me find the remaining plant/animal/wildlife I need to finish everything on a planet
-You have quests that give me unlockables, but also let me unlock those unlockables before the quest. If that happens, at least give me something else so it doesn't feel like I wasted upgrade points

Quests are not a default "good" way to establish motivation for a player in general. 
With that said, here are more general problems
-There is no motivation to farm
-There is no motivation to use exo gear (aside from the sub, I never got to the mech)
-There is no motivation to stay on one planet for an extended time aside from resource farming which is tedious. Maybe consider making resource deposits bigger, maybe on the more advanced stars? 
-There is no motivation to build anything larger than what you need to escape storms. 
-COMPLIMENT: Storms are an example of a decent motivator. "Oh no, a storm. I need to build a shelter or I'll have to hide in the ground." There's a natural sense of urgency, especially in the more intense storms. 
-There is no motivation to go to the red/green/blue starts except for a single element type
-There is no motivation to interact with the wildlife. The ability to ride them is not enough (nor farm, see above). 
-There is no motivation to build good relations with a race or, at least, I didn't see the point
-There is no motivation to do missions for races
-There's not really much of a reasons to do mission in general
-The community stuff is not enough to establish motivation to do missions with others
If I think of anything else I'll add it. Regardless of my opinions, respect to HG for all their hard work. This game has come a long way since what I saw on release.

If you look at NMS, assuming you never heard about the launch issues you'd still be impressed. It offers a rich, vibrant world filled endless possibilities. Yes there is some early grind, but there is enough balance in the game that it can be overcome and isn't a detraction.

The story is meh, not very engaging and actually can be a little frustrating. I didn't buy into the story at all, and actually found it non-sensicle. But you can ignore it, and it is a means to an end..which is the universe.

You have to recognise where NMS has come from, and how much effort the devs have put into it to make it what it is today - at no cost. No DLC, no paid for add ins like Elite is now trying. It started as an overhyped shit show and has come out trumps. Star Citizen is still alpha ware at this point, Elite is trying to reinvent itself and NMS just keeps delivering.

Yeah i'm sure i'll tire of it past 300 hours, but there is always more to explore. Out of the 3 new age space simulators this one has decisively won. In 2050 when Star Citizen is eventually released, or the fraud proceeding have started i'm sure we'll all look back and still be amazed at the turnaround Hello Games completed.

Reviews.117371:
No Man's Sky is one of those Sandbox/Open World exploration games that I can't recommend enough. It's an absolutely stunning game in sheer size as well as aesthetics, so be prepared to do a lot of exploring.

Rest assured that this is not the same game that it was at release. Each free(!) update has added so much in way of content and streamlining that few other games have matched. It's one of the best bang-for-your-buck games you can buy when it comes to free content updates. I've played this game since it first released (on PS4), and while I was in the minority who liked it then, it's astronomically (no pun intended) better now. 

That being said, this game still could be optimized much better. The UI for the menus and such can still be a hassle to navigate, and the tutorials, while better than they used to be, are still sometimes a pain to get through considering you have to redo them every time you start a new save. Bugs can also be an issue, especially when new major updates come out (it usually takes them two patches or so after to fix). Luckily, developer Hello Games is quick to address these issues.

This is one of those games that is very much about the journey rather than the destination (think of how Sea of Thieves handles its gameplay). There are goals and tasks the game sets for you, but the beauty and the "meat" of the game is the exploration and discovery. If you are one that likes reaping big in-game rewards for playing, this game is likely not for you. However, I like these types of games because you can really pick up wherever you left off with no trouble.

Just a few extra notes: the beginning loading screen is always lengthy but there are no other loading screens in the game outside of the one that plays when you warp to another system. The soundtrack is wonderful as well and actively changes depending on what you are doing in-game. Finally, a totally different note here, but this game uses the Vulkan API. DO NOT BUY if your graphics system cannot run it and/or you don't know how to fiddle with drivers and such.

Other than that, it's pretty much what it says it is! I do recommend it, but only if you know you would get enjoyment out of a game like this.

Man has a ton changed in the past few years. I purchased No Man Sky again on the PC a few months back after having retried it on the PS4. I am astonished with how much the game has progressed. Is it to the point where it matches the trailers? Almost... we are certainly getting there.

As a few other reviewers have pointed out, No man Sky has turned into one of the biggest 180* development stories of our time. 

From being a lying pile of shit to a game that can actually hold its own. I have two files going currently; One in creative where I just mess around, and one in normal where Im trying to "play as intended"

Original review:
"No, no, guys. It's a good game now."

Icons and keymappings regularly glitch out. So far only 1 crash in 7 hours, but game alt tabs pretty regularly. 2 times I couldn't even load into the game.

The biggest problem is that even if the game didn't have bugs that kinda fix themselves after a restart, the gameplay is mediocre.
The game has basebuilding, but Space Engineers does everything better + you can build spaceships and vehicles in that game.
The game has space combat, but Everspace does everything better. In this game, there aren't even controls to strafe left/right or controls to lift/lower.
The game has small alien outposts, "missions" and interactions with different species, but it doesn't come close to anything in Mass Effect 1 or 2; or Star Wars KOTOR in terms of quality or even overall atmosphere.

The core gameplay is grinding for materials to get money, to buy more inventory slots, to buy "better spaceships". In reality, the ships don't differ that much. I used an explorer type ship and all fights were way too easy.
The game basically has no story. What it has is a placeholder to remind you that there are a lot of planets and you should go check them out.

What was fun?
For me the fun part was expanding the base on planets, under water and inside the huge frigate. I also enjoyed figuring out different ways to make money in the game. Some of the planets were also pretty whacky/ goofy, which made exploring a few planets fun.

What this game needs is a sense of danger on some planets, so there is a reason to scan animals and different plants. 
Also, it needs to make the space fights more intense so there is a reason to use fighter ships with different weapons.
It also needs a reason to want to talk to different aliens. Right now, "talking" to aliens is basically the same as pressing X to farm minerals.

I played this game for about 100 hours to complete the main story and complete "side quests" just to make sure I'm not being overly critical.

Yes, everything you've heard about this game is [was] true- I bought this game here on Steam when it released. I played for 12 hours. The visuals were disappointing, the controls were strange, there was no tutorial, and there was really no objective. On top of that, the resources and how they worked were, well, as the entire game was- unfinished and broken. After my 12 hours, I closed the game and never opened it again. Not necessarily because I didn't enjoy it, but because the starship's launch thrusters were fueled by plutonium at the time, which was a very... rare resource. I had landed my ship on a deadly planet and could not find any plutonium within the range I could survive without dying to the harsh atmosphere. It was literally unplayable. There was no multiplayer, there was no... anything. It was a complete flop.

Now, hear me out. That was then. Things have changed. And that is an understatement. Only a couple years ago, I was out for breakfast with a friend. He asked me if I had No Man's Sky for my PS4. I told him I bought it on PC at release and never played it again. He told me that the game was better now, and that he would personally take me to Gamestop after breakfast and buy me a copy so we could play together. I soon learned all about the fall and rise of No Man's Sky.

This game is the greatest comeback in all of gaming- ever. The reason the game flopped so bad is because it was simple unfinished, and the partnership with Sony had pressured them into a release date that they never would be able to meet. But instead of leaving the broken mess they made and running off and disappearing with everyone's money, Hello Games sat down and got back to work and made the game that they had promised to deliver. For free. They made it right.

No Man's Sky is now everything and more than it was ever promised to be. Don't get me wrong, it does still leave some things to be desired and it does tend to suffer from the occasional long term very annoying bug. But considering how ambitious this game is, and how small the dev team is, and how far the game has come and so quickly, it is entirely forgivable. This is one of the best games I own. One of the only few games I still use my free time to play as an adult with limited time and lots of real world responsibilities. I have put over 250 hours into my main save on PS4 and I have recently returned to my PC save. I will say that on PC, this game is poorly optimized, but if you have even just a decent systems, playing with ultra settings, you should have very few problems. 

This game now is everything it was supposed to be and more, and more free updates are released multiple times every year- the devs actually listen to community suggestions and take them seriously. And the community is amazing too. The best there is. 

If you believe in second chances, this is the epitome of it. If you don't believe in second chances, you're wrong, and this game is more than enough to prove that.

When i first got this game it was as most of you know completely empty, it was very similar to Star Wars Battlefront (the remake) in that the visuals were amazing but it lacked almost everything else. No quests or meaning. And only randomly generated planets with almost no unique or interesting animals, minerals or plants. And the only difference between the planets was the color scheme or how many sentinels inhabited the planets. Now almost 4 years later it's definetly worth the money, with constant updates filled with content the game is finally up to par with what they promised.

I think they strayed from the idea of completely randomly generated worlds because they knew how implausible that plan was considering how far away we are from that kind of technology, so they have made a large amount of interesting animals and plants that are different in a way that makes every planet fit within a theme. The planets nature often correlates with the different climates that exist within the game, so a very warm planet will have animals and plants that fit that theme. So you might expect that some planets will seem exactly the same but because of the fact that there are so many combinations of things that can exist on a planet and because of the fact that you don't actually visit that many different planets in a playthrough it doesn't feel repetetive. 

The process of upgrading your gear is alot better now with the plethora of upgrades that exist that you can buy with nanites at both space station and the space anomaly. The process of learning the different languages is a fun idea but it gets repetetive after a while and it could be fleshed out more and i hope they do this in the future. The main story is good although alot of it is illusion of choice which feels very deceptive to me. I wish they would either make it so that choices matter or they just remove the choices that don't matter altogether because there is no need for different choices in this kind of story it's just a luxury that is good if executed correctly but not necessary. Also the missions can bug out sometimes and i wish there would be a better way to reset missions because its very annoying to get halted and having to warp to a black hole to fix it.

I haven't had the time to deep dive into the building aspect of the game too much because i've focused on the main quests and pimping out my kit and buying  a freighter instead of doing all the different specialist stations but i think that those missions you do for specialist are often very time consuming and boring i wish they would be streamlined into either longer quests where you can pick more stuff up along the way during other quests or maybe they just remove some of the quests needed to do get the different stations.

Also i understand that this is hard but the world doesn't feel as vibrant as many other games do maybe do to the fact that there is almost no memorable characters except the ones associated with the main quest line you never see characters on planets other than a few exceptions. An idea could be to make Aliens that are out mining or gathering stuff or maybe building bases, would add alot more to the feeling of the worlds cause right now the only one gathering anything is you or in some cases other players. 

Something i haven't touched on yet is the online component of the game and although it is a good basis on which to build on but it feels empty. There is actually no reason to ever be with eachother other than to do missions from the space anomaly together. The fact that everyone has their own quests makes it kinda awkward to play together. When me and my friends started playing this again i finished my quests before them and set off to do my quests while they got stuck because they died when they were getting the first hermetic seal. And after that point we almost never saw eachother again and my friends kinda stopped playing while i continued finishing the story on my own. So there has to be some reason for co-op and i think that there is room for making actual cities and stuff and maybe even make it abit like rust so that instead of having ai to help make the world feel vibrant you could devise a way of making players start their own cities and settlements. 

Everything else is pretty much where it should be i think. Sure they could improve alot of small stuff but in general the game is fun and there's alot to do and i'm not getting bored of it yet though i don't think i'll be playing it after december 10th cause you know, biggest game of all time coming out soo... I'll see you in another year No Man's Sky

Hello Games can confort themselves with the fact that me and alot of other people dont feel ripped off anymore. They can also be happy to know they have big potential for greatness if they think outside the box for new updates. The game has very good visuals and atmosphere but is missing something that defines it. It has alot of thing it could be but they haven't commited to an identity yet so they have the potential to take it to new levels that we've never seen before.

I heard great things of how this game has evolved and grown over the years so thought I'd dive in and enjoy it.

If this is what they call progress, I don't want to imagine the travesty that it must have been at launch.

Yes, there are plenty of things I like about it, but very quickly I grew to notice its flaws, of which there are many.

The graphics are nice and the worlds quite enjoyable to explore, but after only a few planets you begin to notice the patterns and repetition. You go to places that look the same except for a light filter and collect stuff the same way. You scan things which at first is oooooo, but after a few planets just is. 

Once I figured out how to go into first person view the game got a lot more polished to me (no more clanky 3rd person animations). That didn't change the gameplay enough though.

The premise is that you go to planets and mine resources, yet the deposits on your scanner are for only tiny quantities compared to other sources and therefor completely pointless to travel for. Oh yes, and these deposits won't leave your scanner even once you've mined them because it'll still think there's some left.

This is made even worse once you unlock extractors. You find a hotspot, build a little mini base and come and collect the tens of millions a day. You don't even have to be online for it to harvest for you so you can log off at night, log on in the morning and make so much money that every other form of capitalism is pointless.

The economy is also a total mess, with a unit of salt selling for the same as a unit of cobalt, other materials being all over the place made even worse by the unbalanced refining system. For example, it didn't take me long to notice that 2 oxygen (80 unit value) and 1 chlorine (600 unit value) = 6 chlorine (3,600 value)... And because it multiplies a base ingredient, you're essentially creating 2,920 every single time - which only takes a fraction of a second. This problem is mirrored across the whole economy, from mats to ships.

Now lets talk ships. If you were in a space station, you'd assume you could swap your ship out? No... the only logical place to swap ships is the only place you can't. The space stations are also the main place you find new ships to buy. Why is this a problem you ask? because you can trade in your current ship for a discount, but you'll usually find ships you want to buy while doing other activities, meaning you would probably want to keep the ship you're in too. I suppose this isn't a problem if you abuse the economy to make tons of money but once you get a full hanger of 6-7 ships, then it becomes a chore.

And a chore is what this game's UI makes it. It's honestly one of the worst UIs I've ever seen, and even on PC feels like it was designed entirely for consoles. You want to split a stack of resources? trade a certain number of units on the market? well, get ready to scroll through the numbers... that's right, there's no way to type in the number you want (the way every inventory manager I've ever seen allows) and you're stuck with scrolling at an increasing speed, stopping, starting, going up and down to tweak it just right. 

The same sort of awkwardness is true for most things - the early game biofuel generator will only accept EVERY scrap of the fuel you have on you, has no shut off, and wastes all your hard found stuff when you only needed to turn it on for a minute.

Conversations go the same way, with lots of long pauses and listen I just want to right click out, I don't want to wait, left click, wait, left click, wait, left click, wait, okay now I can right click and leave. There's plenty of interactions that will kick you out of transactions as well, making you go through a bunch of dialogue to buy something else.

Space flight and combat is kind of clunky and dull, you can also endlessly blast asteroids for rare elements like gold, silver, and platinum. This again affects how the economy works, but at the same time, if you have a single money farm as the community seems to call them, you can just buy anything and everything you want so there's not much point in gathering. 

Inventory management is also terrible. I'm honestly sick of typing insults about this game now but it's just not well thought out. At all. It's just the worst inventory system I've used in years, full stop, period.#

Ground combat isn't great either... just felt blah. 

And to the main point of the game, exploration... you'll be going to the same landmarks time after time after time. They all look virtually identical and even the odd cool one you find gets old after you've seen a dozen in exactly the same state of disrepair and layout.

Wish I hadn't wasted my money, but that said I got 40+ hours out of it and it was on sale, so I can't complain too much. I just wouldn't recommend the game to anyone else. Seriously, just go buy Space Engineers for half the price, it may not have good combat either, but it's Lego in space, and the base building in No Man's Sky is embarrassing.
