My play hours may look low on PC, but my time playing it on console is beyond 500 hours, so I have plenty of experience playing the game, it's just not on Steam.

No Man's Sky always held a special place in my heart and game library, and is one I find myself returning to time and time again; this game always was fun, even back in 2016 when I bought it on console. And I truly love what Hello games has done with the project, and feel humbled seeing both the game and its community grow into something brilliant. But you haven't come to read my soppy story of adoration, you want pros and cons, reasons for why you should play this game or not. Well, here you go.

PROS
+The Community is stellar like the universe it inhabits; random players you will never have met before will often seek to help you in your ventures, either by gifting you items to help earn Units or leading you to places of interest. The Galactic Hub Project, a fan-based community, is one of many unofficial guilds of travellers.
+The universe is massive. This could possibly be the biggest "open world" game made to-date. There are flaws to this massive size, but we'll touch on that soon.
+Much of the game is inspired by retro sci-fi novel art, with a few subtle references to other pop-culture in the sci-fi genre.
+The music is freaking amazing.
+The story arc is mysterious, and is scattered over numerous sub-plots so it's not all in one place, which encourages you to explore and find all the pieces. (Artemis quest, for example, is given to you right away, whilst others you can only obtain by hiring someone specific or buying a certain object.)
+The game receives occasional free updates, and regular patches, and is still the core focus of Hello Games projects.
+More stuff too. Honestly, it has gone from a fun game to an absolute masterpiece.

CONS
-The universe is so big that diversity in the past was poor. You'd land on a bunch of planets and beside the weather effects they weren't that different. Recent Origins update expanded the diversity, but the issue still remains a bit. Plus, with the universe size, you may not see another play naturally for some time, if at all.

I love this game so much, I wish I could do it true justice in a review, but I can't. This game is an experience, one you need to try yourself to know if it's right for you or not. Though, truly, I encourage you to try it in VR; this game feels like it was always meant to be played on VR.

10/10 Prawn Curry.

Reviews.117722: I wanted to like this game, I really did. After all the effort that Hello Games put into redeeming the catastrophic launch of this title I wanted it to be great. But ultimately, the real core issue this game has is a lack of content. Now, that might seem like a weird complaint for a game world that is effectively infinite, but it's true. After you've visited every type of structure once you've basically seen all the unique, non-procedural generated stuff there is to see. Even the procedurally generated planets start to feel samey when you've seen enough of them. As animals/plants/rocks may look different, but gameplay wise they're functionally the same. Enemy variety is extremely limited, 3 types of robot, like 4 preset hostile alien types, 2 types of hostile spaceship and the rare procedurally generated predators. Combat feels pretty flat and the AI is very exploitable. The base-building was interesting but extremely glitchy for me, your mileage may vary. Though from what I've read my experience seems to be the norm. Making money takes way too long the honest way, making chlorine is 100x faster and easier but very unrewarding. I also feel like this game doesn't respect the players time. For example: You go to a cell tower and get your quest, you need to get/make an item. You get the item(s) you need for a quest, the quest updates and tells you to go to the closest cell tower. You go there and after climbing the thing you have a brief exchange where the guy tells you to bring the thing to someone else, you do so. Go back to ANOTHER cell tower to check in with your guy and advance the plot. Why do I have to keep going to the cell tower? Clearly I have the same device in my ship, they call me on it all the time. Also, why can't I turn in more than one quest at a time at the space station? Why do I even have to go back to the space station to turn in a quest? Why is there a delay every time I want to collect mission rewards? Why can't I skip NPC dialog, especially when I've heard it all before? Why can't I recharge my equipment all at once instead of having to do it individually? Why does the impulse drive not take me directly to the place I want to go most of the time? Why does it take so long to convert matter into other types of matter at a smelter? Especially when you limit the player from building more than 4 close together. Lastly, The gameplay feels very unconnected from the main plot, which consists almost entirely of fetchquests with esoteric dialog dumps in between. Really, the main questline is just confusing from start to finish. It lacks compelling characters or any sort of urgency to make you feel invested. The 5 dudes you meet during the main plot spend their time spouting cryptic nonsense and answering your questions with philosophy more often than not. And the ending is pretty predictable and kind of a cop out, it's a: [spoiler] Reset Button Ending [/spoiler]. Multiplayer could help add some variety, but you could go a whole 65ish hour play-through without ever seeing a unknown player outside the dedicated player hub. I never did, I never even found a previously visited system unless I gate traveled to one. The universe of No Man's Sky is vast and empty, what content it has is stretched to the breaking point. You will likely see all the unique game-play elements within 20 hours of starting the game. After that it's just samey planets and samey fetch quests. Hello games deserves praise for their support of this game post launch, but I can't recommend a game I don't really enjoy.

When I first acquired this game it hadn't been refined to its current level. Coming from Elite Dangerous, my first thoughts were that the colour palette was unbelievably lurid (colourful, sure, but hardly representing anything I was familiar with). Once I had played for a while, however, I began to appreciate that what Hello Games had done was create something very unique and enjoyable. Now those same colours are appealing, the creatures that walk, wobble, fly or roll over the landscape, intriguing and the mid game game-play very captivating and enjoyable. Once the grind of the first few hours is behind you and you begin to get money and nanites, things settle down and you can progress nicely.

The central story and side-quests are there, but the game doesn't care if you follow or complete them. This is great as it let's you live in the game's universe without being forced down any particular path. Everything is your choice but you'll miss a lot along the way as there isn't really much by way of detailed explaining except on the web. So my advice is to do your research as you play for the most fulfilling experience. 

I still don't like certain design aspects of the game; the shape of the normal spaceships is one. They are just a collection of basic shapes that are stuck together; seemingly at randomly. In fact, I don't own any. I discovered from the web that a better looking class of ships existed. Exotics. These ARE well designed. I own six each configured to do different things with my main craft kept multipurpose and nearly maxed out. As yet, I haven't explored the living ship side of things - and probably won't having seen what's involved.

Another strange thing to get used to is the rather random manner in which new things have been added. Take the whole Freighter/Frigate side of the game. Nearly every time I send one particular S class frigate out it comes back damaged. It is rather odd why my top rated crew can't fix some Tiny Motors or Servos that seem to be the most breakage prone equipment I've ever seen. And whoever it was at Hello Games that decided having the frigates composed of a maze of passages that twist all over the ship eventually leading to the damaged parts, clearly wants to put people off playing that side of the game! Why can my crew not carry spares - even if I have to buy or manufacture them? The other frustration is that you cannot sell the ships. In fact there is no mechanism to do this with any ship. You exchange them. It seems where-ever the manufacturing plants are they are not known to you. I would really like to own something that hasn't been around the galaxy a few times. And in the case of frigates, you can only not use them. I would actually like to be able to sell of my overly fragile ones, or be able to armour them better.

The Exocraft are fun, but in a very, almost indestructible arcade way. They plough through the landscape destroying rocks and trees and dive headlong off cliffs and just shake it off. Face a sentinel walker though and something that survives all that becomes suddenly as fragile as paper.. Really? This area feels unbalanced, or unfinished, while being nonetheless great fun.

All in all a great, enjoyable, original game which improves with every update. Well worth your time and money.

Hmm, how to start this off. 

Purchased the game for $60 on the Xbox (windows pc version) App.
Paid another $30 for the same game on Steam.
Total hours of play between both platforms is 200+ hours.

My recommendation is: Worth the money during Rona 2020.

Here is a question from me to you. Have you paid money for the game and 14.99 a month just to play the game you bought? Or maybe you don't pay a dime for the game but have to pay for cash shop items just to progress? Or how about pay nothing at all and get wrecked by everyone else who whaled out to be 100x better than you all the while the game calls itself "f2p friendly"?

No Man's Sky doesn't do any of that. You pay $60 for the game, or $30 if you get it on sale through steam, and that's it. You are NOT beat to death by a barrage of ad's every 2 seconds or being forced to watch ad's just to move to the next stage of the game. There are no cash shops, there is absolutely no way to spend real money to get ahead or make things go faster in this game. This game is a hell of a grind and i love it. 

The developers are still "developing" NMS and patches and updates are coming out all the time. 

If that was all there is to know about the game then my recommendation would be justified, but there is so much more to this game than the positives over every other game that currently exists in this micro transaction world we are forced to live in, but allow me to go into the cons of the game that i've found real fast.

The game is NOT perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but looking back at my time through the last 20 years of gaming, there hasn't been a single game that i would say is "perfect". If there was then all these other games wouldn't need to exist. The game does have bugs and glitches, a lot of games do and a lot more don't even have developers working on them anymore. 

The game is worth the money if you like survival games and like what you see on Youtube. Honestly i recommend everyone that is interested in this game to go and check up a bunch of different opinions on the game via Youtube.

Heres the thing, its not a survival craft game because: you can buy everything you need, outside of permadeath mode you have to actually work hard to die, and honestly there isnt much in terms of things to survive against besides enviornmental hazards that can be largely ignored when yous tart producing industrial levels of sodium.  All that said it is a very relaxing sort of game that has a lot to offer in terms of a casual sims like base builder in space.  The open world (really universe) is kinda neat but a lot of the planets feel the same no matter where you are, there are not differing enviornments in a single planet, and the biome is uniform surface-wide.  Also materials are exhaustive in terms of what can be found 100m from where you land, no matter where it is.  So really the planets are not nearly as large as they appear to be, despite being to some respectable scale they really do not feel varried.  I have a hard time justifying this game over the following:

Subnatuica: superior exploration and survival mechanics
Warframe: superior gear upgrades, unlockables and comabt (not the same genre but still)
Eve Onlnie: superior mmo space mechanics with aprty and ship customization
Minecraft: better crafting (this goes without saying)
Dead island: better customization pertaining to weaponry

I could go on but the gist is that NMS while having a wide breadth of different gameplay loops does not achieve any of them in a deep or dynamic way.  You wake up, get resources, fix ship, find station, find new planet, build base, get resources, upgrade in perpetuity and thats about how the game works.  Threats do not get worse, the main threat you face comes in the way of largely passive drones that can be easily avoided, mega-fauna that dies almost instantly to the non-upgraded starting tool, and ships that may attack you and actually pose a threat but are kinda rare and not related to survival planet side.  The enviorment is about as hostile you could expect, which is good, but even on "survival mode" dealing with ti is about equivalent to dealing with hunger in minecraft, or hiding in a cave.

NMS is a very relaxing game more in line with the sims, than it is with something like Rust, The Forrest, We Happy Few, or Subnautica.  I think its nice to toy around in as a sort of sandbox, kind of like garrys mod, but I cannot recomend it as a survival game as there really isnt all that much to survival.  If you wanna play around with a terraforming mining laser, and build a neat looking base, deffinately a good experiance.  If you are looking for a survival game, or game with a robust crafting element, or combat, or exploration then Id say give it a pass.

Will say I respect the dev quite a lot for continuing the project, and it has come a long way, it just isnt there yet for what its trying to be at the price its asking (I say that even at half off tbh, Id say its worth about $10-$15 max depending on what you are looking for).

I was given No Man's Sky as a Christmas gift from a friend, and I am very grateful for it, and for him.

The love of classic sci-fi runs throughout No Man's Sky, reflected in its aesthetics, background lore, and its premise: the wonder of exploration, with subtle undercurrents of dread. I recognize starship design elements from Star Wars and Battlestar Galactica, and the conversations with aliens remind me of themes in Star Trek. There are probably plenty of other little references as well, of which I have only found a few so far.

The main story I've seen thus far, without trying to spoil things, seems to be trying to get into who you are and what's behind everything (which, like good sci-fi at least since H.G. Well's "War of the Worlds", can get you thinking about our own world and universe).

While yes, explore enough and you'll find elements and patterns repeating in different combinations, that's okay. That's just  you getting the hang of how the universe works, which helps you build routines to streamline things as you go for bigger or more particular things. Hello Games have been working on adding new things, features, and perhaps systems for variety and to do even further justice for this vast universe. The initial learning curve was delightful, and as of this review there is still much more for me to get into.

If you or someone you know would resonate with the spirit of this game, and if you have the time for it, then No Man's Sky is a great gift for yourself or another.

I'll be quick and hit the good and bad points here. We all know the basics by now.

Pros: 
- Huge open-world experience, obviously. You really can just hop around the universe in your spaceship, land on any planet, do whatever you want there, etc. 

- Planets are pretty neat. Yeah they're repetitive, and not just in assets. The assets repeat for sure, but so do a lot of other world features. Still, it's feels worthwhile to search for new and interesting places to explore and even boring planets have plenty of points of interest to explore. It reminds me of Skyrim in this way- even if it's boring wilderness, you'll always find a cave or an abandoned cabin or stranded traveler etc. 

-There's a LOT to do. Trade, explore, quest, build a fleet of ships, make friends with aliens... like you really shouldn't get bored.

Cons
- Prepare to play a lot of inventory management simulator, especially in the beginning. Obnoxious mostly because it doesn't make any sense. I can hold 87,000 more carbon but I can't pick up that flower? Come on. Inventory space is upgradeable later but like... why? This game has hundreds if not thousands of unique items.

- You are forced to quest to unlock basic blueprints and I fucking hate it. Tell me why I have a freighter with 6 ships, 18mil on hand, bases across the galaxy, but my base overseer is sending me on a fetch quest for herbs. And my reward? A blueprint for items I should already be able to build!! In fact the first 10-15 hours of this game (depending on how much you mess around) are just one long tutorial which unlocks the most basic objects like a SAVE POINT (yes you need to craft save points and no you don't know the recipe to start). I'm 27 hours into this save and am still having very basic crafting blueprints trickled to me via main quests and base quests.

The PACING of this game is horrendous. The "this is definitely not a tutorial" tutorial *sucks*. It somehow overexplains and underexplains in its determination not to feel like an on-rails experience. The rest of the game is a lot of fun and you can easily spend hundreds of hours on a single file. I recommend this game but know that it has some serious design flaws which definitely won't be fixed or changed.

Reviews.117846:
Almost everyone who plays games has heard of No Man’s Sky. The unbelievable hype before and bitter disappointment after it got released. Unkept Promises and lies. But Hello Games did, what most developers don’t do. They kept working on their game and released update after update. In 2020 you could say, that No Man’s Sky is finaly the game it was promised before 2016 and more.
And this is the reasonI mostly recommend this game…

BUT!
There is also a side, you barely hear. Because the hype around this game gets dangerously close to pre 2016 NMS. This game has tons of issues, bugs and glitches.

Console port:
First of all on PC you can really feel that it is a console port. The menu, keybinding and options really don’t make much sense on PC. The UI-Design is straight up bad. You have to click multiple times to get stuff done, other times you can’t even use the mouse, even i fit would make sense (looking at you galaxy map) and crafting in this game is more a punishment than a fun activity due to this.
The whole game feels like you would run a console exclusive in a PS4 emulator, not like a PC game.
Also please Hello Games, it is 2020, let me change options in the main menu, not after I start a save.

The Bugs:
The game crashed multiple times when I played it, I fell through the ground a few times, died, lost all items, stuck NPCs, clipping bugs, starships spawning inside your base…just to name a few issues I encountered during 30h of playing. 
The sad thing is, if you search for solutions to the problems you have, you will soon realize that these bugs and problems have been in this game for YEARS.

Missing features:
This game is supposed to be an open world exploring game. But the player can't map, can't mark, can't save POI, the galaxy map can only be opened in space, there are no world maps, the limited markers you can set disappear if you are not in range...you see where this is going. There is tons of features you would assume are in this game, but just aren't.

I just wish Hello Games wouldn’t release half assed Updates like crazy and instead would work out the issues, bugs and missing features. The game itself is fun and until now I never had the feeling that something is missing content wise.

All in all this game is fun, but the issues dampen the whole fun by a lot. So I wouldn’t recommend this game for the full prize. Get this game when it’s on sale.

This game...

I have been playing this game since release, even in a state where many people deemed it too poor to play, but I never gave up on it.

The game was over-hyped; so many grand promises were made that weren't seen when the game first came out, and people negatively rated the game for this...heavily. The developers did their best to appease those who weren't happy with the game, then fell silent for a long time...but they never stopped listening, and they also never gave up on this game. Those promises weren't delivered on release, but they were kept and were worked on to build the game they dreamed of. Over time, new updates for the game were being released; free updates which added more and more to the game: base building, better planets, better story, the multiplayer everyone wanted. What was promised was being delivered because this team of developers never gave up on their game... The story of this team, the story of the game itself, is of redemption. I've built so many memories with friends and while playing solo, explored and uncovered secrets in many systems, met so many nice people throughout this game's universe. I've seen this game grow first-hand throughout the years...and I feel like everybody who has the time to play this game...and never has...should definitely give it a try.

This is why I recommend this game. A game which, despite it's rough launch, managed to redeem itself to be one of the best space sims ever. Thank you for taking your time to read this. Have a good day. <3

I had no hype for this game four years ago. However, I was aware that it had a terrible launch, but the game has been improved since apparently. I started playing just after Origins update was released.

What you're getting here is a space exploration and survival focused game. You document creatures, flora, and minerals per planet. In my experience these work pretty well. There are varied landscapes and some interesting fauna (or lack thereof) to see on the vast amounts of planets that you can explore. Admittedly I would've loved more variety on the fauna and flora seeds for the procedural generation, but there's enough to see and interact with to entertain you for quite some time.

Whilst the game encourages you to be an explorer, you can also opt to build bases that can act as your home or serve as outposts to build resource extractors. Personally I really enjoy this aspect of the game. From the prefabs or parts you're given, you can build simple homes to big farms - whatever suits you. Later on you can also acquire big space freighters that will act as your orbital base and starship garage.

Speaking of starships: flying one from one planet onto another is satisfying. There are a variety that can be purchased, they handle differently and have different stat bonuses depending on their classes. Unfortunately as of writing, there is no way to customize your starship. It would have been great to have that ability. Combat is decent but there is certainly room for improvement in terms of variety of enemies. Combat isn't the focus of this game in general, but what is here is more than serviceable.

The game isn't perfect by any stretch. On single-player it runs fine and I haven't encountered game breaking or serious bugs. Certain issues we have encountered seem to be exclusive to multiplayer. Most noticeable is the base components keep unloading and loading during multiplayer. It can cause some serious base building issues especially with more than 5 people (2 fireteam).

There are a lot more aspects that I haven't covered, but overall it is a decent game for $30. If you're interested but still on the edge about it, I suggest grabbing on sale.

Absolutely brilliant game that is well worth the full price.

Pros:
- Still actively developed with regular updates that add new content
- Devs consistently listen to the community and deliver requested new content, even when it's challenging
- After over 200 hours exploring there's still new and interesting things to discover
- Very open ended. Once you've been through the first part of the story (which is really just an extended tutorial) there's so much you can do, and it's entirely up to you what you focus on.
- Amazing, friendly, generous player base

Cons:
- The biggest issue is quality. There are numerous fairly significant (albeit not game breaking) bugs that have continued to exist across numerous update cycles with no attempt made to fix them. I'd love it if the next update or two focused entirely on bug fixes and QoL updates.
- Updates could use more QA. I often wait for at least one patch to come out before jumping in post-update because otherwise you're likely to run into bugs.
- Not well optimized. This isn't surprising given the scope of the game and the fact that it's developed by a very small team, but it is frustrating that in VR my 1080ti can only play the game at medium graphics settings.
- The thing that adds the most 'challenge' to permadeath/survival isn't increased damage etc, it's the tiny stack sizes that make inventory management (already challenging early game in normal mode) a nightmare

Verdict: 8.5/10

I am somehow disappointed after I found out that No Man's Sky does not emulate our Universe in terms of sizes (like SpaceEngine), but instead planets and solar systems are scaled down by a factor of a hundred. I understand, there must be a balance between realism and gameplay. Outer space is vast, if it is indeed a 1:1 representation of our Universe then travel would be tedious; ships and settlements would be almost invisible in the immense void, if they gone pass you it would be in just a split second because the average speed of objects in space is in the range of kilometers per second.

Those rocks should be spared to certain areas only, like planet rings and belts.

Fantastic game. I saw the Origins trailer and decided to give it a try. I haven't turned it off since.

The exploration is addicting. Planet to planet, galaxy to galaxy, endless beauty and adventure. Jaw dropping scenery. Star gazing at rings of massive planets in an endless sea of bio-luminescent grass, running though lush jungles with exotic creatures the size of freighters, gliding through underwater meadows filled with glittering coral reefs, waking eldritch abyssal horrors, exploring vast cave systems large enough to hold entire cities, caverns encrusted with jewel toned flora -- the sights are truly endless. 

I love turning on my favorite podcast, hopping in my spaceship and losing myself for hours. Crafting and gathering is meditative and enjoyable. The lore is rich and exciting to uncover. Combat is fun and engaging. Really, I have very few complaints with this game and it's absolutely one of my favorites of all time. 

In-game tutorials are limited -- so figuring out the interface and certain functionalities can be tricky. The only thing to remember is the game auto saves whenever you leave your starship. In the very beginning of the game I couldn't figure out where to find certain vital elements to stay alive in a toxic environment, but it's nothing a quick search can't resolve. It wasn't clear how to recharge exosuits and mining beams (you drag and drop the element over the tech icon), and I also wish I knew punching (Q on PC) collects minerals. 

I would recommend a quick 10 minute tutorial on YouTube to learn the basics -- or just jump right in and figure it out yourself. The good thing is no action you take will cause lasting damage to your game. Minerals can always be mined, items re-collected, quests retried, etc. Just don't forget the autosave and dive in -- I can promise you won't look back.

This game has been out for 4 years now. We all know the fiasco with the launch. The disappointment, outright lies, and severe over-hype. However, in those 4 years, the game has undergone extreme changes and improvements...for free. I haven't paid a single penny for any of the content, and there has been an incredible amount of released content, aside from buying the base game. 

The "updates" for this game haven't been small updates to fix a couple bugs. They have been massive additions, any other game would call them DLC, that affect the entirety of the game and how you can play it. Such as the Foundation update that introduced base building. Most games would release that as a DLC package. Pathfinder introduced vehicles. Atlas Rises introduced a story quest. Next update brought multiplayer. Abyss, Visions, Beyond, Synthesis, Exo Mech, Living Ship, Cross Play, Desolation, Origins, and Next Generation have all been large scale updates adding new ways to play and new content. If nothing else, this game has been a testament to how games should progress. Massive amounts of content for free. No charge for any of the content packages released. I'm not a fan of buying a $60 game and paying $20 for every addition of new content. Some games will end up costing you hundreds of dollars for the complete game, but not this one. 

I understand that charging for these updates that were promised game features prior to release would be very bad, more than likely suicidal for Hello Games, but I have to give them credit for all the years of hard work they have put into this game for free. I was extremely upset with the poor state of the game upon release, but they have since won back my trust. I cannot think of any developer that has been able to do that. I cannot think of any developer that has even TRIED to do that. Most just close down and start again under a new name. I nominated this game for the Labor of Love award for this reason. Can't think of any other game more deserving of this award.

This isn't my favorite game, not by far, but it is enjoyable and I don't feel like I got ripped off anymore. I feel that I have gotten my money's worth out of it, and I'm always keeping an eye on this game to see what else is in the mix.

Still utter garbage from a VR perspective (Valve Index). Don't believe the marketing lies that this fiasco has redeemed itself, or at least it hasn't from the perspective of being a VR title. Even in the highest graphics settings this looks like somebody made a joke about what graphics looked like in the 90s. Especially the clouds, although I'm pretty sure there were better looking clouds in the 90s. During my first start, instead of an awe inspiring sight, I was met with a confusing catastrophe of an experience, with bad graphics, way too many slightly random animals that apparently just follow an uninspired formula of four legs and some random mushrooms or gills growing on them here and there.

Despite having just crash landed and suffering from amnesia (which is beginning to be quite an irritating trope for these kinds of games), there is regular traffic in the skies, making it feel less like being on an actual alien planet that nobody has been on before and more like there are people who fly around here that just don't care that you're there. I have to admit that my playing time is very limited and that I'm only seeing things from the perspective of a new user who only uses VR, so compared to somebody who saw the original game on a monitor only and experienced all the improvements over time, my critique might appear a bit harsh or even downright wrong if there is something in the storyline to explain the constant flybys. But still, the planets seem crowded, especially with the amount of animals (like the prey doesn't run away from predators and it's like being in an overcrowded zoo rather than some alien savannah).

The terrain generation looks like a semi-perfect sine wave with some alien features stamped on every now and then. I saw a looney tunes-y rock on a mountain at one point, which made me chuckle, but that was partly also because it looked almost buggy, rather than like an actual rock formation. There were also pillar mountains that looked somewhat interesting, but they seem more slapped on than actually naturally formed (even though I have no concept of what a natural formation on an alien planet would actually be).

Flying in VR feels odd. Partly because there is a huge dead space, so you cannot really make small course corrections, but also because the joystick controls pitch and yaw while rolling is done with the thumb nub, which is about as unintuitive as you can make it. The starship cannot stop and hover, making landings particularly hard to get right. The sensitivity setting helps a bit, but it's still a complete joke. At least compared to other VR flying such as in VR VTOL, flying just isn't designed well in this game. Pulse Jumping for the first time was quite fun, but it still seems unresponsive in VR somehow.

The UI is simply atrocious in VR and doing something like dragging fuel from the inventory to a generator isn't even possible (you have to exit the inventory and open the generator inventory, then click on the slot and select which fuel). But it's difficult to explain the problems with the UI. It basically just sucks, even after you get over the initial unintuitiveness of it all. There are weird out of body experiences when interacting with machines, and sometimes it ends up being rotated such that the window you're supposed to interact with is behind you. Also, compared to Alyx where health is displayed on your gloves, in this game all the things are displayed as floating windows. Sometimes those windows decide to be behind other windows or behind walls. Also, why give people the choice to just leave instead of progressing with the story? The 

It's like they went through the motions but didn't have anybody actually play the thing or have any sense of what makes mining, crafting, building, exploration etc. actually fun. Gathering resources is basically aiming a pistol at a tree and getting a full inventory, then hauling that to a generator that eats up the carbon in a single minute. That wouldn't be as big of a problem if you could craft chests to keep the extra inventory in, or even turn off the generator. Crafting is pressing an empty inventory slot and clicking on what you want, which is about as fun as it sounds. I have to give some bonus points for not having to open the inventory if you want to build more of what you already have, there are a surprising amount of nice little shortcuts like that throughout the game which does redeem it a bit (it's obvious they are trying their best). Building is somewhat how you would expect it, and it even felt fun for a while, but compared to similar titles it's pretty difficult to get a proper foundation for a building in the beginning. I fought my first sentinel, which was basically just me aiming my miner at the thing for 30 seconds and then running into a cave to hide from the retaliation. It was about the most exciting part so far, but compared to something like the headcrabs in Alyx the sentinels are a joke.

I'm sure if you play with just a monitor the controls and graphics are probably not going to be as big of an issue, but if you're buying this for the VR experience I would definitely not recommend it at this stage. I spend more time cursing the UI and seeming lagginess of the game than actually enjoying any aspect of it, and cannot really recommend it as it stands.

No Man's Sky is an amazing open-world / crafting / exploration game. It has it's flaws but it's a game that you can sink a lot of hours into.

The good:
- visually stunning, and great audio and soundtrack
- fun gameplay with lots to do - you can choose your own path and decide how you spend your time
- infinite worlds to explore
- varied base-building above ground, underwater and in space on your freighter
- generous with the resources and lots of way to make the different currencies you need - seldom a grind

The not so good:
- combat is a bit underwhelming, and your weapons are not very good
- the story was a bit too drawn out and convoluted for my liking
- the galaxy map is a mess visually (every dot looks the same but they are supposed to be distinctive) and the controls within the map are frustrating and imprecise
- the game uses Steam configuration for controllers which doesn't work very well - more than half the time, the game wouldn't register my controller on start up (basic Xbox) and I had to restart the game
- procedurally generated worlds does mean that planets and NPCs begin to look the same after a while

This is a fun game with varied gameplay where you can make your own choices. Yes, the story fails to follow this approach, offering only the illusion of choice, and also overstays its welcome. However, you can ignore it all together and decide how you want to spend your time in this game without missing out on anything.

Recommended for people who enjoy exploration and base-building games, and who can maintain an interest in a game where you create your own objectives.

I abstained from trying the game, or watching gameplay of it, until this month. I saw it cheap and so decided to finally give it a try. The curiosity was huge after 4+ years! Especially given the incredibly commendable support Hello Games has given this title for these past 4 years.

The result is a solid 5/10 for me, that's why the negative review. This game, even after all the patches, feels barely enjoyable, and only for a few dozen hours. After a while the same repetitive game loops and the procedurality of it all become too apparent. The game doesn't really offer any real reason to keep up the work, there are few to no rewards beside upgrading tools and ships, and even then they give you very little in term of gameplay addition. I admit there were a few times in the middle where I was having fun, some planets look cool and upgrading stuff is of course rewarding by itself, but then you keep seeing the same things everywhere and notice the upgrades don't really change anything gameplay-wise. And the game just keeps offering fillers after fillers to make you going but without any real reason to do so. Main story fell apart quickly too by that it was not interesting to begin with and that it asks you to perform the same loops you are already familiar with, over and over.

TLDR: Few hours of decent playtime (if bought at a steep discount), some nice visuals, and almost enjoyable upgrade system. It falls apart after realizing it revolves around few basic loops, and that there is no real reason to keep doing them except flying around planets and collecting data or upgrades that have close to zero impact on gameplay. Main story was decently boring too. I fully understand now the rage from people buying it four years ago at full price. 

EDIT: But I can't avoid but compliment Hello Games for investing so much time and resources into continuing this game development for free since launch. Even though the game is not to my taste, it is well received by many many other players, something evident just by the comments in this review. And that for me is the important aspect of game development, making most of the players happy. I'd say, even if I give a negative review, I count this as a great redemption arc since that infamous launch. Gj HG

Not recommended.  The tutorial is bad and very long, especially in multiplayer.

My friend bought the game for me and we've been playing Survival mode for TEN HOURS already and we're still not past the UNSKIPPABLE tutorial.
The game seems like it would be fun if it would just let us play it!

The tutorial will often advance for one of us, but not the other.  For some steps, sharing a base seems to work, but for others there's no other way to progress except to make separate bases.  We constantly have to battle the tutorial to make progress, having already understood what its trying to teach.

This game would be a lot better if the entire tutorial was scrapped and we could simply do what we want.  The tutorial feels like everything bad about game tutorials, it's unskippable, on rails, buggy, patronizing.  We have to restart the game, try to complete the task at each others bases, try skipping ahead to the next stage of the quest that the other person is on, etc etc.  It's a total chore.

Although No Man's Sky had a rough launch (probably one of the worst game launches in history), HG really has redeemed themselves. Updates are rolled out regularly, and each update is free and comes with fresh new content that will satisfy long-time veterans and travelers who just began their journeys.

The game itself looks amazing, every single planet is different and contains secrets and anomalies that are waiting to be explored. You get to build your base wherever you want, and there are so many options in basebuilding from anything such as metal parts to farming to a music synthesizer. You also command up to 6 starships, which come in all sorts of sizes and colors, and finally you get to command one massive capital flagship, which stores your starships and can be warped from system to system.

The main storyline is amazing as a tutorial for newer players, but it's not really the main point of the game. Once you beat the storyline that's truly when your journey begins, and the infinite amount of planets and star systems are open for you to explore, at your own pace and desire.

I highly recommend this game to anyone wanting to play an open-world, sandbox style game where there really is no strict progression or direction players should go.
The Mixed reviews on steam are due to the massive amount of negative reviews this game got on launch (which I think the game deserved, it really was a crappy launch), however HG has more than redeemed themselves, and the recent reviews are mostly positive as a reflection of that.

I remember hearing about this game before it launched.  It looked gorgeous, and the enormity of the universe was intriguing.  I wasn't into gaming at the time, but this game caught my eye for sure.  I bought this game in Jan 2019 before I even had a PC to game on. I even paid full price (foolishly not realizing steam sales existed)  I tried using my poor linux system to play this in 2D.

After I built my gaming PC (for VR), I knew this title was coming to VR and waited with bated breath.  It took a bit of testing to find a config that was usable, and I will admit, it didn't look awesome due to jaggies. But the idea of  being inside this game still exhilarated me.

I had already done some small part of the game in 2D, but the chance to play it in VR from the start (essentially) was awesome!  I overlooked the graphical issues I encountered and took in the wonderous sights I saw.
I could launch my ship from the ground and into space, while I was in it, without a cutscene!

Some may not care for this type of game, it is generally a game about isolation and solitude, even in a universe with aliens that you regularly encounter.  It has a building and farming mechanic cycle that persists deep into the game.  I don't mind this concept, but some may.

Over the past 18 months Hello Games has changed this game by adding tons of content and switching it to a more multiplayer friendly game.  I have to say,  it is impressive the amount of content updates that have been released for free.  In some ways altering the gameplay (for the better) but always growing the game in new directions.

No game can be everything for everyone, but this game is a damn fine space exploration game with a story, that also has some multiplayer aspects that can make it enjoyable to share.  In 2D this game looks awesome; in VR it suffers from performance demands and noticeable aliasing. But I'm always happy to play in VR because I feel more immersed in the universe. Over 300 hours later, I will say this game can be so much fun, and has enough variety for even the pickiest of action gamers to satisfy.

Come fly the No Mans Sky!

Reviews.118654:
Don't get me wrong, this game isn't for everyone. You also need to realize there is something in here for everyone. But only if you're willing to put in the time. As my friend puts it, there are "menus within menus" that can be a bit confusing at first. I've been playing since day 1, so my perspective on UI and UX can be a bit jaded. That doesn't mean it still needs some work. The hints, albeit not obvious in viewing, can be helpful - be sure to read. There are a LOT of items and resources to keep track of. I recommend using the 'NMS Assistant' app that you can find for iOS and Android. It details everything you can find in the game and what you can do with it. The app was made by a fan, so if you find it helpful, maybe give the dev a little something (the app is free).

I play primarily for the exploration. I love the idea that every planet's terrain is procedurally generated, giving countless possible landscapes to see. Which is an even bigger draw to making videos in the game, in places no other player has ever seen. That's crazy. I have since made 20+ high quality cinematic videos (some of which feature other prominent NMS community figures), planetary focused walk-abouts, tutorials and other random content within the game itself. Not to mention the creation of several photo books from the Photo Mode available in the game. A necessary feature for such a game. Again, something that needs some refinement.

There are things in this game I haven't seen until 500 hours in, even 1600 hours in (and not just because of all the *FREE* updates over the years). The surprises are numerous, given you dedicate the time. The community is the most inviting place to ask questions to help you along and maybe cut your time in half with certain things. 

All in all, it's the sci-fi Travellers dream, minus the time travel trope. The aesthetic is captivating, and the things to do are countless. I mean, you can make your own chiptune music in the game for crying out loud.

Honest (2020) Review, (From the mind of a simple critic) Industrial Gamers! 

Gameplay. This game offers you to be whatever you want to be from the start. The main/side quest helps players learn things about the game and unlocks useful items. All 100% up to you to decide whether or not you wish to pursue them.

Graphics. The amount of visual overhauls this game recieves with each update is crazy. And on top of that their "Next Generation" update is arriving soon. I'm astonished how they can keep making an already beautiful game look even better!

Controls. Absolutely 100% Simple. 2 hours in you'll master the quick menu as well.

Sound. This game is FILLED with ambient sounds, pair that with the relaxing music that overlaps it and you have the recipe for one relaxing game to take your mind off of things.

Difficulty. When you start you will hit a learning curve. The game offers so many items and on top of that it's own periodic table, it's kindof hard to keep track of it all. Besides that, npc difficulty isn't much of a threat after you get the hang of the game.

Final Rating - I vote this game the "LABOR OF LOVE AWARD" every year for a reason. They stood up against a community and said we won't give up until we give you the game we promised! They've given that and MORE. Much respect to Sean Murray and his team, can't wait to see what other project you all have in store for the future!

Overall, No Mans Sky succeeds at putting you in the shoes of a galactic wanderer as they progress from being ship-wrecked on a random planet, to having a fleet of capital ships and star-hopping to the center of a galaxy populated with beautiful planets. 

 There is an underlying story that feels more esoteric and philosophic than rich and engaging; there is a Skinner-box aspect, where you gather resources to improve your ship/multi-tool/exocraft, in order to better gather resources, etc. without really having an end goal. These are less than ideal, but in this application are fit to serve. That is, they are not the point of the game, but rather things to drag you to the point. The point of course is to fly around in your spaceship and explore all these beautiful planets.

As someone who enjoys exploration in their video games, I was super excited for NMS leading up to it's release. Frankly, it failed to live up to the hype, initially. I chose to not be overly disappointed in it, but found the criticisms (basically, the universe was kind of empty, and some pre-launch promises were not fulfilled) to be valid. In light of this, I was delighted upon picking it back up over the summer to find that they had taken the criticisms and worked to address them. I have found that the game has really become one of the best space exploration games on the market.
Reviews.118761:
This game is the definition of 'labor of love.' It came out 4 years ago, with a host of issues and unfulfilled promises that condemned the game's reception after launch. Instead of moving on and writing this game off as a lost cause, the developers doubled down and set off to implement every promised feature into the game, and many more.

The game now features a robust, cross-platform multiplayer; a huge variety of vehicles; massively customizable base-building process & options; revamped procedural generation that added lots of variety to planets; a more coherent main story; and so on.

While the game is not perfect, it has significantly surpassed the greatness that the developers initially promised and didn't deliver at launch. That is more that can be said for most games that don't meet the hype. Highly recommend it.

I'm recommending it because it's not a bad game, and I did enjoy it... here comes the "but"

They for SURE made this game drastically better than it originally was, and they added a ton of stuff. 

But for me, it's still severely lacking:

-The questlines aren't very long, including the main story line
             Individual missions are also very boring. It's the bit of story and lore that brings life to quests early game, but  it doesn't last long.
-Brunt portions of the game can be finished in an afternoon, so to speak.
             You need a lot of salvaged data that you found just under the surface of the ground, and located with your scanner. You use this salvaged data to unlock all buildable parts. You can get the few hundred that you need to unlock everything in an afternoon. 
             You need a lot of nanites to unlock all your tech for your exosuit, ship, exocrafts, and multitool. Once you get a food processor, you can pretty easily figure out how to make a few higher grade food items. With the food in hand, you go to the anomoly, and feed that lumpy potato alien all you got! You get anywhere from 10-200+ nanites per food item. Go there with 200-300 food items and you'll have all your tech. Tedious and a bit time consuming, but easily doable.
             You need a lot of money to buy a decent ship, multitool, exosuit slots, frigate, freighters, tech modules, etc... 
You mine a bit of cobalt, sell that for a few 100k, then go get just a bit of Chlorine (easily bought from a space station) and buy an EXCESS of oxygen. 10s of thousands if you can afford it. Put Oxygen and Chlorine into a medium refinery for a return of 6 Chlorine 
 for every 1 of each. Chlorine sells for a lot, Oxygen is cheap and you can buy a few thousand at a time from stations. 
             So that right there is all your currency and unlocks done with almost zero effort put in. 
-The multiplayer experience is almost non existent.
            You can be in a group together, sure. You can build bases together use the same home world, sure. That's about it. No questing together, unless you want to include the Nexus missions which are a joke. I have a way faster PC than my buddy, half the time I can finish the quest before he gets to the planet. How is that a multiplayer mission if I can EASILY solo it? 
           It feels like this is turning into another one of those games where you have to "make your own goals", only because of a lack of real content. Which if that's how you want to play it, that's fine enjoy yourself, but it's boring to most. You can only see crazy RNG animals and planets so much before it loses it's luster. 
-Bases building is sort of pointless. You only need to for quests and convenience. 
           Taking the time to build a facility to make money can be fun, but if you're to that point, you probably don't really need money that bad anyways. 
-Given the points above about the easy progress of things and base building, all but one of the exocrafts are useless. And REALLY disappointed the cool mech looking one is such. terrible. trash. The only good exocraft is the big 4x4, for hunting down salvaged data faster. 

All of that being said, it IS a fun game, and I DO recommend it, but after coming back to it, starting from scratch, and playing for 40ish hours... I'm almost done with it again...

In the end, everything in this game, lore, quests, progression, everything... is just too shallow. It's comparable to Fallout 4, where it has it's strong points, but everything in the game feels like "modules" that were made separately and, in the end, all slapped together. There's a disconnect.

No Man's Sky is a very true to form depiction of what the Sci-Fi genre was originally all about. That feeling of wonder and discovery, of not knowing what was out there. A beautiful selection of colors and design aesthetic really make the backdrops of space stand out in that classic early Sci-Fi style.

The team at Hello Games has done an amazing job of continuing to support their game well past launch, with a host of bug fixes and performance improvements. The expansive amount of new content and the addition of multiplayer continued to build on what they had already worked so hard on. They have my respect for sticking through all the troubles the game has had over the years, and my continued interest in their games for their genuine attempt at something surreal.

However, I can't recommend No Man's Sky. Although the game has come an impossibly long way since it first released, the game itself is still incredibly superficial. Underneath all the pretty colors and nice aesthetic is a horrible repetitive resource grind, that offers little (if any) change as you continue playing. The initial two hours of gameplay is the entire game, there is nothing past that to offer accept a change in scenery (which is also very repetitive).

The game totes an entire realities worth of "content" with the same level of depth as your local convenience store. Planets just blend together, you being to notice where things have been reused over and over again. Space stations are all the same, every single one is identical to the last. Reviews.119146:
The central pull of No Mans Sky is exploration, resource gathering and character progression through technology upgrades. Delivering wholeheartedly on the fantasy of being able to go anywhere in an infinite universe is straight out of Star Trek, as is landing your ship on an alien world and knowing you are probably the only person who will ever set foot on it. These alien worlds are incredibly diverse and even come with their own flora and fauna. From pink-grass to water-worlds, the variety is incredible and with the addition of photo mode, makes for some excellent screenshots. 

Whilst No Mans Sky delivers whole-heartedly on its premise of every rock, tree and planet being procedurally generated, it does come with some drawbacks. Aside from any bugs or glitches, after visiting a certain amount of star systems you will notice that the variety of these worlds may start to thin. Although I will credit the Hello Games team here for continuing to add in new world options to spice up the procedural generation. 

Survival and Permadeath modes come with added risk as you are more likely to come across planets with increasingly hostile flora and fauna as well as inventory limitations and higher upkeep costs for your life support systems. Fall damage is surprisingly unforgiving here and I’ve had a couple of almost save-wiping close calls. Once you mitigate this with up to six S-tier shield upgrades you might as well be playing on normal mode again, especially considering the myriad ways a player can quickly build up a stockpile of units and nanites to buy there way out of problems with new gear and starships. 
Money isn’t hard to come by as you Indiana Jones your way through abandoned alien structures in search of valuable relics, scrap abandoned starships or set up an automatic mining colony to begin raking it in. In what would be a premium currency in any other game, quicksilver is used to buy special cosmetics and can only be earned through playing special missions on the nexus player hub. I have to applaud Sean Murray and the No Mans Sky team for refusing to add any microtransaction chicanery to the game. 

In your travels you can collect up to six starships which can be summoned in a pinch to make for a fast getaway. Starships come in five flavours, from the dummy thicc hauler to the zippy fighter, but if you are in the market for something a bit more sci-fi, look no further than the weirdly-shaped exotics. I’m still scouring the stars looking for the elusive squid ship (squid noises). 

Base building is a satisfying, yet resource-hungry way to make your mark, but don’t expect to be able to build the space mansion of your dreams right away. Another thing to chip away at is building up enough space credits to be able to purchase a swank new capital ship. My personal favourite looks suspiciously like a Venator from Star Wars, the Clone wars. There is also a Warhammer 40K version for fans of the series.
 
As well as holding tons of resources in its cargo bay, the freighter holds all of your collected star ships and has a command bay to direct your fleet to go on a mission. Once assigned, the fleet they will physically travel through the galaxy which absolutely blew my mind. Your new mech exocraft can be also be called in from your freighter when you are planet-side in a way that mimics titanfall. 

Although you will spend most of your time alone in this vast colourful cosmos, No Mans Sky has an excellent player hub- The Nexus where you can purchase suit upgrades, admire each other’s ships and join in missions together. There is also 30+ hours’ worth of story to play through although I’d consider it side content that is done naturally as you play involving several characters and the titular Atlas obelisks act as a bread-crumb trail of story objectives. Whilst the central objective is to reach the centre of the Euclid Galaxy, it acts as more of a ‘prestige’ system then a conclusion to the narrative so be warned. 

The scope of No Mans Sky and its procedural generation system is its greatest strength and sometimes its biggest drawback. That being said, No Mans Sky has solidly delivered on its original premise and in doing so has redeemed itself in the gaming community. With more updates to come, now is an excellent time to jump in and experience it for yourself. 
Score: 10/10

Reviews.119191:
Okay okay, No Man's Sky.  You got me.  I was on the hype train back in 2015 and the release of this game was, well we all know how it turned out.  It was a lot of fumbling around and figuring out how to continue your vision in the wake of that horrifying launch.  A lot of people thought that you couldn't do it, and look at the game now.

This game has been patched with the utmost care and love and in its current state it is amazing!  Far better from the initial release.  This game allows you to play casually and just sit back and enjoy the weird universe that Hello Games has put together, and I love it.  I love the cross platform multiplayer.  You can play with Console, PC, and VR players all at once.  The VR support is not the best, but understandable considering the type of VR this was designed for.  Fix that and I would probably live in this game.  That said it's still amazing to play.  I don't think its worth $60, but if you got the $30 when it goes on sale it's a good game to pick up.

One of the most challenging things I've done was make it to the Centre in permadeath mode.  This game really does deserve the Labor of Love award this year.

For some people this is probably a fantastic game, but I expected something different.

I bought this game on it's first day of release. You don't need me to tell you how disappointing that was. 
However, they brought out a free update. It made the game playable.
Then they brought out another free update. It made the game fulfil the promises they initially made.
At this point, the devs were beyond praise - here they were, still making FREE updates to continue their legacy as the space exploration / crafting / survival game everybody had wanted. But there was still MORE.
They brought out yet another update - still free (Unlike another certain sci-fi Bungie game) to ADD content that no one had even asked for.
Time and time again the developers have added to the game and more and more this game gets more beautiful, more complex, more content bound.

I can now really *feel* like I am genuinely staring up at a planet from my own, hovering on my horizon like my own Jupiter moon, watching the enormous variety of flora and fauna, each behaving in their own unique ways, knowing that I can hop into one of my spaceships bartered from an alien and move onto a completely different solar system to explore new surroundings.

Simply, and un-ironically, a game out of this world.

Players who may enjoy this game: 
-Those who enjoys a soft exploration. It is unlimited, but not complex. 
-Base builders. Lots of potential, from a giant xenomorph shaped tower to a low orbit space station.
-Sightseeing lovers, a whole lot of beautiful vistas to be amazed.

Not the focus of the game, they are present, just not expanded, so be aware:
-Combat. Simple and effective, just not exciting in the long run.
-Story. A mostly linear one that can get really intriguing and mysterious, but not really deep or long.   
-Coop/Multiplayer. You can easily get on a game with your buddy and enjoy it, but the core gameplay doesn't encourage much of sticking together for the most part, no challenges or difficulties that require a party. 
If you set personal objectives and goals, it can be achievable.

Props: Althought the game's Story ain't Witcher level of insane, it is the perfect example of how to tell very interesting plots and get holds of you by just using text. No expensive cinematics nor special effects, just badass writing skills.

The main selling point of the game, which is complex procedurally generated worlds to explore - falls extremely short of my expectations. The reason being that the procedural generation is too simple, and after visiting a few planets it becomes clear that the only differences are basically in colour. 

 - All planets are basically mono biome. You will never see a planet that contains a jungle and a desert and a polar cap. You basically see the entire planet the moment you land.
 - Landscape features are very uninteresting. There are mountains of various intensity and occasional stationary bodies of water on some planets, that's it. This, again, reinforces the whole perception that there's nothing to see outside of your landing zone.
 - The universe is empty. I understand this is a bit of a plot point, but it doesn't really make the game more interesting. There's like 3 spacefaring civilizations, and nothing else. No primitive societies on some worlds, no ancient ruins of forgotten civilizations. All the artefacts you find look the same and don't tell any stories.
 - Even flora and fauna is repetitive. Sure, you get weird critters on some worlds, but the "dangerous flora" like the venus flytraps or the explodey gas blobs - are exactly the same on any planet. No need to cautiously approach a strange plant on a jungle world wondering if it might be carnivorous.

I feel like the game could use another 5 years of development focused entirely on procudural generation before it can actually be interesting as an exploration game.

To the hardcore PC gamer that wants to "beat" this game. You won't like this game. It's not meant to be beaten. It's a game to have a great time with other people, or even explore planets, name creatures, plants, and planets, build massive bases, fight to save different star systems from hostile sentinels, have massive dogfights in space, upgrade your equipment, explore new ideas, and most importantly adventure! ALSO THE VR IS AMAZING.

TLDR: game used to suck, doesn't anymore.

I only got into this game this year, I think it suffered in its early iterations for poorly communicated expectations but it's clear the dev team really did love this game and the updates that come out our enjoyable expansions to the experience.

Know what to expect and you will love it. This is a game about flying through space, exploring, discovering new planets and creatures. It has some base-building, some crafting, some sporadic combat objectives. First and foremost though, it is exploration. It's designed to make you feel the grand expanse of space, it feels infinite. Sure it is procedurally generated and you'll quickly know the limits of that, but I've never looked at a map in any other game and just been blown away by how it goes on and on seemingly forever, and there are thousands of players out there that you might by chance cross paths with (extremely rare), but there is a hub you can go to and start multiplayer missions or chat.

If you want a space sim that is like Star Wars which is about dogfighting and grand spectacle battles, this is not for you. If you want to get into the cockpit of your very own little spaceship and just see where the hyperdrive takes you, then bum around this infinite world and have fun doing so.

There's so much one could say about this game. I tried to be brief, but I rambled, it seems. [b]TL;DR[/b], absolutely worth it, not too too difficult, great and fairly existential experience.

First, [b]the elephant in the room[/b], and what this game is probably most famous for: they kept at it and stuck around even when the game had, arguably, the worst kind of launch any game could hold. Internet Historian did a really good video on it that I highly recommend. 
The game was released incomplete and lacking in promised features, on top of being extremely buggy. At the time of its release, I was an Elite: Dangerous player who looked onward at the burning ship that was this game with a mix of pity and spite, thinking of it as receiving its just deserts. Early access bait-and-switch/exit scams of this kind were new and common in those days, and that line was already being tread by Star Citizen (which I hope to one day have a PC capable of playing).
While it was released too early and with seemingly false promises, however, the studio behind the game did something unexpected: they respectfully accepted every refund of the game and kept working, because they do really seem to care about making a great game. 

And that they have, imho, as many of the previously promised features have been added one-by-one, and I have quite happily enjoyed the time I spent exploring its infinite universe and learning its story. There is still so, so much more they could do, and I'm absolutely excited to see what else is in store and where the story goes. In its current iteration (heh), though, it's quite an enjoyable (and existential) experience, so far. 

[b]The music[/b] is amazing and right up my alley, on top of being of a style that's fairly in-vogue, I think, with its futuristic, glitchy, a-bit-experimental, and existential tracks. I often listen to the soundtrack while doing other things, when I'm not feeling my typical lo-fi hip hop stream.

[b]Visuals[/b] are not the most realistic, but can be quite wonderous. I'm upset that I do not have a more powerful setup capable of witnessing this game on higher settings, especially with the more recent update which sought to improve the look of planets and such. All those subpar screenshots...

As for [b]the story[/b], there remains several mysteries which I am interested to see resolved ([spoiler]what is happening to the Atlas? Why is it manifesting in this way? Why did the people who run the Atlas seem to have abandoned it? What's going on in the "real world?" Why did what happen to Artemis..happen to Artemis, exactly, and how did we get those transmissions like that? etc. etc.[/spoiler]), but the so-called big secret about the universe was very predictable - at least, to me, it seemed a no-brainer that [spoiler]the Atlas was some kind of computer and the universe(s) are simulations its running as some kind of test (well, now, it's trying to understand what's going on and so is modeling the real world to understand why it's being "hurt", but I'm not trying to get too in-depth here), and that, to a debatable degree, we weren't "real". It seemed to make an attempt to..like..make it debatable that we were in a simulation and that things were or were not real, or were simulated, as determined by dialog, etc.[/spoiler] If it's supposed to be questionable or up in the air, then it's not questionable enough, to me, or gives up the 'truth' a little early. [spoiler] While it was fairly predictable to find Artemis 'dead', it was still fairly heavy, I feel. Null's panic about losing everything after all he's done was pretty real. [/spoiler]

[b]Gameplay difficulty[/b] can be as chill or action-packed as one makes of it. A creative mode is in place for those who just want to build and explore (of which, the majority of the game becomes about - meet with people, explore the universe, play missions, find cool ships, and build wondrous  or fantastical bases you would happily call home), while some amount of danger awaits those who play normal, survival, or permadeath. Normal has generous material inventory stack limits and some amount of damage reduction, which will be fine for most who don't opt for straight-up creative mode. Survival feels like the way the game was meant to be played. Permadeath is just for the achievement, really, but isn't so hard.
Getting started is the hardest part. It's already a little tricky when you already know what you're doing, but it can be brutal when you're new - especially if you start out on a fairly hostile/dangerous planet, which was the case for me. It's hard to figure out what you need to do as you're taking weather damage and quickly running out of oxygen as you run around like a chicken with its head cut-off looking for the things you need to avoid it and survive. Once you get past this initial scramble, get into your first ship, and take off, things ease up quite a bit. You can begin gathering a small stockpile of necessary materials, so that you can make longer treks looking for upgrades and more stuff you need to progress even further.
I highly recommend most to stick to the story mission prompts at least a little ways, before going off and trying to do your own thing or start building the most amazing base ever, unless you're on creative (I haven't played it, so I don't know what all it gives you, to start). I decided to do this (go crazy, building right away) and eventually realized I could have gotten some very nice upgrades much, much earlier, like a storage container blueprint, had I progressed just a bit further in the story, i.e. [spoiler] access to the anomaly, base computer mission blueprints, a crashed ship, etc. [/spoiler]. Without spoiling it, I'd say to go at least as far as when you start getting prompts to interact with your base computer for blueprints, as well as access to the big multiplayer hub at which one can unlock all of the upgrades.
As mentioned, permadeath ends up being not-so-hard once, well, one figures out how to not-die, obviously - which isn't so hard, in this game. Everything that can kill you is absolutely avoidable or preventable. You will just die a few times in other modes as you figure those things out the first time you encounter them. I'm surprised more people don't have the "To Live Forever" achievement, honestly. Getting off the first planet is the hardest part, as you may get unlucky with material accessibility or a harsh planet - past that, it's fairly smooth sailing through the main questline.

[b]Gameplay, itself[/b] is, again, as chill or as action-packed as you make it. It's a lightly difficult survival-building game, of which there are plenty flavors around. Building bases is fun, and can be done anywhere - claim a little slice of the universe to be permanently yours. Build your dream home, or dream city. Enjoy exploring procedurally-generated star systems and planets with a wide variety of flora, fauna, weather patterns, geography, and so on. My favorites are water worlds or volcanic planets [spoiler] following anomalous planet types like planets of light or the spooky orb ones [/spoiler]. Moving around and performing actions in this game is fairly solid and smooth. Fighting stuff is not too complicated - it could be a little better, but it's not an FPS or action game. I figured there'd be more hostile fauna, but dealing with the environment is almost enough. The actually-hard things you can fight seem too hard, if you don't cheese it somehow. Picking up eggs that causes a swarm of monstrosities to spawn all around and [i]right next to you[/i] that can launch you all the way into the nearest ravine, for one. Large AI walkers that are fairly easy to fight while running around or hiding in a building, but more than a match for my own mech. I was quite disappointed about that, as the first thing I did when I got my own 'mech' was to try to fight a walker - and be subsequently annihilated.

This was a game I had written off for a while. Too little content, gameplay that was too simple, little better than a few hours of fun.

The amount of updates, love, and passion that has gone into this game since then has absolutely blown all expectations out of the park. This game is excellent, especially to play with friends, and holds things to keep the interests of both casual explorers and loot goblins alike.

There is a lot more variety now, not just in terms of planet types and creatures, but in terms of missions to accomplish, things to build, equipment to find, and random interesting locations to explore. The planets are widely varied and very interesting to explore, with a lot of very unique environments to check out. Ships handle reasonably well on mouse and keyboard, and the game feels relatively intuitive whether you're repairing an old ship, or managing your fleet of freighters.

Visuals and audio are quite good. Not the absolute best in the world, but they suit the game very well.

Particular downsides continue to include some issues with multiplayer syncing, environment manipulation wonkiness, AI detection wonkiness, and a steep drop-off in replayability after you've explored much of what the game currently has. However, these bugs are relatively rare and not very serious for the most part, and there will be dozens of hours of gameplay before you reach the replayability cliff.

I definitely recommend!

There is something immensely satisfying about reaching a planet or system that no one has discovered before in a "shared" universe. This "shared" universe is what makes any discovery feel satisfying -- I know I can share this planet or weird creature with friends or strangers online, and they can visit that planet if I give them the "address". 

Despite having pretty decent multiplayer, I wouldn't call this a multiplayer game. Multiplayer is less stable, and while there are co-op missions you can do together, and while you can collaborate in base building, you will have a limited experience if you only expect to play multiplayer.

This game is first and foremost a singleplayer exploration game in a shared universe -- the core gameplay loop is travelling from planet to planet, system to system, naming your discoveries along the way. Base building is something fun you can do, and a good way to make money, but I've played 40 hours without making more than a simple base with a portal (I look forward to creating a more in-depth base as time goes on). 

The best part of this game is that despite already being a _good_ game, the potential for being an even better game is amazing, and Hello Games has proven over the past four years that they intend to make this game what it was hyped up to be. I am _SO_ excited to be able to play this game long into the future.

Tl;dr If you expect to only play this game co-op, you might not have the best time. If you don't like open-ended games, you probably also won't have a good time.
