Reviews.119979:
Seriously, this game is amazing and worth every penny, especially on sale. don't let people discourage you in any way about it. you'll see them everywhere, complaining about the game being horrendously flawed (ironically, this group of people always have hours in the thousands) or pulling out the "list of things sean has promised us". if there's anything that these two groups have in common, its that they are completely unable to see the good side of things. even if this "good side" is constantly in their, and everyone else's, plain sight. 

i do understand though, the fair complaints and arguments besides those who don't see the game for what it is. indeed, the game's mechanics are shallow and lack complexity. indeed though, the game may look like it, but you shouldn't expect some hyper-realistic space-sim-to-end-all-space-sims. it's not a perfect masterpiece, nor is it the enormous game that everyone in the HypeTrain.tm expected it to be.

*but*. that isn't what No Man's Sky is about. 

the point of No Man's Sky is to relax, and have a journey. the devs didn't make any of the systems complicated, even though it’d be a very easy thing to accomplish. that’s a purposeful decision; that’s not what they want you to look for when you play No Man’s Sky. the game's all about simplicity and eye-candy which both take you away from the stressful thoughts of managing complex systems. it offers you many, many small yet sufficiently interesting options that you can chip at when you feel like it, and otherwise lets you do whatever the hell you want. 

this lack of solidity, and therefore abundance of freedom, is what No Man’s Sky is intended to be played for, and is what splits it apart from everything else. it’s what makes the experience feel special and fun. yes, it may feel empty to those who look for a purpose to be handed to them. but for those who create their own purpose and go with the flow of it, this game is great. it is a pure, devout sandbox, and this is what you should expect if you intended to dive deeply into No Man’s Sky. it absolutely is a beautiful, enticing space simulator that will draw you in as soon as you realise what its true purpose is. 


I am nominating this game for the Labor of Love award. sean spent so much effort on this title, and it's insane. he's still not stopping with these free updates, even if he's done much more for us than we'd ever expected. It really is a love for the game and its growth that keeps him coming back to it. and since its release, not once had Sean asked for any extra money, whether it be in-game currency for cosmetics (we have Quicksilver missions for that, no cash involved) nor DLCs. it truly is a Labor of Love.

Do note that there are still quite a few bugs, so if that kind of thing bothers you then you might not enjoy NMS.

To start out with, I know I have a small amount of time on this game, but my friend has more and thinks exactly the same.  

I truly wished to be able to love this game.  I absolutely adore flying in space, exploration, shooting space weapons, and the thought of ground conquests are super intriguing.  

I went in not knowing what to expect other than graphics and going straight to a planet's surface from space.

Pros: Huge potential, great graphics, wonderful idea.

Cons: Almost 0 fun.  They literally forgot to add fun.  Flying isn't fun, shooting stuff isn't fun.  They placed far too much time into what they believe is "realistic".  Planets are exceedingly similar, these little bot guys attack you for no reason.  You fight them for no reason to gain nothing.  Avoiding them is super annoying.  

You have to farm just to survive or travel in space.  Which might be okay, right?  Wrong, you have to farm all the time.  You just farmed for space fuel for 30 minutes?  Congrats! Now you can travel a small distance at a semi fast speed!  Is that realistic?  Honestly, yes it probably is, but its not FUN.  

This game literally has no valuable content.  The height of the experience is flying from space down to a planet.  It's all downhill from there.  Just endless farming, but gathering materials isn't the only grind.  You also have to spend time crafting materials.  Which takes a ton of time even with machines.  

This game is essentially just a MMO level grind without the subscription.  A sandbox type, but without the standard fun.  Too much work involved for even a minimum amount of fun.  

The grind exists to blind players to the fact that real content is basically non existent.  Don't believe me?  Download or buy the game called Freelancer.  It's literally hundreds of times more fun than this.  No hardcore grinding, no survival stress, and EVERYTHING IN IT IS FUN.  Flying is fun, dog fights are fun, missions are fun, different weapon effects are fun, and even trading is fun.  Custom mods of Freelancer are light years beyond this and FREE.  Yet even the base game has plenty of ship models and systems.  Way more quality than NMS does.

By god, use Photo Mode and make yourself a very sweet screensaver gallery.

A very enjoyable game. It never gets boring, there is so much to do and so many places to go, locally or light years across space. The mechanics are, in the main, surprisingly simple to grasp which makes understanding and figuring out the inevitably more in-depth elements less arduous.

A vast, sweeping playground which blends flying, questing, collecting, surveying, building, swashbuckling and exploring on whatever scale takes your fancy. This is in addition to the multiplayer element upon which I am unable to comment.

The Devs have been taking damage often times unreasonably in my opinion for it seems to me that many players, getting caught up in the relative minutiae of the game, lose sight of the incredibly ambitious aims of this creation. There are some issues and omissions, some glaring, but nothing in my experience so far, that stifles my enthusiasm or desire to go back whenever real life relents into this vibrant, constantly moving universe of adventure. 

I particularly enjoy the relative lack of enforced combat in the game. This really makes the game, though potentially challenging in so many other areas, far less intense and more relaxing. You control the tempo of your movements and activities.

I also really, really like (and am impressed by) the vibrancy, life and, most importantly, the extra, highly interesting and enjoyable, dimension that the teeming NPC aliens and indigenous creatures, bring to the game with their customs, languages and the lore surrounding them and the universe in which you all travel, interconnect and co-exist.

No Man's Sky offers us a seemingly limitless, sprawling, beautiful, utterly exciting and absorbing universe and experience which, in my opinion, most definitely stands apart from and, at the very least, shoulder to shoulder in its own right with the likes of Elite Dangerous, Eve and Satisfactory.

2. Make creatures much more environment-specific, it's weird to see the same types of creatures in wildly different environments
3. Somehow improve the HUD and waypoint system, I've rarely had a harder time in a game just orienting my view to the direction of the thing I'm trying to reach, both on planets and in space.
4. I wish space travel had a feeling more like the X-series of games, not sure if it is the graphic quality or just the lack of depth in the field of vision in space, but it never feels epic enough to me. This contributes to the pretty boring nature of space battles.
Overall though, the game is trying to do so many things that I need to give it some slack. Also, despite the frustrations for a new player, it actually does develop and get more fun and engaging once you get out of the initial few star systems. My advice is spend as little time as possible on the many boring worlds, and keep moving on to worlds you find interesting, since there are sooooo many.

This game is minecraft in space with a pretty chill community, while it dose have a story and missions to do both are fairly shallow (not bad, just not deep) so you pretty have to make your own entertainment to get the most out of the experience. While both the exploring and base building are the highlights of the game, both can be grindy early on but pay off in the long term as you unlock new tech to make life easier, unfortunately the puzzles and combat are rather dull and lack any real challenge which in turn makes things like space battles play out like an old Starfox game and the derelict freighters seem more like a cheep haunted house. Kinda fun but lacking any satisfying punch. 

Plus yes this game has more bugs then a roach motel, some of which are game breaking like flying into the anomaly only to glitch off the map or watching animals have a seizure cause their stuck on a rock. But on the flip-side Hello Games is working hard to address and fix many of these issues even if progress is often annoying slow at times and they honestly seem to listen to their customers when it comes to working on new content. This is refreshing in a time when it seems like most game companies couldn't care less about... well anything outside of squeezing more money out of whatever customers they have left.

It's not perfect and it's not for everyone, honestly if your looking for hardcore space sims with grit-your-teeth space battles then you probably want something like Elite Dangerous but if your looking for a nice chill game to kill some time with and maybe even chat with some decent people then you could do a lot worse then No Man's Sky. Remember, all the updates are FREE! You buy the game, you get the game, you play the game. No paywalls, no loot boxes, no micro-transactions, no BS.

Don't let the hour count fool you; between PC and PS4 versions I've spent many and many-a exploring the galaxy. Once upon a time, that galaxy was a smaller, duller, lonelier place. I explored it anyway.

Yes, No Man's Sky had a rough start. Yes, it didn't have every single little thing promised at launch, although there were a few of those "unkept promises" that only existed in the minds of the people complaining about them. Yes, it had bugs, although in a world where Bethesda Softworks exists I don't really know how people could act like No Man's Sky was some kind of outlier in that respect. Yes, once upon a time, the galaxy was incomplete and broken. But I explored it anyway.

As the months and years crept by, I'd leave the galaxy to do other things. Other times and other places - and not a few real world problems - took me away from seeing what there was to see on the next pale dot in the sky. As the time passed, the galaxy changed. It grew, it drew itself together, coalesced like a cloud of stardust into what it was always meant to be. And I explored it.

From building a base of operations to piloting my first Exocraft; taking on the captaining of a freighter, and diving into the secrets only a water world can keep. I found new friends in the Anomaly, and I crept through dead, haunted ships floating forgotten among the silent asteroid fields. Hundreds of worlds, dozens of systems, always looking past the horizon to the next thing to see, and remembering all the unforgettable things I had gone through in who knows how many Iterations. What's my goal today? Creep a little closer to whatever lies at the center of things, crash through a black hole and see where chance takes me? Maybe investigate that weird planet on the far end of the system, or see if I can't track down that last alien life form I haven't seen before I head back to the stars. Always another discovery to make, another milestone to reach, if you'll explore. Just like I do.

Hello Games didn't just fulfill their promises; they went above and beyond, and here's hoping all the naysayers are eating their words. From a humble, troubled beginning, never asking a penny more than the price of admission, we went from a shell of a game to something really special. A near-infinity of places to go and people to meet where you can do things however you want to. Trader, mercenary, explorer, I've been all three, and so can you. You could come along on this grand journey with the rest of us that stuck it out, that kept searching, kept trying to see what was over the next horizon. You want my opinion on what you should do?

You should come spend some time under No Man's Sky.

Reviews.121156:
Not based.

--Extremely limited overall proc. generation even four years after release. 
-Mineral and plant generation is all from the same table of generic plants/rocks -- there's no single unique mineral/plant. Once you've seen a mineral or plant, you'll see it a million more times in different or indistinguishably different colors.
-Same-y resource plants and resource crystals. Almost (if not every) planet has these likely to prevent softlocking. As far as "Dangerous flora" oxygen flora goes they widely look the same across a handful of variations, many of which share the same planets. As far as "resource flora" goes such as sodium or oxygen flowers, they share one single model on every planet. The same accounts for Carbon, Sodium Nitrate, and DiHy crystals which all look exactly the same and are present everywhere. 
-Animal generation is ever so slightly more diverse but you'll quickly realize you're in a universe that only has a couple dozen different animals in it. 
-Same-y anomalous planets. Unique biome planets are not so unique. Once you've seen a planet with a specific glitch biome, like pillars of light, you've seen them all. Minor differences may be accounted for with mega-exotics that just contain sized up versions of regular flora, or a color filter. It's a gimmick.
-Proc gen terrain kind of really sucks. Geographical features such as caves are endless tubes and at the end of the day are indistinct. Above ground features lack several common, naturally forming aspects of terrain, such as rivers (outside of extraordinary circumstances) that create believable planets.
-Planets typically have one "biome." There's not much creativity in this department. The biome differences are very subtle and usually only noticeable by plant types and color filters, without really changing the atmosphere. There's little sense of place.
-Horribly modeled solar systems that are just a handful of planets and endless asteroid fields. It's monotony of the worst kind. No asteroid belts. No comets. Nothing that could define a system. They're all the same infinite asteroid field with 2-6 planets and 0-1 space stations depending on inhabitance.
--Terraforming sucks. 
-The terrain manipulator's "terraforming" function (by way of reshaping and smoothing land) is terrible. I'll be honest. I don't think I've found a 3d game where Terraforming is done well. But this certainly adds to the list of "horrible terraforming features"

--Controls are dreadful.
-The game feels like playdough. It feels like I'm encouraging my character to keep moving but he's an obese, asthmatic 80 year old man. With the terrible FOV and you get a recipe for disaster. 
~Flight controls leave a little to be desired on many of the unwieldy ships, the flight model definitely isn't perfect but I don't think a more realistic model would fare well in this game.

--Horribly gimmicky updates, or lack therof.
-Ships are uncustomizable. You cannot change a single visible ship part on your ship. You cannot repaint your ship. You can't even obtain a skin for your ship type (the easiest thing they could have added). Despite all of your prowess in being able to create and attach complicated technology such as weapons, thrust, scanning, and landing/takeoff systems, you somehow cannot make the easiest of edits to your ships. 
-Ships are barely tune-able. Like the lack of customization, you'll find yourself incapable of making meaningful edits to the performance of your ship beyond providing synergy bonuses between like pieces of technology. No optimizing power or upgrading parts, no minmaxing armor and shields. It's all a very basic and obtuse ship model that is at the whim of the same three RNG stats - Damage, Shield, Hyperdrive range.
-Devs adding variety? Hardly, they add content such as an organic ship type that you can grow. Sort of like those foam capsules you drop into water and it turns into a dinosaur. Or more 0.01% rarity exotic ships. Or they let you expand inventory slots. Anything but meaningful depth to the selling point of their game. 
+On the bright side, the freighter and frigate mission management has promise, with all of its own shortfalls. 
-The freighter and frigate content has many aspects but so little control over each of them. You cannot control who is on your crew in each ship, or customize any of the ships you buy beyond hardware upgrades specific to them and their performance in missions. They can gradually "level up" supposedly but there's very few ways to invest in this content other than casting your net out widely to maximize profits.

-The cultures of the game suck. Every single system has the same extremely spread out and isolated populations. None of them form cities. All of them form 1-3 person colonies on inhabited planets. There are no civilized planets representing these widespread factions. None of them are rooted to any particular area of the galaxy. Everyone is PRECISELY spread out as thin and diaspora'd as possible. This leads to a lack of real meaning to their existence, they serve only as artificial alien factions that hold no real place in space, not even a city or a village. There's no primitive (pre-space exploration) worlds in space either. Of course the game devs will back this up with the unique existence of Atlas and all of the other lore but it's all such a dreadfully boring excuse for an uncreative alien population. While they dip their toes in exploring some key differences between the main three species (Vy'Keen's warlike demeanor, Gek's businesslike focus, and Korvax's devotion to science and history) it is largely superficial at the end of the day and reflects in no way their appearance, ships, space stations, or colonies which are all the same minimalistic garbage.

+The base building is fun, despite being a grind. There's lots of room for creativity with a mix between prefabricated and manually fabricated building pieces. Power generation for these buildings sucks variety wise, but it makes up for it in at least having the decency to possess a battery system. The resource automation is simplistic but acceptable for what it is. 

-Overall, the devs seem intent on keeping a game model that takes as much freedom away from the player as possible in a game that's supposed to be about the freedom to make your own path through a universe. 
-For a game about exploring the universe, it sure is shallow. 
-Hello Games wants NMS to be like many games, but doesn't devote enough time into developing the depth of the mechanics it adds to make them comparable enough. Whether this is through caution of not wanting the game to borrow too many mechanics from one place and thus lose identity, or pure laziness, is indeterminate. At the end of the day, they play it too safe and there's no staying power for any of the features they've added over the past several years. No long term goals. No concrete efforts you know you can accomplish beyond grinding for few and far between cosmetic furniture, or engine trails, or a unique helmet. At best you are accumulating resources, but these resources don't have any fluid or intrinsic value after you find an S class ship or Freighter you like (which, again, could take hundreds of hours just to find on your own RNG-wise).

The game has no real sense of depth or discovery. You will never find anything original, nor will you make anything original outside of maybe a base.

As a pal of mine says/said: It's a mile wide and an inch deep. This rings true years later.

In conclusion: Go play other games (Elite, Empyrion, Space Engineers, etc.) instead because this game has failed at combining aspects that all sorts of games succeed in on their own. No Man's Sky is a shallow husk that adds a very thin coat of paint to itself every few months.

For those that enjoy open cohesive worlds and freedom, this game is a treat.

I'll start with some objective criticism to get it out of the way and then offer some objective praise for those that are on the fence, and finish with why I think the gestalt is so magical.

Turn offs: This can be a fiddly game. You'll spend a lot of time in the menu, especially in the beginning, and inventory management is a big part of the early game. For me, this was tempered by the consistent feeling of progression as your inventory expands and you learn how to better prioritize and evaluate the items. Also, due to the enormous number of activities you are capable of doing, there are a lot of different controls and menus and  ways to access and travel through them and the world. It's a lot to learn and it's not often intuitive or well explained. For an old school gamer like myself, this is not a barrier, but if you don't have both the time and inclination to experiment with the controls and menus until you get comfortable, then you may bounce off this game. Sometimes you run into graphical glitches and bugs. I forgive this because it's immense and I'm impressed at what they manage to accomplish, but don't expect a seamless audio/visual experience.

That's honestly all I would warn you about. I have run into some bugs, locks and crashes, but the development team is so active that they've never failed to patch it more than a day or two after I discover it. Which leads me into what is great about this game. It's not just a massive world full of possibilities, it's growing. When I first started playing it, I put in dozens of hours over an extended holiday weekend, and it just kept surprising me. If you're reading reviews you've likely heard how large the physical world is, but it may not be quite clear how much there is to do in it. I won't let on too much because it was such a joy to be blind sided again and again with a completely new activity, and most of it can be ignored if you don't like doing it. That said, I really like it all.  To top it off, before the entirety of the features had unfolded themselves to me, the devs released a major update that included even more things to do. The community is active and friendly too. There's not much need to engage in the multiplayer elements if that's not your jam, but if you ever do you're likely to have one of the most wholesome interactions you can find on the internet. If you like the aesthetic of classic sci-fi films like star wars and blade runner, you'll probably fall in love with the art direction like I have. The lovely music and design are featured in the trailer videos, but the understated story that you unfold as you complete the game is really a hidden gem that suits the genre equally well.

Perhaps that wasn't all that objective, but it's really hard for me not to love this game. When Breath of the Wild came out, I thought I was ruined for all other games because of how it made me feel. It just felt so good that anytime I'd start a another game, it would feel too cramped or constrained or it just wasn't a world I wanted to escape to because it was too drab and unspectacular. This game doesn't feel the same, but it does at least match it. It's that perfectly balanced combination of a massive world that isn't just delightful to your senses, but rewarding to explore, with enough direction to keep you occupied and enough freedom so that you can really get lost in the experience.

In conclusion, I don't think this game is for everybody, but for those of us who enjoy the experience I've described, you can't do much better. 

Also, it goes on sale all the time, but I almost regret not paying full price. I don't know how the devs sustain the pace of free content generation that they do, but the value proposition here is easily the best money you can spend on a video game. Obviously, I can't back that claim up with any facts, but needless to say, I'm grateful to Hello Games for their continued commitment to their customers. Whatever happened at release has been more than made up for.

Reviews.125504:
The game runs well for me - although my PC should be more than enough for a game like this. My specs;

CPU: Intel Core i7 10750H
RAM: 16 GB 
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 Ti 6 GB 

Graphics

Hello Game's have elected to paint their universe in a cartoonish aesthetic covering everything from the planets you'll discover to the procedurally generated funa and flora that inhabit those planets. That isn't to say that the textures are low quality with some lovely details - especially lighting effects. There are a few options to alter graphical settings to fit your rig. Unfortunately, due to the procedural nature of the game, the draw distance is rather poor. Flying down to a planet's surface or flying through it's sky you would think that each planet is a barren wasteland with nothing but hills and valleys, until you begin to fly closer (and slower) to the ground which is when the beautiful terrain will finally load in the assets. 

There is also a plethora of customisation options for you to explore. Base building is in-depth and rewarding - among some of the best moments in the game is discovering other player bases or having them explore your own - and you can customise your own character with (free) unlockable cosmetics. 

The game has had a recent update to the library of assets the game uses to create the worlds you'll explore, so if you were here before and thought the variety was lack-luster, then maybe give it another look. 

Music, Sound, Voice

The sample variation that is played while exploring is a little lacking in variety but all are used well. Nice atmospheric sounds as well as ship engine and multi-tool effects. NPCs aren't voice acted, instead they speak with grunts and cherps with a text box telling you what they're actually saying - so long as you have translated enough of their language which is done through discovering lexicons throughout the universe. 

'Wild' aliens you discover on planets are really lacking in variety when it comes to sound, where seemingly all prey/predator creatures share a very shallow sample pool. Again, although the variety is lacking, the quality is strong. 

The music is relaxing but doesn't come in as frequently as I'd like. A decent variety in samples, again all to a high quality, will accompany you through your journey across the stars. 

Moment-to-moment gameplay

No Man's Sky is a typical survival game. You'll be spending much of your time managing resources to be used as consumables (for ship/exosuit maintenance, base building, upgrades etc.) and exploring the cosmos. There are daily and weekly missions for you to take part in with other players. 

The usual three pillars of a space game are here too, that is mining, exploration (as stated above), and bounty hunting.

It has to be said that the combat in this game is not a driving factor. The combat is servicable at best, but again, there are options for you when it comes to how you want to tackle and given fight (rain down hellfire from your cockpit, use a giant mech to vaporise your targets, or blow them up with your multi-tools grenade launcher attachment) as well as who you fight.

Mining too is more akin to Minecraft than Elite Dangerous; do not expect any deep core mining or even the need for specilaised mining equipment, instead you'll be upgrading the base equipment to allow you to mine tougher materials. 

Exploration is really the name of the game here, and in my opinion this is one of the best exploration games on the market, especially when you engage with the community.

Needless to say No Man's Sky had a 'rough' start, but the dedication of the team from Hello Games shows a true love for the game and its community. Constant free updates that expand the game in new and exciting ways keeps the game relevant even after long periods of play. 

This is a must have for any survival/space game fan!

Reviews.125572:
No Mans's Sky is a game I overlooked until a couple years after it was released.
All of the hype surrounding it before launch and the epic fail that was its launch was kind of off-putting, but damn, Hello Games deserves mega props for sticking with it, eventually delivering what they originally promised, and as of this review, much more.

The scale of this game still astonishes me even after 60 hours. There's so many solar systems to visit, so many planets to explore and even if before the Origins update they all shared some assets it was still exciting to find that paradise planet that would be perfect to base on (Only to be let down because it has high sentinel activity :c ).

The gameplay is good. Nothing exceptional but it does the job and makes sure to make a point of travelling a lot.

The graphics in this game are great, the detail of the planets even better, but best of all is the atmosphere. Standing on a cliff looking off into the ocean, knowing that it's almost guaranteed you will be the only person to ever see this particular view even if there are many like it.

It extends far beyond this though, because if you ever get the chance to play the game in VR it becomes one of the best VR experiences I've had. Actually *playing* the game becomes more exhausting while you're in VR but every once in a while I'll load up my main save and just go sightseeing or flying around in my ship. Suddenly you realise the size and depth of things you didn't before on a monitor and it all becomes so much more immersive. You see the planets in the same way you would were you actually there.

Overall, I can highly recommend this game. It is a stunning example of what games are capable of these days and I thank Hello Games once again for not giving up.

I recommend based on how far this game has come since it's reception on launch. My personal experience has been at odds with this recommendation, with frustration interjecting a largely dull and frankly boring time with this game across platforms and at launch and afterward.

Personal best parts of this game:
The rare 'Stunning Vista' shows that this game can be beautiful and full of a sense of wonder like the first time of playing Minecraft a decade ago.
The seamless transition between planet surface and space is almost perfect and lends itself to realizing the fundamental vision the devs had.
First 30 minutes to 1 hour of being on a new planet have a feeling of wonder as you see what this planet has to offer.
Upgrades for self, ship, and tool have a good balance of cost vs. reward.


Personal Detractors:
Dying is too much of a setback in the Survival .
Everything is grindy, excessively so in many instances.
Player movement feels slow and clunky.
Some keyboard controls feel like a console port or afterthought.
Flight mechanic is simply bad when compared to other games with similar feature.
Hostile creatures persistently hurt you, disregarding damage or pathfinding.
No way to get rid of Sentinels or aggressive fauna if Sentinels are nearby.
Gameplay loop is a bit misaligned with half of quests being focused on base building and increasing relations with factions and species and the other half rewarding exploration.
Mechanical gameplay is lacking active choices and strategic options such as cover, dodging, stealth etc.
Terrain is hit or miss on blocking line of sight where hostiles can target and attack you through base walls and underground without being able to retaliate.
Basic survival resources are always available, however all actions requiring same resources always looming.
Interaction with NPCs feel trite and dialog boils down to randomness regarding results with no personality inherent to individuals such as interests, and preferences.

I'll start out by saying that I intentionally avoided this game when it first released, and for quite a while after.  I wasn't going to give a developer money when they, to put it lightly, underdelivered on almost every promise they made about the game. After hearing from multiple friends and reviewers that I trust that it was now worth playing, I decided to relent and give it a shot. I came into it expecting a pretty generic procedural exploration game; what I got instead completely blew me away. There is an actual feeling of wonder, of being out of your depth in an alien environment operating on its own somewhat inscrutable rules, that the game conveys so well that I can't really put it into words. In addition to the exploration that was so much better than I expected, it also has a story that hits surprisingly hard, and following the story naturally results in the player exploring the game's mechanics in an approachable way.

This game is the comeback story of the century in regards to gaming, and if you've been holding off based on the problems at launch, you should really give it a chance.

[ORIGINAL]

I decided to give this game a try in mid 2020 and so far spent 80 hrs on it. Most of the time went to my home (base) building, which I found as the most interesting feature of this game. For those who love home building in Fallout 4, you definitely need to try this. As for other aspects, I found this game too lacking.

The exploration aspect of this game, which should be the main attraction, however is quite disappointing. Firstly, if my observation is right, all planets (moons included) are static and the sun revolves around them at a fixed interval, making up a day. I can understand the real simulation may involve a complex or slow algorithm but this is the biggest let down to me as the beautiful sky is nothing more than a static randomly-generated image. Moreover, a planet is apparently homogeneous in climate as I can't find a noticeable different in latitude. Details such as rivers or forest are also not presented. There are species (no human so far. I wonder why) but I have not found any civilization - city, town, or even a village. Only a few types of identical building, such as trading posts, can be found on most planets.

The main story line (as well as sub-quests) is boring. The plot was more like a chore and gave me no motivation to run from system to system. There is no human voice and you can't give your avatar human looks. (why?? Do people nowadays like to have a humanoid body with an exotic face?)

Flying your "starship" is another let down. I know it is for the sake of algorithm simplification but I found space and atmospheric travel identical. Apparently there is no gravity on a planet but THERE IS air drag in space as your ship slow down without applying the acceleration. I know this isn't a flight simulation game but this is over simplified. I can't help feeling like playing a kid game.

There are many other minor issues such as unrealistic space color/contrast but that can be decently fixed by a mod. Resource gathering is also repetitive but you can get over it with a memory editor.

Overall, I would only recommend this to anyone who love to find a beautiful plot of land to build a villa. For others, I doubt you would find this worth your time.

Reviews.131489:
[b]"No man's Sky" instantly divided the gamers' world on its release and continues on the same route nowadays. It packs some good elements, but a lot of problems too. The overall atmosphere is great combined with a sense of greatness, vastness and relaxation. The colorful visual aesthetics are pleasant and you will find big amount of technologies to discover. Also the developers take the credit for fully supporting their game and constantly releasing new free DLCs.
The main problem is that the developers promised an exploration adventure but they did not gave us motivations to do so. In fact the game is about the daily routine of an interstellar entity and how it improves its base and equipment through buying or crafting new things. After a while the game becomes repetitive, the universe seems not infinite at all (every planet looks similar to another you have visited before), there is no real purpose on what you are doing and there is a bunch o bugs here and there.
The game is nice but it looks more like "Sims in Space".


Manometer: 6/10[/b]


The good
- Nice visual aesthetics. The graphics are minimal and the color palette is great. You will find a lot of planets that will force you stop and take a screenshot.
- Great overall atmosphere. You feel the vastness of the universe along with some loneliness feeling while exploring. You feel small. It makes you dreaming.
- It is one of the most relaxing games I've played. You can always escape inside its world after a harsh day.
- There is a great variety materials you can gather. You can always learn new recipes and combine them to every possible way through refiners and others machines.
- There are so many ways of customizing you character and you base. There are so many different ships, vehicles and technologies to discover (from agricultural to energy supply machines). There are so many decoration things for your base to choose from.
- The controls are well designed and easy to learn. Some elements of the gameplay can give you great satisfaction (like activating the pulse engine).
- The sound design is at a good level. You will find a big variety of electronical and robotic sounds and a good variety of creatures and environmental sounds. The music is subtle and manages not to become boring even after many hours of gaming.
- The story is interesting as of its philosophical approach. Don't expect twists and intrigues from the story although It gives you a tempting choice in the end.
- The galactic map is well crafted. The solar systems, the planets and the moons appear to have some scientific consistency. 
- Good photo mode. Gives you a lot of options (angle, fov, focus, vignette, time control and more)
- The developers deserve our applause for releasing so many free DLCs that added a ton of things and fixed a lot of bugs (although it is not  our problem their decision to release a crappy, beta game back in 2016).
- You will find an active and big enough in-game community that creates some cool stuff. Although the world is vast there are always some available ways of communicating with other players (or playing some missions with them).
- Knowing that everything in this universe is online and accessible to everyone, the ability of naming the new systems and planets you discover makes you feel like a great explorer contributing to humanity.

The bad
- After a while you will find no purpose on anything you do. After a certain point you get bored of the exploration and the missions. You have that feeling that you have seen everything and nothing new is about to come. The developers' promise of a huge exploration game starts to fade and the only thing that remains is base and character upgrading. But for what reason? To show off to your friends? The game does not give you motivations.
- The procedural generated world does not really work. They talked about a vast amount of available different ecosystems to explore but at the end everything seems less designed, random and repetitive. Every planet and every creature on them consist of the same elements you meet again and again. Each time only the combination changes. Even more there are no rules of which creatures inhabit which planets. Everything is everywhere. This is definitely lack of design work.
- The missions are terribly repetitive and boring. This is an obsolete open world game approach. It just drives you (without giving you a particular reason) through the map from place to place to gather some staff or to kill a sentinel and then come back for the reward. The buildings and the NPCs you meet are the same after a while. The NPCs say generic things and they have no interest at all. I know that the main story is here mostly for learning reasons but it is extremely boring too.
- The graphics face some problems. The flickering is extremely visible and all the things tend to pop up when you get closer to them. The pop-up especially creates some serious gameplay problems. The game is too demanding and won't run properly on ultra preset even if you have a beast machine.
- There are some major collisions issues that ruin the immersion. Creatures intersect other creatures or objects while walking, pieces of ground suddenly appears inside you base and many other weird things happen. These issues will cause you some problems while moving your character too.
- These pirate ships that randomly appear and attack you are too annoying. They just delay you from what you are doing. As of the space combat, it is too basic and arcady.
- The majority of the DLCs offer only visual additions (staff for decoration and base customization). Even the exocrafts don't really add anything new to the gameplay.
- Some random freezes happened while speaking to an NPC. When this occurs the only option you have is to force stop the game.
- I experienced several crashes on desktop. I lost some gaming time too.

Reviews.134148:
This game has honestly been increasingly getting better with every time that I play. I first played this game back in April 2017, and even then when the game was not really finished, I still absolutely loved it. There are few games that I would consider to be personally meaningful to me, however this game honestly has made an impact on me. It has shown me that there is importance to development and effort, even with setbacks, and seeing it come from the lowest of lows, and grow to what it has become today, only furthers this point. It is still getting updated, has a beautiful community, and is truly a fantastic game.

Note: The bugs described here are subject to change.

The gameplay is well thought out, but not too complex in the variation of "key strokes" or options and is very responsive to user input both in "keyboard and mouse" and "controller" configuration / format. Try to keep the keybindings set to default if you are on keyboard, as changing them does have the possibility of hindering some gameplay aspects.

Visually, the game is beautiful. It utilizes procedural generation however, and this can result in some small bugs while mining. There is a chance that you could fall through the world if you are trying to "speed mine" using the "Terrain Manipulation Tool," which is not a problem as you will automatically be teleported to above ground level and you will not immediately die from fall damage. Though this is both good and bad, as sometimes when mining, there is a chance that you could be randomly teleported above ground as well, but overall both bugs are very rare and are easily avoidable, managable, and/or fixable.

There are only two major bugs that need to be addressed and I have found the solution to both. The first is Landing your Starship. Sometimes the landing sequence becomes unavailable and sometimes there is a chance you could get stuck in landing mode in the right circumstances and although getting stuck is rare, the sequence becoming unavailable is not and can be very frustrating at times. There are two solutions to this, the first is to either find the nearest landing pad or have a friend build one which counters these, the second is to simply keep pressing "E" or whatever keybind you have "Landing" set to. 

The last and biggest one is multiplayer. Sometimes the syncing isn't correct and sometimes No Man's Sky can go into what I call "Offline Mode" where you can see other people online and even be in the same star system or in a space station (there are more but I will not be spoiling the game for anyone in this review) and you will not be able to see them in game, nor communicate with them. Another thing that can happen as a result of this same issue is that if you have previously played with someone and get stuck in this "Offline Mode," you can see what was last loaded but any new changes to bases will not load in, even when you and your friends are online at the same time. The solution to all of this is unfortunate but effective.

You first have to get in game. Then while logged in, you must wait at least One Hour before you will be able to see other players again. If you can't see anyone at first, go out of the system you're currently in, and go back in, and you should be able to see / connect with your friends or other players. This has not been occurring recently (as of November 26, 2020) but it is a common problem that I have been seeing online and have experienced myself. 

Otherwise the game is amazing, and I Highly Recommend it to anyone and everyone who is looking into more information on the game. The price may seem high, but it is more than worth it, and you truly to get everything and more out of what you pay for it. 

- TacoCatProductions, Euclid Iteration Operation Analysis & Management.

So, now having invested a serious amount of time in this game I can't honestly keep this review negative, despite the less than impressive start.

In the beginning I had massive issues with highly regular and, due to how the saves work, progress slowing crashes. After 6 hours with no less than 6 crashes, and basically one of those hours being nullified by said crashes, I had it and tried to refund the game. And the steam refund page says that outside of the standard refunds under 14 days of owning the game and 2 hours, if you have a proper reason to refund you should try and it'll be individually vetted.

So yeah? I'll call that a blatant lie. If you ever consider Steam to really mean it when they say "Refunds are designed to remove the risk from purchasing titles on Steam", they're joking. If a crash per hour isn't a reason to refund a game a few hours beyond the normal 2h, then what is? Do not trust Steam refunds. I've tried it 3 times for a game that crashed once per hour, so I'll be dismissing Steam refunds entirely, and instead buy more stuff elsewhere.

So about these crashes. No Man's Sky has massive beef with alt+tabbing. Like 40% chance of crashing on every alt+tab kind of beef. This can be mitigated to a 10% with using the "Switch to" function in task manager for whatever reason, or, in my case, actually 0% by turning the game to borderless. If for whatever reason switching the graphics settings to borderless doesn't jive with you and you alt+tab at times, honestly avoid this game for now.
After switching to borderless the game still has the occasional random crash, but we're then talking about a more bearable once per 10h or so. Sometimes other stuff happens too like FPS drops in menus that prompt a restart, albeit at least a restart on your terms.

With this out of the way, what about the actual game? First of all, be cautious of jumping right in with Survival/Permadeath, because by far the most brutal challenge to surviving, the game throws at you are the first minutes. The very first planet I started my very first survival run on was impossible to survive. Like, after looking back at it with 100h+ playtime genuinely not doable. Even if you're like me and you prefer harder difficulties, play the game a bit on normal, learn about recharging your gear, farming and repairing, the usefulness of caves, and then go back to Survival/Permadeath. Also be advised that these modes drastically reduce the ability to stack resources compared to normal and you're signing up for that deficit permanently. We're talking 9999 stacks in normal and 250/500 stacks in Survival/Permadeath. If that kind of inventory management doesn't sound like your cup of tea, go normal.
With that aside, I had only one other glitchy, but still with better shields avoidable, death.
So very much unlike in many other games I know that feature permadeath, here you can actually do it. That is do it without being flatly guaranteed a glitch death with the mere question being when, not if. I only played Permadeath until I got the according achievement, but that's still unthinkable with many other games that somehow feel the need for a permadeath mode, but consider polish and bugfixing to be quartiary or straight up irrelevant.
Looking at you here, X series, as much as I loved these games before X Rebirth. Or Darksiders III even lol. I'd never trust these games with permadeath but yeah, No Man's Sky can do it reasonably. That is if you get past your first planet, survival really is pretty much up to you and you only. I wish I could say this of even one other game with permadeath.

After that though the galaxy is your oyster. Or more like 255 galaxies, and yes the number of planets and systems per galaxy is fairly realistic, and also yes, you can go wherever the hell you please. No invisible walls here. The planets are definitely way smaller than earth, but if you want to walk around one on foot, we're still talking hours or days depending on the planet, so you're probably never gonna explore any single speck of any planet unless you make a concerted effort across weeks so there'd be no advantage to bigger planets anyway.
Don't expect any crazy underground adventures like Starbound or Terraria though. The caves, although they exist, are usually neither big, nor varied, and the bedrock really isn't deep either.
The story I found to be starting slow, but engaging when it gets going, the crafting not insane but satisfying too.
The exploration is generally unlike any other game, particularly because of the absolutely insane scale. The only thing I know that compares is Starbound with FU, that however just in 2D and well, with much worse FPS due to terrible optimization, funnily enough. NMS actually seems fairly decently optimized outside of the occasional menu FPS drop.
You will eventually see most of patterns of the procedural generations, and big surprises are probably going to stop happening after the first or second hundred hours but this game tickles that exploration fancy like no other.

Also the background story behind NMS is quite the doozy too. The devs found themselves caught between a massively unreasonable hype and corporate release requirements, leading to one of the most disappointing game releases ever, yet instead of doing what most game companies would've done (cough, EA, cough) they took the massive amounts of cash they raked in and actually lived up to the hype over the passing years.

My last review was made just before 40 hours, which I personally feel isn't long enough to truly appreciate everything this game has to offer. Now that I've finished most achievements, beaten the game on permadeath, created mines for every practical resource, and have a near limitless supply of the ingame currencies, I feel I can finally review this game for what it truly is.

The world's biggest come-back story. As stated by some others, I also believe the reason this game came out in the state it did is because of Sony pressuring them. I learned from Internet Historian's video that Hello Games took a deal from Sony for publicity but that quickly went sour when Sony kept pushing the due dates stricter with little leeway and then proceeded to advertise the game mostly for PS4. Despite the initial backlash, Sean Murray and Hello Games stuck it through. In the face of the toxic wasteland and endless ridicule the internet can be, they stayed with their dreams and finished something truly amazing.

The music adapts to your actions throughout the game by mixing different audio tracks together from the several songs in the OST. A majority of the OST is post-rock, which is a very beautiful genre and fits the "just sit back and enjoy" motif the game takes once you finish the storyline. Some tracks are true masterpieces, which I'd compare the likes to This Will Destroy You, namely Supermoon by 65daysofstatic.

The planet types are various but not too varied that every new planet is something entirely new and unfamiliar. The main threat in the game, Sentinels, have their presence informed to the player very plainly, either through a directional indicator on screen or a descriptor of their activity/hostility on the planet. This makes planets have different levels of hostility towards the player, and unless the Sentinels are very explicitly explained to be immediately hostile to the player, they're mostly harmless.

The transitions between space and other objects are nearly seamless. The only things that can break the immersion are how landing is handled, but I don't mind how handling is held, personally (landing is automatic). The shaders are beautiful and what was initially promised is now there, and more.

My only complaints for the game:
- Bases cannot interact whatsoever. This means if you have an S-tier Electromagnetic Power Hotspot and an S-tier Deep Level Mineral Deposit more than 600 units apart, it's impossible to connect and use them both (bases have a diameter of 600 units)
- There are a lot of visual bugs - important, VISUAL. They have little to no impact on gameplay, but can often break immersion.
- Once finishing the game and choosing no at the final interface, the journey to the center of the galaxy is excessively long.

This game already has satisfied everything they promised yet HG continues to deliver more content. Thank you, HG.

You would think a game built on procedural generation would get repetitive... but there's so much to do, that issue is minimal at best. What can you do, you ask?

- Play the story mode.
- Earn units and nanites from missions or trading.
- Obtain new ships and ship upgrades to become stronger in ship-to-ship combat.
- Explore planets to find technology blueprints, cargo, and artifacts.
- Build a fleet of frigates that you can send on missions from your own Capital freighter.
- Locate crashed ships and salvage them for parts that you can use on your main ships.
- Claim land on planets and build bases for item storage, farming, mining, or racing.
- Feed creatures to obtain animal products, or ride them as a mount.
- Cook hundreds of foods using said products, meat, and/or wild plants.
- Interact with other players on the Space Anomaly, and undertake special co-op missions.
- Build land and water vehicles you can speed around with on planets.
- Role play a roaming trader, buying and selling special trade goods.
- Play in VR, and interact with both VR and non-VR players.

So... yeah. Have fun!

*This review will change when I reach the center of the Euclid galaxy*

***This was written prior to Synthesis***

No Man's Sky, we all know what it is. But 3 years later, does it hold up? TL:DR, yes it does, just not at $60, wait for a sale. If you want to know specifics, keep reading.

-Visuals
The game is beautiful and landing on a moon just to see the planet hovering above you or over the horizon looks fantastic, especially if they are ringed. Volumetric clouds look amazing and feel like they have depth, though upon entry and sometimes if mountains are too tall the clouds will render over things, and water can render over the clouds sometimes (This did not occur pre-Beyond update and can only assume it's related to the move to the Vulkan graphics API). If you are in water and are sitting above the surface (with the camera out of water) you can still see bubbles and other underwater effects.

-Gameplay
Running around the planets and exploring feels very good and if you enjoy the constant strive to upgrade your equipment and don't mind grinding a little bit, you'll find the game very satisfying. Most planets feel unique enough to make a lot of them feel new, but some planets (Such as the snowy planets) you will be bored of after the 3rd or 4th time encountering one. Space feels lacking and I wish they could add more stuff to do, other than grind for valuable resources or kill an occasional bounty.

-Exploration
Once again, running around feels good, but that doesn't matter if the environments are boring. Most of the time, environments look stunning and you can travel for hours and find new animals, plants and minerals. However, eventually you will find planets that visually look exactly the same as previous ones with animals and plants that, again, look literally exactly like previously discovered ones, especially on anomalous planets.

-Multiplayer
Multiplayer generally works well, and playing with friends is fun! You can complete missions with random people or with friends and get rewarded with in game currency or other things.

-Bugs
There are quite a few, but the most glaring one was when I was in an Atlas Station and quit the game, when I reloaded my save I was flying in my ship inside the station. The only way to fix this and not lose hours of progress, I had to kill myself by shooting missiles into the invisible boundaries.

-Developer contact and bug reporting
Contacting HelloGames for suggesting new ideas, requesting changes and fixing bugs is easy! They have a contact page set up that can easily be found on google, and they seem to read all mail. For instance, I have a 16:10 monitor, and for a while the game's UI did not scale properly to odd aspect ratios. I submitted a request to add support for the aspect ratio, and a few weeks later they patched the game and the aspect ratio was working flawlessly!

-Verdict
No Man's Sky is honestly my favorite game and a technical marvel, 18 quintillion fully explorable planets and moons across 255 galaxies! This game is undeniably the largest game, possibly for all time and the engine works amazingly! Sean has spoken about using it to make a Skyrim/Zelda esque RPG, and I think that would be a wonderful idea! If it can make an entire universe, think about what it can do to an entire world! The game holds up very well 3 years later, and with continued support from the developers, it can only get better from here, though I would advise picking it up on G2A, or on sale.

**Post-Origins and after reaching the center of a couple of galaxies
-Verdict 2
My opinion on the game hasn't changed after more than a year and over 400 hours of playtime.
Hands down the best space game on steam and of all time. I've played Elite Dangerous and
Star Citizen, however I found Elite fairly complex and hard to get in to, plus the fact you needed
an expansion just to land on empty planets/moons up until recently was kind of disappointing.
Star Citizen is fucking awesome, but far from finished as it stands and isn't the easiest game to run.

TL;DR: buy the game it's really good especially after Origins and Next Generation

TL;DR Summary: An overly ambitious concept game from a team who clearly know how to dream, but not how to execute. As a result, the game remains in a permanent beta state that, as of now, just barely fulfills the promises made five years ago - once you get past all the bugs and quirks.

Don’t let my play time fool you, those 294 hours are not an endorsement to the quality of the game, rather, they are a sad testament to my personal flavour of obsessive crazy, and the combined result of three separate instances of trying out this game. The first was launch day, where I had pre-ordered the game only to find it wouldn’t even run on my rig, despite my specs grossly exceeding the minimums – though that actually made me lucky, since it let me refund the launch price and then watch the overwhelmingly negative reviews roll in. The second was about 18 months ago, after one of the major updates, where I repurchased at a much lower price, messed around for a few hours, and quit out of boredom. It was only on the third try, after the BEYOND update and watching a friend stream some gameplay, that No Man’s Sky finally hooked me.

Looking at this game’s spotty history it’s clear that Hello Games are a passionate group of artists who genuinely want to produce their vision, but I cannot help but imagine their development meetings being similar to two first-year college students, one a first year physics major and the other first year philosophy, both stoned out of their gourds with quality weed, discussing the universe and its purpose. A lot of crazy ideas, most of which only sound brilliant to them, and the few potential diamonds that come from their ramblings barely understood in the garbled memories and shorthand notes found the next day. They came up with an awesome idea, and presented it in a surprisingly dark and ominous setting. But the development is clearly scattered and on “valve time”, with priorities shifting from update to update and questionable focus (such as three times as many different types of craftable food than types of planets. I wish that was a joke). More than three years later, it’s still in an unpolished beta state, riddled with bugs and severely lacking in quality of life features, and with the clear understanding anything can be changed and corrupted with each update, even the core procedural generation that might just rewrite the entire universe. 

So how did this mess hook me? The aforementioned setting. It’s not apparent right away, which is why I missed it on my second try, but as you progress past the initial survival scramble and start dipping your toe into the vast stellar ocean, a bunch of small things you notice soon snowball into a simple realization.

[b]The universe is rotting.[/b]

There’s something fundamentally wrong about the state of the galaxy, and rotting is the best word I can think of to explain the feeling. This is not a (cosmic scale) young and growing universe like our own; the universe of No Man’s Sky is old, and under its sheen of being fully settled and populated, it is decaying, like some infection is slowly and irreversibly destroying it. And given how much of that decay is tied to logs and notes that are the only communication in a language you understand...[b]you might just be the one of the viruses[/b]. 

Because you are alone. There’s three races that cohabitate all known areas of the galaxy – the [strike]Vulcans[/strike] Korvax, the [strike]Klingons[/strike] Vy’keen, and the [strike]Ferengi[/strike] Gek – but it seems not so much as that they have conquered the galaxy, as that they merely inhabit it, inheriting a network and technology and entire civilization that came before, and that for some reason has disappeared, leaving only artifacts and the omnipresent Sentinels to police the universe to their unwavering lawful neutral agenda. And in meeting those races, it is clear that you’re not one of them. Their languages are garbled to you, but they seem to treat you with respect that borders on fear. Only when you explore, wandering across planetary landscapes littered with discarded trash, broken machinery, and abandoned crash sites, will you eventually come across a language you understand. But that will bring you no comfort, for these words either come as creepypasta extracted from the slime covered computer of an infested and abandoned building, or from some ancient relic that predates the three races above, or from some freakish entity, glowing and ephemeral, speaking either of nonsense or of certain doom. Like them, you are an anomaly. 

[b]You are a Traveller.[/b]

So yeah, it hooked me.  But as said before, the actual mechanics of how this all works, of the gameplay that you go through to make the story progress from there, and that fulfils the original promise of “endless exploration in an infinite but shared universe” falls flat. It is incredibly grindy, repetitive, poorly optimised, and full of stupid bugs that even the most basic quality assurance procedures should catch. All the reviews seem to quote “wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle”, and I’ll repeat it since it’s 100% correct. There are only 9 planet templates – which, if you’re generous grows to 15 if you count “with oceans” and “without oceans” as different, but I don’t – and only the rarest two of those templates have any meaningful subtypes. The challenge curve is negative, because the universe is so generic that nothing changes with your travels aside from you personally growing stronger with upgrades to your suit, weapon, and ship. And those upgrades take forever, as the increments of improvement are often so minor, or only available at the whim of RNGeezus. So you just keep going to the same places, and doing the same things, over and over and over and over and over and over and over and it gets mindlessly easier every time. By the time I reached the centre, I had to travel through 297 systems, and since I [strike]wanted[/strike] obsessively felt I had to “tag” every planet, that meant I landed on and at least nominally explored (as in, stood in one place and scanned everything I could see) 588 planets – so yes, I cherry-picked systems that only had one or two planets whenever I could.

And then, after 294 hours of that and finally reaching the centre, you apparently stop and write a negative review. Because, like I said, personal flavour of obsessive crazy. To hammer home the point, I was going to end with just a laundry list of stuff that annoyed me, and kept the game from ever being fun, rather than something I just felt I had to finish.  Which would have been fitting, because just like this review wouldn't have had a proper end, neither does the game. This list was as of the BEYOND update, and is scattered, incomplete, and only loosely organized. Again, like the game itself. 

But it's so long, it would make the review exceed the word count. Too much ambition, not enough execution. So it is fitting, after all.

After 4,600 hours of playing the game since Foundation, I can say I've enjoyed it for the most part, around 85% of the time. The Origins Update really spiced things up, adding biome variants, a ton of new assets and more mountainous versions of the original 10 terrain archetypes. I can happily recommend this game as most of the grievances I have are, in some shape or form, alleviated. Though there are multiple walls of text below on the game's flaws, overall I feel very, very positive. So go buy it and have some real fun! Because I feel it's just going to get even so much better from here. Keep it up, Hello Games!!!

1 - There are just TEN kinds of terrain generation in a game with QUINTILLIONS of planets. Thankfully, more mountainous versions are added, so that's at least 20. One can eventually find out all 10 of the "new" terrain generation but due to how most, if not all of them look really nice and majestic at the right settings, it is going to take a quite some time before it starts feeling repetitive. At the same time though, I wish there is even MORE than just 20. Way more.

2 - While the variety of colors has somewhat increased in Origins, there still could be more. The filters (e.g. black and white planets) add some sugar and spice to the current color palette but it can do only so much. There are still just 4 water colors - blue, green, pisswasser yellow and red. There are just 6 sky colors - blue, green, yellow, orange, pink and light red,  The filters make the colors good enough to suffice for the time being. More color variety please! WAY MORE!!!

3 - Flora and fauna levels. The variety of flora and fauna levels has returned somewhat but it still needs work. The ones with "few" flora are usually ones with specific assets. There could be planets with medium or low levels of flora but not specific to one set of assets. For fauna levels, it's more of a bug actually. I've seen planets with no fauna have "high" or "copious" amounts of fauna.

4 - Even MORE variety! Origins is a variety update but there could be even MORE!!! One really good reason why is each biome has multiple descriptions (e.g. for the lush biome: Verdant planet, Paradise planet, Overgrown planet, etc.), at least 10 per biome. Either adjust the procedural generation for all of them or brute force it - Create assets and conditions unique to ALL descriptions, which is going to be a ton of work because there are over 100 of them. But I think it is going to be so worth the hard work. Maybe a new "biome" is in order as well? An ecumenopolis biome with its own unique assets and descriptions (e.g. City planet, ecumenopolis planet, megaconglomerate planet, slum planet, etc.)

5 - I don't know why, but building a base, especially larger ones, can get FRUSTRATING. It is how annoying and sometimes, difficult it is to place base parts. Not to mention bases getting buried due to terrain regeneration because the "Base Terrain Edits" meter is moody and inconsistent or the builder hasn't visited the planet or played the game in quite some time. Some relatively simple things even require multiple weird steps to make, like stair "railings". Others will be "invalid" due to Atlas knows what. Can't everything just snap easy-peasy and validly so we can much more easily build stuff? We can easily delete a wrongly placed floor tile or wall, instead of dealing with the annoying invalid invalid invalid oh my goodness why is the wall having a seizure invalid invalid invalid everything?

6 - Sentinels. These things are a threat early-game, a bit less mid-game and a joke end-game with good equips. A buff to sentinels is needed, especially the stupid AI and the ones at higher wanted levels. Or for every planet, there could be a heavily guarded sentinel fortress which, when destroyed or defeated, will lower or completely eliminate the sentinels for a period of time or forever. They get really mad at me for mining 1 Ferrite Dust but when I'm destroying over 9000 Ferrite Dust by using the Terrain Manipulator, strip mining and destroying the planet down to its core, they don't care? Sentinels are utter pieces of sentineling sentinel! They are sentinel! Yes, I'm using sentinel as a curse word because THEY SENTINEL.

7 - Powerful end-game events, threats and enemies are still missing. There should be optional end-game threats that can seriously challenge even the most heavily armed save-editing gazillionaire, especially in survival and permadeath. Some suggestions - A powerful corrupted AI in some Korvax systems that need to be dealt with at its core. A spacefaring hive mind insectoid race hell-bent on destroying the galaxy hanging out in abandoned systems. Interdimensional a**holes that caused the disappearance of all sentient life in some uncharted systems. A powerful Atlas Entity gone rogue (reckoning) in some Atlas Interface systems. Heavily-guarded sentinel fortresses which, if destroyed, reduces sentinel activity by one notch or completely stops all sentinel activity for a period of time or forever. Sightings of a No Man's Sky version of Herobrine. A very rare and difficult end-game quest which rewards the player of visiting the land of the almighty deity wearing a plaid shirt, surrounded by his benevolent demigods at his command. And more!

8 - Missing essentials in combat. No melee weapon. No ability to crouch and sneak. No ability to push or shove things, which can be useful against green insectoid bio horrors.

9 - The little things. There are still a lot here but it doesn't feel as annoying now. When firing your weapon, instead of instant response, sometimes the avatar will twitch the gun for a second before firing, even if the weapon is already drawn. This has screwed me many times in intense battles against sentinel walkers and quads. No button to manually draw/undraw the weapon. Unpredictable and twitchy ship handling, even in fighters and exotics with a full suite of S-class pulse engine modules. The clouds still don't look as awesome as the NEXT trailer. Why do star systems always need to have life? I encountered star systems with nothing but dead planets in Foundation and Pathfinder. Planet-wide storms occurring at regular intervals. Pirate attacks at regular intervals (e.g. in a peaceful system, around 7mins in normal mode, 3mins in survival and permadeath). Getting attacked by pirates in a supposedly uncharted system. Sentinels in an uncharted system. Derelict freighters looking the same on the outside save for color changes. There are still a lot, but it's definitely getting better for sure. Anyways!

I can happily recommend the game as of the Origins Update. There were significant improvements too many to list here. Maybe there will be procedural in-planet dungeons and maybe even... VILLAGES, TOWNS, CITIES AND CITY PLANETS WITH BUILDINGS THAT HAVE ACTUAL PROCEDURALLY GENERATED INTERIORS!

However, the game still needs more polish, adding more stuff while keeping it relatively bug-free.

Thank you for taking the time to read my overly long review of the game!

I got this game strictly for VR. I always wanted to play it before, and after many years of updates and Hello Games redeeming themselves, I finally pulled the trigger.

To start, I have a high end rig and this is just not optimized for VR, very hard to play without having issues on INTEL based CPU's (or so I have read). 

I have an i7 8700k and a RTX 3080 and play on a Vive Pro w/ Wireless adapter (the wifi adapter puts extra strain on the cpu too). I played with a gtx 1070 last spring and had the same issues as many, frame drops and just a terrible experience. There is a guide of things you can do to fix the game I will put below. Some of them work, some don't. What worked for me was setting my desktop scale to normal (had it at 120% scaled up, turned off 2 of my 3 monitors,  changed my CPU setting parameters to 4 to 2 instead of 6 to 4 (stock settings for CPU in No man skys, but will vary and more can be found on the reddit page at the bottom). Tweaked some Nvidia Control Panel settings for performance and changed the DPI on the program (reddit link for more info). Put it on a Solid state drive... AND THEN VIOLA!!!!! Still get drops some times but the game is much better. 

My rig shouldn't have a problem but has struggled. So happy to play, this games really fun and relaxing. Index controls kinda suck so have to rebind them though.

Reviews.148068:
[b] Positives [/b]:
- Phenomenal game which has improved substantially since launch. 
- Tons of content:
[list]
      [*]10-20 hour campaign
      [*]Multiplayer hub for finding friends to play with and multiplayer missions
      [*]Space combat, 
      [*]Tons of randomly generated content with more appearing as you approach the center of the galaxy
      [*]A variety of different goals and ways to "progress" (more on why it's in quotes later)
[/list]
- Frequent content updates
- Interesting environments
- Countless upgrades
- Dynamic economy

[b] Neutral: [/b]
- You have to make your own fun once you're done with the main quests. The game does a good job of guiding you through it's content with it's quest system, where you can basically turn anything into a quest with multiple steps which will be pinned to your screen by pinning a recipe or goal in your logbook, but it's up to you to decide what you want to engage with and what is fun to you. You can explore the galaxy and hop planet-to-planet, you can be a merchant who trades with players and NPCs (you can automate resource collection eventually), you can catalogue all of the life on every planet you visit,  you can journey to the center of the galaxy, et cetera. Whichever path you take is up to you, and while some are significantly more enjoyable than others, they all have enough content that you can focus on one or just vibe and do whatever you feel like in the moment.

[b] Negative: [/b]
- The game has always been, and probably will always be extremely buggy
- The game runs terribly on old hardware and the minimum specs will not get you anything close to presentable
- The graphics shown in the trailers and screenshots are only possible on recent mid-range or high-end hardware, the terrain looks like putty on anything less (little to no grass, weird shapes/textures)
- In multiplayer the tutorial objectives can sometimes fail to trigger until you restart the game, and if your friends make too much progress they can trigger your tutorial quest objectives before you're ready (this doesn't apply to story quests, it mainly applies to base building tutorials)
- The starship controls are passable at best and cumbersome at worst
- Combat is incredibly easy

Highly recommend this game in spite of it's flaws, there is a ton of content and there are countless different ways to play this game. The game receives countless updates every year, and it's finally something I am proud to recommend.
