No Man's Sky was a very overhyped game before it was even released, but not long after its release, it was one of the worst games to have ever been released, It was a successful failure. You more than most likely know what I am speaking of. If not, Google it, I don't have time to explain.

Thus leaning towards its downfall, but, over the coming years, more content was added, quests, vehicles, new biomes, third person, etc. This then brought the game up from its grave to try and show the players that this is what our game is. The reviews weren't as harsh, the reviews came up from mostly negative to negative/mixed. 

Nevertheless I still wanted the game, I had watched YouTubers play the game and it looked quite fun. I will admit I was one of those people who overhyped the game but came to a realisation that it was a hot mess and not worth my time. UNTIL the newer updates and newer content was released. I eventually caved in and bought the game. I thoroughly enjoyed the game, I was immersed, it was fun, it gave me lots of new things to do and shit to see. This then wore off after about 20 hours in or before that for that fact. Here's why:

The game is huge, like stupidly huge, in fact it's so huge, the whole your mumma is so huge/fat/big jokes flew out the fucking window, this game is way to fucking big. (18,809,587,245,234,916 planets or some obscure number). This was overboard. After discovering atleast 10 planets, you come to a realisation that the next however many planets you visit are just reincarnations of the first 10 planets you've been to. The design is the same, the layout is the same, its all just the fucking same, it's like the devs just said fuck it, slap a new name on these planets and just use what we already have. It's a chore, like really, I would rather mop the floors than fly to the same planet for the 9 billionth time.

Quests. Oh boy. Ok, in no way am I saying the quests are shit, oh wait, I'll probably contradict myself by saying that, ok yea I lied, the quests are just the mailman simulator, all they ever consist of is, fly here, find that, talk to this, make that, use this, do that. That is every damn quest and it is seriously infuriating.

The grind, oh here we go. There are a lot of ships in the game, ranging from classes to different shapes to just plain old fucking obscure. There are also frigates and freighters in which you can buy or get for free if you are lucky, you can build a fleet so to speak. The problem with this is they're so fucking expensive. Here's an example, I had like 1 million credits and I thought I was king, I found a ship that looked fuckin sick, so I decided I'll buy it, yea that's when I realised that it was 90 million credits. Like holy fucking shitball Tuesday, how the fuck do I make that much money, is that even possible. This then brings in the endless fucking grinding. This was when I found out that you can find crashed ships and claim them as your own, that was pretty cool until I found out that repairing them costs just as much as buying a ship brand new. 

Gameplay, now gameplay is quite fun, well I'm assuming that since this game is so fucking unoptimised that you'd think Bethesda had some part in the development of this game. Like fuck me, I went from a 4GB GPU which ran the game at around 40-50fps on low, I then moved to an 8GB card and it somehow made my performance worse. Now that I think about it, 40fps wasnt that bad especially since I could actually play the game, now the game runs like that one African Olympic runner who is built like a brick shithouse but is somehow coming last in his race. Hopefully this actually gets fixed in the future because I would love to play the game if it was actually optimised.

Here's some positives to the game for anyone who actually wants to know what I do like about the game.

-Character Customisation is quite unique, multiple races to choose from and cosmetics to equip.
-AI ships are always flying around planets and space, it brings a sort of life to the game.
-The freighters and frigates that jump from the game's discount lightspeed is quite astounding.
-Most materials aren't too hard to find unless its Solanium, that shit doesnt exist.
-Graphics are amazing but you can't witness them unless you have an NASA super computer which is probably meant to tell big mean motherfucking world destroying aliens to not harm us as we come in peace, but we know that's a fucking lie as humans are lying backstabbing murdering cunts. Wait what was I on about?

Ah yea that's it I think. Listen if you want this game, go ahead, I'm not judging (I am), just be prepared for what I have stated in this review. If you don't encounter any of what I said in this review, you are obviously lying, are indeed a world destroying green motherfucker or your game is the immortal copy in which it has no issues and you are enjoying every second of the game (hopefully).

-------------------------Original Review------------------------------
After 256 hours... I feel I am now qualified to write a review.

I watched the launch in the news.  I saw the masses of disenfranchised gamers declare the game garbage.  I waited and saw an update later.  I still resisted the siren song of "new game!".

Finally, steam put the game on sale.  I went for it.  I played it and loved it and put my heart and soul into it... for a few days (weeks).

I made a new game because something went wrong with my original save.  I chose the maximum difficulty because the first save didn't seem like an authentic experience.

One day I "paused" the game via 'esc' and came back to an empty, non-existent game.

Undeterred, I created a new game on a lower difficulty, determined to play to the "end" and see for myself what was good and what was bad.  I had an open mind.

I played.  I ignored the fact that I had to visit forums and search on google to figure out why I couldn't connect to the discovery servers and why I didn't have a group quest.  I ignored the fact that when I chose to try to login to a different player's game, my own game seemed bugged, and my pride and joy, my first home base, turned from a temperate desert planet into a frozen planet.  I ignored the fact that jump jets would fire off if I tried to do a short jump.  I ignored the fact that at some point the hazardous planet achievement ceased to increment.

Then one day, I logged in, short on patience, experienced multiple bugs within minutes of logging in and decided to give up on the game as a failure.  When the quest indicators say "go to this system to accomplish this quest" and then I go there only to find the "hold x to find out where the hell this quest might be" button, I have to call it a day.  I had to quit.  I just don't have the tolerance to put up with this many bugs.

Should I have left sooner?  Probably.  Parts of this game were very calming and enjoyable.  Parts were extremely questionable, and lend themselves to declaring this a failure of untested schedule-satisfying trash.

In the end, I had a decent gaming experience, despite the incredible amount of bugs that I encountered.  But overall, this game is (still?) not for the casual gamer (or any gamer) who wants a "finished" game, with few bugs that are hard to find, and a relatively smooth experience that leaves them feeling like their money was well spent.

I recommend this game to experienced users who are capable of identifying, understanding, and working around bugs.

I do NOT recommend this game for everyone who does not meet the criteria of my recommendation.

---NO MAN'S SKY REVIEW---

A bit late to update the review, but here we go. This year, Hello Games blessed us with a number of updates for NMS. Most importantly, however, we got Origins, which is a complete overhaul of the game's most fascinating and technical aspect, procedural generation. New planet types, new biomes, more randomized terrain generation with more elevation, more flora, more fauna, more everything to give players like me, who've spent countless hours in this game and have seen everything a new, rewarding experience.

--------------------------------------------



Old Review:
It's 2019. Hello Games has released its 5th massive No Man's Sky update after years of hardships; BEYOND. Like with NEXT, this update completely revamps the game while still maintaining its core characteristics which are what you'll spend most of your time doing: Exploration, Survival, Farming, Mining, Base Building, Trading, Crafting and of course, Multiplayer. 

--------------
It's true, however, that BEYOND launched with a lot of bugs, glitches and optimization issues that weren't there when NEXT and Visions were released. This is normal as they're a small team working on what's basically a 'triple a' level game, and they'll fix it eventually. Instead of whining and nitpicking, it's best to help the developers identify what issues need to be resolved so they can be fixed as soon as possible.
---------------

Now, I will not lie to you...
Is the game grindy? Yes. 
Is it repetitive? A bit, yeah. 
Is it fun? Absolutely. And this is the most important part. 

Despite its flaws, the game manages to be very entertaining. Every experience you have will be different and unique despite the feeling of familiarity whether it's scanning animals, surveying planets, looking for monoliths, gathering resources, et ceterap; it's a fundamental aspect of open-world/sandbox survival games in general which contributes to their replay value and the truth is, No Man's Sky manages to execute it perfectly. 

If you're a fan of Minecraft or Subnautica, then No Man's Sky is the ideal game for you. If you don't like games like that, then you won't like it and no amount of improvement is going to make you like it. So avoid wasting your money and avoid making a review after 0.1 hr's of gameplay nitpicking and complaining about something you knew you weren't going to like. Otherwise, we welcome you and whatever constructive criticism you may have into our community.

This game still has a long way to go, and I'm excited to see what Sean Murray and Hello Games have to offer. 

--------------------------------------------

In space no one can hear you lie...........
Luckily Sean Murray lied in front of camera so we all know the BS that came out of his mouth. I avoided this game 2 years ago because it looked like an indy title and I was still playing Elite Dangerous so why bother with this. If Hello Games had run away and hidden in a closet then I probably wouldn't have bought it now either. But apparently they have improved the game so I thought I'd buy it and see what all the fuss was about.......... plus I was bored and couldn't find anything else to buy.
No Mans Sky is a survival space game with combat on the ground and in space, some trading elements and exploration. You start on a random procedurally generated planet with nothing but a gun that can turn stuff into resources for you to gather. And you have a broken ship that you have to use those resources to repair. Your environment suit is apparently defective as it doesn't last 5 minutes without needing some resources to get working again. Your ship, once repaired, can only take off 4 times before needing resources. Your gun can shoot for about a minute before needing resources. And so it goes on. Every time you start making progress you hit another resource wall. 90% of the game is gathering resources. Needing resources to power stuff is fine but not to this extent.
So on you go, gathering resources, upgrading your gun and ship. Finding more items that require yet more resources. At one point you find a fleet you can take control of which, you guessed it, requires resources before you can start using. Maybe there will be more updates to make having a fleet more interesting but aside from sending ships out on missions there doesn't seem much you can do with a capital ship. You can't even save your game on it.
The combat in NMS is pretty good I have to say. Both the ground and space combat work well on the gamepad (didn't use mouse/keyboard so can't comment). On the ground there are things called Sentinels which cover pretty much every square foot and get all antsy whenever you start collecting resources or, heaven forbid, start shooting the wildlife. These things are fricking ANNOYING! They seem to be there simply to make resource gathering more difficult, which in itself is there simply to make playing the game more difficult.
There are some base building aspects to the game but as the point of the game seemed to be telling me I need to keep moving towards the centre of the galaxy building bases on planets seemed utterly pointless. You can build rooms inside your capital ship as well but again they seem pointless as the only rooms I seem to be able to make are corridors and a store room. A save game room would be nice.
The No Mans Sky experience is an interesting one. There are moments when I genuinely thought "WTF?" in a Space Odyssey 2001 kind of way. But then there are moments where I thought "WTF?" in a "What Were They Thinking" kind of way.
The music seemed to be just some synth noises and at one point completly corrupted to the point I had to take the headphones off until the game loaded and I could turn the music off in the options screen. The sound of NMS just feels very underwhelming.
Once you have landed on a few planets, gathered resources, scanned a few animals and blown up a couple of pirates the game seems to repeat itself. And that is where the problem lies. No Mans Sky is trying to be everything to everyone when it only succeeds at being something to someone....... or something. If they had set the game in a single system and concentrated on making that system interesting and varied instead of massive and similar then I would have had more fun. People seem to want to make clever games instead of fun ones. "OOOh look we made a universe of cookie cutter planets aren't we clever". Yes you are, but I'm still gonna give you a negative review.

Graphics - 7/10
Sound - 6/10
Playability - 6/10
Lastability - 4/10
Overall - 6/10

Plus I wouldn't have recommended the game because of the obvious rendered screen shots still showing on the store page. Disgraceful.

EDIT: Steam says I have played this game again and would I like to amend my review. Ok I will. Yeah no, still don't buy it,

[h1]Introduction :[/h1] This game caught my attention during December 2016 when the Foundation update introduced the base building mechanics. Before that I didn't find the original scope of the game very appealing, it just looked like another 'open world sandbox' game except with procedural generation and a space theme.

However since I started playing I feel it has improved in most of the other main aspects as well like exploration & discovery, progression and social aspects; each to a varying degree so far.

[h1]Game Modes :[/h1] You have four choices when it comes to starting a new game - 'Creative' mode: No resource extraction or crafting necessary and I believe you can bypass acquiring most if not all blueprints though I'm only sure about those required for base building. Basically a good mode to try out everything possible in the game without worrying about progression. You can also proceed with the storylines I believe but I mainly utilize this mode for building mock bases before implementing them in my 'Normal' game mode which has standard progression and survival mechanics. 

A step above you have 'Survival' mode with harsher survival penalties along with relatively slower progression and finally 'Permadeath' mode if you prefer absolute risk versus reward experience and willing to spend extra time to spare.

[h1]Locations :[/h1] You start on a planet which is part of a star system, each of which can have up to 6 planets in total and up to two planets can have one moon each. Each star in the star system will have a colour - blue, green, red or yellow; each possessing planets with distinct stellar resources and also affecting the probability of the actual type of planets they can possess. 

Basically some planet types are more common and some are quite rare especially Anomalous planets. I don't know whether the colours of stars and their respective planet types, occurring are affected by getting closer to the centre of the galaxy as rumoured because I never tried reaching there but if it is true indeed then that is a positive aspect.

[h1]Planets :[/h1] At the moment each planet has a specific main theme like Toxic, Barren, Radioactive, Hot, Cold, Earth-like, Anomalous or Dead; each of these further having many sub descriptions like a Cold themed planet could be a Sub-zero planet or a Hiemal planet though they mostly resemble each other from my experience. 

Water-like bodies can occur on each of these planet types and they usually retain the traits of the respective planets atmosphere though magnitude can vary like for example the amount of radiation in and out of the water body. Dead planets have higher life support consumption and lower gravitational pull. 

Elemental storms can occur on planets depending on their descripted properties. Planets with harsher weather descriptions do indeed have more frequent and severe storms. This is one aspect of the game which has been consistent throughout my experience. 

I do wish storms would actually be more of a local phenomenon than being planet wide at least on non extreme planets in my opinion and actual direct or indirect visual and/or audio indication of a coming storm would be more immersive. Currently it can feel artificial or simulated after a considerable amount of time.

[h1]Flora :[/h1] Except for few planet types like Dead planets, most planets will have Flora depending on the planet type there are certain 'native' plants and/or trees you will come across on each of those planets, like Mushrooms on toxic planets, Conifers on cold planets etc. 

Variety in size, shape & pattern and colour does exist but after considerable amount of time they will definitely look similar. 

Density of Flora can be related to the planet's description regarding its Floral density however I have personally found this to be inconsistent at times. 

Introduction of additional defensive and aware plants in the 'Visions' update is a welcome step to change the existence of plants into something more than just a source of Carbon, elementary gases and other substances.  

For the future it needs to be introspected if there can be additional meaningful purpose of harvesting or allowing large scale farming of native Flora to achieve larger goals for example say, large scale refining, manufacturing in factories which don't functionally exist at the moment.

[h1]Fauna :[/h1] Again not all planets will have Fauna regarding which you can check the planet description. Overall it seems most of the Fauna species are inspired by real world specimen both which currently exist and some which are extinct some of which include birds, domestic animals, wild animals bipedal carnivores resembling Jurassic era predators and long necked herbivores; some of these are relatively rarer so don't expect to find a planet with most or all the above. Though it can be a good long term goal to achieve for sure.

Carnivorous Fauna will attack you or another nearby non-carnivore and if they succeed in slaying a prey you can notice them feasting on the corpse or well at least pretending to feast to be more accurate. And that same behaviour is shared by the herbivores as well. Yes they pretend to search for food, look around and run in fear when you or any carnivore is around but besides the ability to feed the smaller ones on ground thus making them follow you for a bit along and thanking you with their poop there isn't much of any other kind of interaction they possess currently. 

So just like my suggestion regarding improving the importance or relevance of existence of Flora, similar mechanics involving Fauna like herbivores in herd not just grouping up but actually defending themselves against lone carnivores by forming formations, grazing or feeding near their favourite food source, finding or heading towards a nearby water-like body and carnivores waiting near them in the shadows of the nearby vegetation or in the water-like body and other similar scenarios can definitely be implemented in the future I believe. 

[h1]Aliens :[/h1] Now regarding the actual named NPCs of the different races, you have to start with finding point of interests where they are usually found like Space stations, Trading outposts on planets and minor settlements and depending on their race, your reputation with their faction and their own mood you will have somewhat limited dialogue options mostly involving learning new words, gifting them factional antiques, receiving new point of interest markers, missions and/or quests and in some rare occasions they might present you with a multitool or upgrade module which can be quite helpful in early game.

However that is mostly it regarding NPCs currently. They do react to your actions or dialogues but they seem pretty much static besides that. In planetary trading outposts especially you can notice how they don't even utilise chairs or seats already present in all standard trading outposts but instead they bring their own. 

Not much else to suggest other than the ability to see NPCs actually flying and exiting their ships, mining asteroids and also maybe see your own NPCs you hire in your personal base walking around and helping in the maintenance or upkeep of your base modules though the later mechanic isn't really present in the game either unless you count farming plants and flowers.

[h1]Progression :[/h1] Regarding progression it isn't deep like a RPG game but there is a decent tier and class based system for Multitool, Starship, Exosuit modules, Exocraft modules and Freighter. You also need to obtain blueprints, mostly from Manufacturing facilities and some from quests which might be part of the storyline itself. 

Base building which is quite welcoming to creativity though not without flaws is also something you can see yourself spending a lot of time. You can have more than one base by the way so don't implement all your ideas in one place to prevent potential performance issues.

A story of redemption.
Making promises is a risky business, never more so than when expectations are high. Even though most people know, at least by a certain age, that expectations should be kept grounded, realistic, gamers, as a crowd, often find it hard to cut and measure their expectations within the bounds of realism. I know this because I am one myself and have fallen for my own coterie’s foibles time and again. The reason that gamers are prone to this weakness is because we want to believe, we want to believe hard, and when we are told - sold, in fact - that a title is coming out to satisfy all our gaming cravings, then there are few of us who can hold steady our cynicism against this siren’s song. Because we want to believe. We’re soppy romantics, really. 

And so it was with No Man’s Sky.

In reality, this is more of a criticism of the sales and marketing departments employed by games publishers - indeed, by any large company - rather than a criticism of the developers themselves. No, the developers weren’t blameless, of course not, but if we blame them for giving in to the lure of marketing hyperbole and the promise of unrealistic returns of investment, then we must hold ourselves equally culpable. It’s only fair.

No Man’s Sky would have been just another reminder to guard one’s expectations, to fall in love with promises at one’s own risk, but instead, it’s become something else; something more than that, both more positive and more compelling. It’s the story of developers gritting their teeth against the vitriol of a scorned player base, a hostile media back-lash, and memes, countless memes of cynical, sometimes comical, disappointment, to finally deliver the experience that we were sold - that we fell in love with - in the first place. It’s the story of how a creator, if they truly believe in something they have made, should never abandon it, never let it fall by the wayside, gather weeds, choke in the gutters of failed dreams, though it would be so easier to move on to something else, something new, something less trammelled by the tinge of disappointment. This is the story of constant work, of interminable care meted out over years to resuscitate something the world thought beyond hope. This is a story of redemption.

I can only speak for myself here, but I can honestly say that No Man’s Sky, now, doesn’t merely meet my expectations - it surpasses them. With every update, in point of fact. I suppose, in a way, this is my story too: a story of how I learnt that sometime, very rarely, you can believe; you can fall in love; you can hope and not have that hope dashed against reality’s unforgiving shore. At least, if you’re willing to weather the storm for a while. Or two years, in this case. And perhaps there’s a lesson in that, a lesson with a happy ending, for once. And who doesn’t love a lesson in a story, especially a story of redemption?

TL;DR
I love this game, you should too. Buy it, and join me in the stars, where you too can fall in love with your own piece of the untouched sky.

Edit: 11/20 - Almost exactly two years after my original review, and the game continues to evolve and improve with each update. Absolutely outstanding, and always worth coming back to.

I waited until this game was on sale in 2018 to buy it. As of this review, I've played for 100 hours.
If you want a game with a rich story, compelling characters, difficult challenges, and stellar writing, look somewhere else.
If you want a game to zone out to, maybe while playing Netflix in the background, or listening to a podcast, you're in luck.

Pros:
[list]
[*]Cool technical achievement, being able to go from planet to planet without loading screens*
[*]Boat loads of randomly generated ships, multi-tools, upgrades, planets, flora, and fauna
[*]Multiplayer, so you can travel the galaxy with your friends
[*]There's even a story, if you look closely.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*]Side missions are quite limited. The missions that are there are pretty repetitive
[*]The interface is medium good. Finding where you're trying to go can require going to space, only to return to base, or a station, and take a portal to your destination.
[*]Bugs can make certain missions impossible to finish, and even be deadly, on occasion
[/list]

*I'd count traveling between systems or using a portal as a loading screen. You watch a cutscene and have no input. It's a loading screen.

I'd recommend this if you get it on sale, and also like games like Minecraft or 7 Days To Die (or similar games)

[Edit 11/27/20] Since written, they've released dozens of expansions. I haven't played them, but based on the trajectory they were on, I'd still recommend it.

I love this game, however it has some flaws and I do not think it is for everybody. (Version 1,57 "NEXT")

This game is basically a modern version of "Elite (the version from the 80s/90s)" or "Scape Velocity".

It is a space game where you move from system to system buying and selling goods, the difference from the games of old, is that in this game the map is galaxy-size x 256+ (almost endless) there are billions of systems each with procedurally generated planets.

You can jump into your ship and go anywhere, anytime, literally. See that distant moon on the sky, let's check it out. It is a technical feat that at least once has to be experienced, it changes one's perspective on what space games should contain in the future.

Just edit the review to note that all the hours I have spent on the game have been by using Steam Proton on a Linux computer. This game works like a charm in Linux.

This game has fantastic visuals, some of the scenes you bump into are beautiful, sometimes the views are so good one gets distracted by the landscape and forgets what is it what you were there to do, it is that good.

As it is the 2010's it has to have crafting and most of what you can do in the game to move around is tied to that, the crafting on itself is not bad, not too good either.

The reason for the crafting not being great has to do with two issues, managing the inventory (pain in the neck), and the game's poor job at explaining what is that you need to do on a given moment. Knowing what blueprint you need and where to find it is confusing most of the time. Long term it doesn't get in the way and in the end you enjoy the game, however this could have been thought a bit better, perhaps adding some kind of blueprint tree in the GUI.

The inventory management problem is that it gets in the way too often forcing you at times to abandon your location and go to a different place to exchange items. It does improve over time a bit as the game progresses, you can expand the storage slots in your suit and that makes the inventory less of a problem. In my opinion normal mode should have a larger inventory at the beginning of the game while survival and permadeath should have the current size it has now.

The biggest flaw in my opinion is that all systems required for survival on a planet consume fuel and boy it runs out fast, so the constant grind becomes a chore real fast. It is so bad it gets on the way of the game's biggest mechanic, exploration. The grinding makes exploration unnecessarily tedious.

The second flaw is variety, once you've seen two planets of any given category you have seen them all. Why the devs choose not to include many more different types of plants baffles me. The most glaring lack of variety is barren moons, they are almost always rock and always brownish.

I have high hopes that these flaws will be ameliorated over time as Hello Games has been producing a steady supply of updates and patches addressing many issues in the game.

Even with all the flaws I thoroughly recommend this game if you have both patience and enjoy space trade games.

Fast forward to today, and no man sky is what it actually should have been two years ago. Much more involvement, better mechanics, and most importantly multiplayer. This game lacks excitement. There is no direction and really no end game. There is no real enemy and the missions are loosely based and not very exciting. If you’re looking to accomplish a bunch of missions in the traditional way it’s not this game. Half the time you don’t know what to do, where to do it, how to do it, and why you’re doing it. There is no strict structure to this game. You just exist, and how you go about that is up to you. 

Despite all of that I absolutely love this game. I play this game when I want to relax and enjoy the scenery. Unlike other games where you’re pushed to finish missions or one up other players this game is about you and your journey. I saw one review say something along the line of, this game helps you learn when it’s time to move on and can be applied to your own life. Are you just going to stay in one solar systems for the rest of your play time, or are you going to move on when it’s time or move on because the prospects of the risk may reward you so much more than what you can get now. 

This is not an exciting game in the usual way that games are exciting. It’s exciting because you never know what you are going to see next. It’s exciting because you can build a home the way you want home to be. It’s exciting because of the journey. That’s why I love No Man’s Sky, and why I think someone who loves the journey will love it too.

The studio cried itself to sleep after release day but that following morning it awoke with one goal in mind, to deliver the gaming experience that they always wanted us to have, that they think we deserve. So over two years, they worked and they worked, fixing bugs and adding content. Improving the game with every update, every build, every code commit.

Until one day, they release NEXT. Their hail mary, the thing everybody always wanted... Multiplayer.

I picked this game up in the sale for £20. I played it, for seven hours. Straight. This game is incredible. Simplistic in its design, elegant in its execution. There are some things that the tutorial doesn't tell you until it's absolutely necessary which I love, it doesn't hold your hand and keep you in a protective bubble like most new games do.

It requires you to look after yourself and your ship, gather oxygen so you don't run out of life support on your toxic planet and die, collect fuel so you don't have to sellotape your thruster button down to get to the next planet because, without fuel, it would literally take hours instead of minutes.

So far I'm only 8 hours in and I feel like I've scratched the surface of what this game has to offer. I would recommend this title to anyone, thoroughly enjoyable and worth every penny.

Review at Patch: Update 3.12 Next Generation Patch
Hours Clocked: 533 (207.6 at last review update)

- Updated Review -

No Man's Sky is hardly the game it was at release. More stability, more content, and actual multiplayer. While the basic gameplay loop is the same, there is a lot more variety than ever before. On top of that, every single content patch has been free. No DLC, and no cash shop.

While there are plenty of things to do, inevitably there will be some gripes. Ship customization is still in need of a bit more love, although recent patches have made upgrading that ship you love to be much better. Until you find that configuration you want, it will be countless hours hunting one down for the perfect combination of parts and of course, the perfect color.

The game is far more stable than ever for me, as much of my crashing issues have almost all but become non-existent. So much so, that I don't recall the last time my game crashed at all.

Overall, I do recommend No Man's Sky more than ever, but I won't fault you for waiting for a sale. With 533 hours in the game, which I've had since the game came out and many more hours planned, I think it is safe to say the game is worth it more than it has ever been now.

- Previous Review -
No Man's Sky is a space survival exploration game, where you play a "Traveller" that awakes stranded on a strange planet. The basic premise is you explore and mine resources on planets on foot, by ship, and by exocraft. Head to space to explore, fight other ships, and mine asteroids.

I'll say that multiplayer was never a priority for me, and that I played mostly solo. The newest patch while I did sink enough hours to finish the "story", the incentive to continue really falls short.

**SPOILERS***

Upon finished the main "story" you are given the choice of moving to a new galaxy. In doing so, you are transported there with a broken ship, much of your tech broken, and it as if the old galaxy never existed, so all your bases are gone. Fortunately, all your ships and freighter retain their inventory, which is not a total loss. Did not check to see if the materials were sent to a specific structure that collects deleted bases however.

***END SPOILERS***

Overall, I offer a lukewarm recommendation for No Man's Sky. This is a borderline because while I enjoyed the game, a number of serious bugs really hampered my enjoyment.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Multiplayer added!
    [*]Lots to do, from exploring to fighting space battles.

[/list]

I want to tell you about my hectic cycle-of-death experience in No Man Sky. (There is a review in here somewhere I promise) (ALSO MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS)

So following the Artemis/Apollo story arc, I was lead to a frozen planet. At the time I was also looking for Frostwort. For some unknown reason these frozen planets have extreme Sentinel activity. So each time you are seen, you are attacked. When I arrived on the planet I found that it also had large lakes and rivers. (These should be frozen solid in -100 Celsius temps, but that's beside the point). I also had been searching for a water planet to mine Kelp Sac so discovering these waters was harder than finding gold. I took this rare opportunity to kill a few birds. Complete mission tasks, get Frostwart, get Kelp Sac on the same planet. Great, right? Oh, did I blow myself, hard.

So the best way to avoid sentinels is to construct your exocraft (I use the Roamer) on the planet, so if they come annoy you, summon craft and haul ass. I mined the Frosties till I was bored, then moved onto the Kelp. Did that till I depleted all the resources in my locale then surfaced to return to my Spacecraft and exit the system. As I was flying out, I don't remember what, but I saw something that made me land again. I landed, on this really rocky cliff near the water. As soon as I got out, sentinels were on me. I got back into the ship and thought, fuck it, I'll just leave. Launch! ...nothing happened... Oh, no fuel in the launch thrusters, fill 'er up. Out....of....Plutonium. Great, now I have these fuckers shooting me while I search on foot for some, during the extreme cold weather conditions. Exited ship and scanned immediately. Nothing...Not a single stick of it in my radius. Too close to the water I guess. Tried summoning the Roamer...out of range. Roamer is far, (about a 15 minute walk). The Roamer Geobay was closer, but not by much. A 13 minute walk, or should I say, swim. Yep, the bloody thing that was gunna save my ass was 13 minutes across a would-be-frozen lake. Nothing to do but book it. Sentinels and all. The "hazard suit" (small Half-Life gag) was diminishing about 20 seconds per recharge and I did not have a lot of Zinc/Shard in my pack left. None-the-less. I continued to swim for my life, Sentinels still on my tail. After about 5 minutes of this I ran out of shielding, but I did find land. Scanned immediately. Found the Plu! Oh no, Sentinels are killing me....fade to black. 

I awoke. Still in the same location (?) I had not experienced this before so didn't realize you respawn in the same spot. I picked up my grave, rescanned and, uh-oh, Senti's are back.....got to the plutonium. I frantically mined as much as I could, at the same time, cycling weapons, trying to blast those little bastards. I thought, even with this Plu, I will never make it to my ship or Geobay. What the hell do I do? Then I had a quick thought. "I'll warp the Plu to the ship, charge the thrusters and summon it." But just as I warped the Plu, another death came over me...I pounded my fist and cussed. 

Ah I see the light again. To my excitement the Plu made it to the ship! I grave robbed again. Charged the thrusters, summoned ship, boarded and pounded the launch button. I cannot explain the relief I felt once my ship was floating, away from those deathly Sentinels. I collapsed in my chair. 

Worst 7 minutes of my NMS life. It's a pity the other four and half thousand minutes felt like work. 

Note to Hello Games:
Please either reduce the amount of resources needed to construct things, while also reducing the cost of items, or increase the amount for resources gathered from things, and the amount of money earned. I don't need to go to work at the end of my work day, this is a game, it should be fun to play, not a task. Second request, please make building your base a more free hand feature of the game. Angles are important and add to uniqueness. Building on angles can be done, shouldn't be a "work around", it should be a feature.

EDIT: Changed my review because I had spent 30 hours building an underground base, and the game glitched out and filled all the terrain back in. All the materials still there. You can't use the multitool indoors, so I would have to delete everything in order to remove the terrain again.

EDIT2: I have changed my review again cause the game has improve a great deal since I wrote this. Still lots of bugs, but it's waaaaay better now.

Like many other reviews you might read I have had mixed feelings based upon my chaging experiences of this game. I have come down on the side of recommending it though.
When it released it is fair to say it was not the experience that the developers wanted for the players, and after showcasing elements that were clearly not in the launch release I don't think any developer would intentionally piss off its customers in such a way. It was unfortunate, but if you calm yourself and give them some time to fix things and add the lost content then what you have now is a robust space exploration title with plenty of things that make it different enough from other space games out there to make it worth a punt.
The visuals are excellent. The look and feel of the environments are really good and the criticism that they are all a bit samey is kind of missing the point that they are all generated from algorithms and not hand crafted by teams of level designers, so you trade off the variety for the truly massive number of places you can explore as a result. The problem with a finite set of levels is that if they are good you always want more but that next location is not available because no-one has built it, in No Man's Sky you can literally go wherever you want, explore anywhere. Nothing is off limits to you and for that I think paying the price of having similar looking planets is one well worth paying given the exploration opportunities it affords the player.
I like the ships, although they do seem a little random at times this is a small quibble. 
My biggest annoyance is with the galactic map, I would like to see the map have a bit more functionality. Look at the Elite Dangerous map and emulate that. Again its a small point but something for the devs to look at maybe.
The content that has been added since the launch added nerw game modes and embellished the whole experience for players to be more aligned to all the showy intervoews and videos that frew us to this title in the first place.
I would say that if you have bought it and left it unplayed after the inital launch then give it a try now with an open mind and see if it still annoys you. If you are new to this title then I will recommend it, it has alot to offer, and is a well contructed title in its own right with plenty to pique your interest and keep you coming back for more.
There are quite a few other titles in similar settings on Steam but they all offer just one aspect of No Man's Sky and this title has alot more to give if you give it a chance.
For me its a return to older style of games which rewards the time you put in rather than handing a pre-designed experience to you in a series of orchestrated cut-scenes and linear levels. This is a much slower paced and organic experience that is really driven by you as a player and I think that some of the more reactionary reviews, expecially at the time of launch, just missed the point of the game and what it had to offer.
Put in the time and make an effort with this title and you will be rewarded with a different experince, something new and fun which will have you coming back. I would leave the "Journey to the centre of the galaxy" thing though, anyone remember the expensive galactic hyperdrive in the original Elite??

[h1] My review of No Man's Sky [/h1]

=======================================================================
**UPDATED 2020:**
After so many updates this game has finally became what it was always meant to be, one of the best space oriented games out there
=======================================================================

This is written by someone who pre-ordered... (*sigh*)... but still enjoyed and played the game intermittently.

No Man's Sky is a game that is for a specific group of people. It wont appeal to all, much like a lot of other games, it has a community of people that enjoy it for what it is and others that dislike it despite the new updates. The new updates add a lot of features to add either story content and emotion into the game or add brand new traversal mechanics, or even entirely new things like calling a planet your home and building a gek'nip farm on it. 

The game features hours and hours of content, this varies from following the newly added story to creating your own path through the stars. Each player can experience wonders, some by having an intense dogfight, others from finding a planet with an interesting environment.

Some of the survival aspects may feel repetitive at first like constantly refueling the launch thrusters, but after you play for a while and understand ways around making specific treks out just to get fuel for them it becomes less of a worry and more of an idle thought.

If you are planning on buying the game, do more research into the game, into its mechanics, into the general vibe you get when you play, and remember that it is built around survival mechanics, so that you will be fueling/ recharging things along your journey.

Multiplayer is now fun, you can also just plug in coordinates to the "stargate" and travel anywhere so you can join others and group up, follow communities online by simply seeing the glyphs posted online, there is so much to do it has been a constant go to game for fun (their is no local co-op, all players must have a seperate system) all i can say is gameplay wise and fun this game went from something worth 4.99 on release to something i would easily pay 100 dollars for. hats off to the developers who took their time but did not leave a poorly launched game behind them, they are continuosly adding new content even 4 years later with no DLC costs etc. you buy the game and thats it. If you are looking for call of duty in space, this is not it, this game is not focused on extreme combat, its focused on exploration, community, discovery, ship / weapon / spacesuit building, and designing unique bases on worlds you find. the design peices easily let you create something great thats not cookie cutter style and yet not blocky ugly and serve no function like minecraft. they are really your homes with technology you need, you can also design all kinds of mines for resources that run themselves, self replenish and are usable by anyone that gets to them.

If you are at all interested in space exploration and calm gameplay you should buy this immediately, you will not be let down, you will be amazed by it, just get through the initial "i need to survive and find and repair my ship" stage (about an hour) and the universe is yours, creative mode also exists but i suggest you never think about doing it that way, creative mode ruins the fun just as creative mode ruined minecraft for anyone besides small children.

buy it and enjoy! oh BTW i have 700 hours of gameplay on the xbox one on top of my time on steam

[h1]A great gamel, but takes some getting into[/h1]


[h1]Updated Review[/h1]
I'm a newcomer to this game; I get the feeling this will be an ongoing opinion. But It has grown on me the more I play it as I have got more used to the way things work within the game. When I first crash landed on a horrible frozen planet, I had no clue as to what I had to do so that I could to get off this frozen wasteland of a planet, OK there were some prompts but performing simple tasks was a challenge. Things became particularly difficult once the mining beam ran out of power. It took a while to realise (and research) that the good old Neanderthal method of hitting things with the multi-tool worked! Also during my initial stumblings, I kept on incurring the wrath of the Sentinels. I am now much wiser, and they no longer kill me for destroying things.

They've now added a lot more content and it has now fleshed out the game adding a lot more to it. I've only just scratched the surface of the new content.

I couldn't find any Zinc to complete the necessary repairs to get my spaceship flying again. Resulting in a long trudge to a small centre with a Landing Pad where I was able to sell some items which I'd accumulated while aimlessly wandering around and buy some Zinc. Eventually, I managed to take off after all that and end up in another hellish planet that was so hot. 
There is some hand holding in the game to get you started but working out hitting plutonium with the multi-tool could be used to recharge it. Albeit very slow.

At the start, this game came off as cold and harsh and didn't immediately pull you in like some other space games I've played such as Empyrion Galactic Survival. But it may be exposure to those types of games that made it feel cold and harsh, or it could simply be that I happened to be stuck on a cold, harsh planet. 
I didn't think I was going to stick it out though and came close to stopping. But the game gradually grew on me, and now as I have more possessions such as a ship with bigger slots, an Exo suit with more slots, Numerous Exocraft  it is getting a great deal more interesting

I find I end up looking to trade up to ships with more slots. So consequently I never have any money spare. I need to be patient and save up for that nice 48 slot ship. I so far have not seen an option to trade in my old ship though, as you were able to do in the original version of Elite. (I haven't played Elite Dangerous so don't know if you can in that.)  Upgrading slots in your Exo suit can start getting expensive as each extra slot after the first free expansion costs 10,000 units more.

As you travel through the game while heading to the Galactic Core, you mine and collect relics or other objects for trading or constructing items. The one thing that you need to remember is not to be a hoarder. I keep forgetting and ending up running out of slots as I keep significant amounts of Resources with me. Just in case. So a tip for you, do not horde things on you or in your ship, as you limit your ability to make a profit. My base probably will end up on an episode of hoarders! As I have containers full of resources just sitting there waiting for me to sell for significant profit, but I just can't seem to part with my precious horde.

There is a lot I have still to do and have resorted to reading some beginners guides to get some tips, although most of them are for the original version and the subsequent updates have changed things.

Such as previously you could find signal scanners to find abandoned bases, crashed ships, etc. To use these signal scanners you needed to create a bypass key for them. Now you can build the signal scanner. 

I'm playing the Normal game mode which offers what they call a chill experience, but there are other modes:
Creative 
Survival
Permadeath

I have played Permadeath and Survival; They are a great challenge to even get to your ship. I've had to make many restarts with those two modes. They feature much more aggressive pirates that the Normal mode and resources are much scarcer

So overall for me, this game so far has been worth the money I paid for it. I admit I did pick it up recently for 40% off when it was on sale for the Pathfinder Update. I had looked at this game,  on and off, since it's release, but the large numbers of negative reviews for it put me off. But Now I'm glad I took the plunge, and for me, it was well worth getting past the first few hours of the game.

Once you repair your space ship, you can travel faster, but it burns plutonium every time you take off.  One drawback of the game is that key assignment is only partially implemented. This game appeals me much more since the latest Patch/Update.  I would describe my play style as "Deliberate" as opposed to "Hectic". I enjoy the slower paced gameplay which is probably due to my advancing years and lack of a really good twitch reflex. Overall the game is seriously lacking in some departments, but it's not a deal breaker for me.

The Idea of discovering new Tech/Items could be a little less Linear, but I'll take it.  I also like the Freighter idea coupled with onboard storage. A degree of customisation always ticks the box for me.

I don't like the flying experience, this seems repetative and boring for planetary travel, I would have prefered Sustained Jetpack Flight for Planetside exploration. The constant need to refuel the launch booster is at best a PITA. On a planet wide scale the same Biome can be pretty boring. The Inventory Management is a Huge Pain, but it can be done without too many tears. The space stations while working seem unfinished somehow, like a work in progress.

Still as I bought this game without prior expectations I don't find myself experiencing the collosal Butt-Hurt that some people have. It occupies my gaming time without too many negatives, I'll call that a win.

TLDR: Get it on sale if you like space/exploration/sandboxes. 

NMS is a comeback story of the decade and by 2021 it largely makes good on its promises - and in many ways exceeds them. Post-launch support has been continuous and largely exceptional. My problem with that is - would we have seen any of this if the game wasn't met with the backlash it received on release in 2016?

The only issue I have with the game as is now, is that the new and delayed features that are now in it feel somewhat disjointed. You can tell the release feature list was largely a wishlist, and that features were being implemented across multiple updates. This lends a feeling of discontinuity to the gameplay experience. 

Like many sandboxes and similar games, NMS is also quite shallow despite breadth. This may or may not bother you. 

I personally think it's a fun title now, with exceptional support and breadth of content, but the depth is very limited, and the whole experience is absolutely not a £40 game - it never has been, and charging that 4+ years after launch is a bit a of a pisstake.

Edit: Changing my review to a positive, but leaving up my writeup. They have definitely redeemed themselves, though I've never managed to get back in to it.

*I hate that the company got any of my money for such a blatently lied about game (see everything said and shown about the game... just look at the steam screenshots!)

I think value comes in to question when deciding if I could recommend this game. It is great for what it is. BUT, it’s overpriced for what you get and the promises made both through interviews and even the preview videos are a hard pill to swallow when they’re blatantly missing. Here’s my thought in nice easy to read point form. I’ve played for a while, exploring planets and seen quite a few.

Pro’s:
- Huge galaxy to explore
- You can land on and take off from every planet
- A cool variety of things to do
- Relaxing game to play

Cons:
- Flying your ship. You can’t really fly your ship. It feels like you just guide the auto pilot. If you’ve ever played a racing sim with turn assist turned right up to the point you couldn’t turn the other way if you tried, that’s what this feels like. Unlike the preview videos of you zooming through a planet and dodging scenery, if you get anywhere near to the ground, your ship points back up (to the point sometimes where if you try to pull up, it believes your leaving the planet, takes control and points you straight up to the sky. Let me fly my ship!
- Landing your ship. I found it easier on the PS4, and way harder than it should be on PC. Trying to land where you want with the above auto pilot is a pain and really sucks out the joy of having a ship
- Planets repetitive. Yes they change, but after you’ve seen a few, it just feels like a colour palette change. A lot of the things like Plutonium are the same everywhere, so you come across each planet full of the same models. Which takes away from the idea of having to learn the new planet. You never need to explore to find where you might find that plutonium you need so badly. The majority of the minerals all feel and look the same galaxy wide.
- Planets are bare. All the planets feel like a big plane, scattered with some generated objects. They all seem to have caves and ditches too. It starts to feel like Mass effect 3’s endings. Basically the same thing with a different filter. The geometry seems the same everywhere
- The weather. “Storm incoming”… this should be a challenge and drastically change what you see. But the sky during a ‘storm’ is the same and all you really see is the plants move lots and your life support drops quickly. You’re not blown around, no loss of visibility, no dark skies or approaching sand storms
- Nights and day? I would expect night should be night. It was flaunted about having cycles, but I only ever notice it’s night, if I get a warning about extreme night time conditions
- Ship variety. I may have missed something here, but I never saw or got the feeling that the ships handled differently. A brick of a freighter seems to handle the same as a small fighter.
- Crashed ships. GREAT idea, but boring implementation. I would love to find a rare crashed ship that will take Heaps of resources to fix and reward me really well for the effort. But every ship you find is only about 1 or 2 inventory spaces bigger, which hardly feels like it’s work it, as you can’t upgrade your slots on a ship. So even if it looks cool, it’s going to be replaced quickly
- Dangerous wildlife… Where is it? I never once felt like I had to scout a creature out first before approaching. 
- Dangerous planets. Where are they? I have not made a single upgrade on my character to better handle a planet’s environment. And that feels silly. Where is the part of the game where we were not going to be able to visit a planet or would barely survive until we upgraded our suits to work.
- Goals. I have been following the Atlas path and I’m at a point that when I find a new anomalous station, everything they give me I already have. So even that part of the game feels ‘over’
- Maps. There doesn’t feel like there is one. You can’t waypoint a point of interest to easily find your way back there. So if you find a crashed ship or something and have to leave the planet, it’s near impossible to find again
- Multiplayer. I wish they had just said it was single player only and only named objects would appear. I know the odds of running in to a player is almost 0. But I loved the idea that I might see someone zip past. Multiplayer net coding is hard and would cause problems if lots of people got together, so I’m not sure why this was promised and why they didn’t announce its removal (other than to sell more copies)

What I’d like to see:
- Let me fly my ship. Maybe turn on advanced flight and accept I might crash and need to repair my ship
- Big effects on planets. Pitch black nights, big approaching sand storms, roaring storms in the sky and whatever else to make the player worried. And make them deadly. I want to look on the horizon and see a poisonous sand storm coming and feel a little fear
- Give us varied gravity on planets
- Lets us push our graphics up and fill a planet with the generated fauna and animals.
- Make planets different. I’m happy to struggle through lots of barren, empty, lifeless planets. Then feel the rush of excitement when I find that amazing lush green planet teeming with life. I will be compelled to explore it
- Make the game dangerous. I came in to No Man’s Sky expecting to die a lot. It was sold as a semi rogue like, where survival was an ever present challenge. The only challenge I’ve felt so far is try to land my ship on a landing pad
- Variety! There’s a great engine that can generate random creatures, plants and everything. Use it to change the building’s layout. Don’t use the same models on every planet. The player is smart, we can be made to explore to find a resource. 
- Give me more reasons to explore. Cool artefacts or recipes hidden deep underground or hidden around a planet. I would like to have a reason for exploring

Conclusion:
All the planets feel the same thanks to generic geometry, repetitive common resources, repetitive hotspots and weak ‘conditions’. The game is not a survival game, as it’s too easy. Your ship is an unresponsive thing that’s not much fun to fly. The game gets repetitive quickly with little hope for change or variety later. Once you have a ship you like and a bunch of recipes, it’s kind of just a pointless grind to finish.
Do I like the game? Yes. But it’s more of a meditative game than an actual game. Think Minecraft with enemies disabled, no building and you just mine materials which you use to replace your pick axe. I have enjoyed it and will continue to play for a little longer, but I just feel some more features would have made this great. If this was a $20 game, I would be raving about it and the cons wouldn’t matter, as it feels like a great little homemade tech demo where you just explore a generated galaxy. But it was sold as a big game and described as one too with lots we could do in it.

I love this game.

I know a good many have what they consider legitimate reasons for their reviews, which I'm not going to argue them, to each their own. This game has in scads what I like to do, which is explore. I am still seeing brand new things after playing 270 hours as of now and counting. Ive been to over 100 star systems and crawled over more planets than I can count. At this point, I've maxed out 10 of the 10 milestones and am nowhere near done with this game. I will be playing this for a long time.

If you like exploring, this game is for you.
If you like seeing amazing vista's and sometimes like to find yourself just staring at the view, this game is for you.
Some reviewers hate the inventory system, I consider it a mini game in its own right and it's VASTLY more complex than a good many reviewers understood or took the time to figure out. Choices have consequences here. Just carrying around everything you might need all the time is boring (IMO) in an exploration game.

Just go into it eyes open, it is an open world, survival, exploration game, with light PVE combat.

Performance on my machine is excellent for the most part, i5-4690K, GTX970, 8GB ram.
The game runs smoothly and I maintain 60+ fps nearly all the time.
I've never had it crash or otherwise misbehave besides what I pointed out above.

I recommend this game to anyone that likes to poke around and explore, take their time checking out this or that in no particular rush. This is not a game with a clear end point or objective, its never ending, which suits me fine. It does have a story which is slowly revealed thru learning the various languages. Maybe some day Ill run into the center more likely by accident, maybe not, Im in no rush.

I bought it at $60 and don't feel ripped off AT ALL. I've easily already gotten $60 of entertainment from it and have plans to get a heck of a lot more at this point.

The only reason this game is getting this poor review is because peoples was too hyped about the games and the launch didn't deliver for the price. But hey... different taste for any gamers out there....



--------------------------------------------------
Now, to a neutral review.
81 hours of gameplay.

You start up on a planet with a broken ship.
You need to collect ressources to fix component
Then you get to choose your path. 3 choices you have.
1- Free navigation, so you goto whatever system you want to go
2- The way to the center
3- or the atlas path.
In anytime you can switch to atlas path/free navigation or way to the center.

- Exploring planets/ systems:
Each planets are somewhat unique. Different flora/fauna and in density as well. Some have no life (fauna), barren, frenzied sentinel(attack on sight), water/no water, caves etc etc. Each planet has different ressources and building from other allien Races.

In space there will be astroid field where you can collect ressources, freighter that sometime send distress call. (once saw a 39 enemy attacking freighter), and a random 2-3 pirates forcing you into combats. You can raid them if you like. Then... there is the space station. So space is pretty much empty right now.

- Ressources:
to my knowledge you can't find a planet with all ressources on it. There will always have carbon, iron, zinc, plutonium, thamium9, platinum and titanium (from sentinel) then it will have about 2-3 other random ressources on the planet. Altho, there is more than one planet/moon on a system. so on a system you could have all the ressources needed. Some ressource hace icons, so when scanning you know whats what. Other wont have icon, but are easilly recognizable.

Suit/multi-tools/ship slots:
You'll start up with barelly none on all three. You will struggle at first to know what to keep. But your suit and multi-tool can all be maxed at 48 slots each on the very 1st planet you start off. It just take a little money and finding the building for it. Your ship slot upgrade cost a crap load of money. But you can look for crashed ship and take or salvage it. Crashed ships are +/- 1 slots from the current ship you have. Its a long process but it cost you nothing. ships at 24+ slots start to cost alots for as little of +3-4 slots.

Tech:

Race/language/reputation:

The base game is fantastic. The planets are luscious and extremely detailed with lots of variety and diversity. Some planets have nothing too special or unique for them, but even those are fun to mess around on. Even then, it makes the ones that do all that more rewarding to find and explore. 

The game is frequently compared to Minecraft but in space, and I'd say this is accurate, but with more much more of an edge towards exploring rather than staying stagnant at a base.

The game is very grindy, but I love it for that. Its something to sink hours in. Its a good "filler" game, a game I like to play inbetween other games.

One main thing that gets underappreciated is the sound effects; they fit the gameplay perfectly and genuinely add a lot to the game. For example, the sort of "crunch" sound you hear when mining things has grown to be ultra satisfying to me. Same with the sound that plays when mining ores or lifting off your spaceship. Similarly, lush, unique soundscapes are produced for each planet you go to. They're awesome and create a delightful ambience to your voyage across the galaxy. All in all, the sound effects are very well done and create a delightful soundscape to the worlds you visit.

The VR mode encapsulates everything this game was meant to be. It has lead to some of my favorite VR moments. Combat is visceral, intense, and heart pounding. Mining feels very satisfying and enjoyable. 

Discovering planets, places, and species is absolutely magical in VR. It feels like you're truly hopping from world to world. The sights you see look splendid. You'll leave the game with distinct memories from each place you went to.

The game isn't perfect in VR however. There are definetly more bugs in VR than the base game, and when they do happen, they interrupt the immersion immensely. Sometimes the menus can feel clunky. Usually most of my vr runs end because it started lagging out of nowhere, and wouldn't stop even after waiting it out. This usually only happens after several hours of playing, but is still annoying when it does happen. Sometimes it stops, but other times it doesn't. The bugs don't ruin the experience, however; I would still recommend No Mans Sky.

This game is best enjoyed, in my opinion, to a nice album or interesting podcast. I find its easy to sink tons of hours into No Mans Sky when I do so

 I give it a 9/10. The game is immersive, beautiful, grindy in a good way, and rewarding in long term playthroughs.

I stand by my review below as a critique of NMS at release. Turns out, this game really did just need 2-3 more years of development. Today, it's actually pretty great. Strongly recommend if you're looking for a chill exploration game.

Original review:

I bought the game on the strength of the trailers (featured on Steam), the listed features, and public commits from the developers that came in the form of videos, interviews, presentations, and development preview videos on sites like IGN. 

The game I bought does not match the game advertised.

Many of the committed/demonstrated features do not appear to exist in the game, including air combat that originates in-atmosphere, wingmen and flight formations, dynamic atmospheric maneuvers (aka, flying low/under/around objects), pack-behavior in fauna, and so on. I played about 15 hours, in hopes those features would be unlocked; I've unlocked about 50% of achievements, but so far these features have not yet materialized.

Game performance is sluggish, buggy, and prone to crashing, even on a higher-end PC (4690k/GTX 980). Pop-in and this ugly "materializing" effect are rampant. Textures are muddy, and even running at 1440p the game has pronounced sharpness issues.

The game performs like and is featured like an early access game with 2-3 years left to develop. I do not purchase early access games for exactly the reasons I described above.

I requested a refund, as the game I purchased does not match what is described, demonstrated, or marketed. Steam has denied my refund request (I am definitely over the time limit).

I hereby rescind my previous review.

[strike] After spending about 85 AUD on this game, I really, really tried to enjoy it.

And for a little while, I did.

I looked past the sluggish interface, the 
terrible graphical quality, and the flight mechanics that made you feel like the game is holding your hand everywhere.

I genuinely enjoyed this game for a short time, albeit probably because I came into it with minimal knowledge of it - I was aware of the hype but I didn't know much more about the game other than that it was supposedly a pretty space exploration game. (I have around 200 hours logged in Elite: Dangerous, hence my initial excitement about this game)

But eventually, the game just became boring.

For example, even the simplest tasks were unnecessarily long - I'll never understand why you manually have to add fuel to your launch thrusters. 
It seems like an unnecessary step in a game that cuts all sorts of corners when it comes to "realism."
The constant cycle of crafting electron vapour, then crafting antimatter, then crafting a warp cell, probably wouldn't have been that bad if there was any variety in the planets and moons in the game.

I'm aware that the game harbours something in the ballpark of 18 quintillion planets/ systems, but that number means nothing at all if every planet is essentially based off the same formula.
If I were to describe how it feels, it feels like the game's procedural generation settings are set to 1/10 on the random scale, when they should have it set much higher. A massive universe isn't much of a selling point if every single celestial body is functionally identical.

Things only got worse for me after I began to notice these glaring issues in the game - I began to read into the history of the game and what was promised.

No Mans Sky, as it is today, is not the No Mans Sky that Hello Games promised us.
It feels like an early access game with a triple-A price tag.

I tried really, really hard to enjoy this game, but I just can't anymore. I'll be attempting a refund, even though I've got nearly 15 hours on record, because supposedly some people with longer have still gotten refunds too. I suggest you all consider it.

Warning - some spoilers ahead.

I had heaps of fun in the beginning, as the game starts out very promising; there is seemingly tons of things to look at and while you're doing the initial "get better gear" stuff it's pretty fun and visually pleasing.

However..after a relatively short while, you start seeing a lot of repetitiveness.  Even though everything is procedurally generated, you begin to see a lot of very obvious patterns in the content, AI interactions and environment. It feels like the same few ideas and designs are just rehashed over and over. Tasks given to you become more like a chore than anything else.

- The storyline is virtually non-existent, vague and pretty lacklustre (explore the galaxy at random, follow Atlas' path, or go to centre of galaxy)
- NPC AI is extremely basic; same 3 races of aliens saying the same things over and over ad nauseam.
- Spaceports are all identical inside and feel very basic, empty and barren.
- Planets get very tedious after you've seen 10-15 of them.  The 4 different planet hazards (cold, hot, radioactive or toxic) have essentially identical effects, bar the name.
- Most (if not all) planets have the same resources, so you can find pretty much all the basics you need on any planet.

All in all, was fun for the first 20 hours, then really starts to feel shallow and unfinished.  I never followed the hype (literally discovered this game's existence about 6 weeks before launch) but feel that, given the little content currently present, it's definitely not worth spending $60 on.

As a final note, the game is also very poorly optimised and ridden with really bad bugs, such as savegames not working, stuttering GFX, random FPS loss, CTDs etc.  The patching so far fixes one thing but seemingly breaks something else.  In essence, this game feels unfinished; great idea, great framework, but just not fleshed out.

EDIT - this game has done a full 360, especially with the extremely well done VR experience.
As such changing my reccomendation to "positice"

I was one of those early buyers of the game and OH BOY was it way too green by then. The one thing that it had was its algorithm, which could truthfully deliver millions upon millions of variations of planets. That too was a bit rough around the edges, but it worked.

Thankfully, however, Hello Games didn't give up on the game, much like others have *cough cough ANTHEM cough cough*.

All of the things Sean and the team had promised or at least brought up by then, have delivered; online multiplayer (now up to.... 32? players?), seeing people's creations, a mission system, several spaceships, exocrafts, freighters and pretty much all that encompasses these elements. The algorithm has been refined; now planets have a more "grounded" theme to them and feel much more alive, not to even mention they have since delivered on the variance of creatures, flora and fauna.

While the game has improved immensely now, it's still not without flaws: from disappearing bases to random clipping, disappearing quests, unbalanced "mid" game (it's so easy to get 75 million units and that can break the whole progression in a heartbeat for example), graphics and performance still need to be refined slightly, and multiplayer and multiplayer instancing need some looking into.

That said, the game HAS finally delivered. And while reaching the centre of the galaxy is no difficult feat (which is mind-boggling considering just how many planets there are), the experience and zen-like vibe it has fixed that huge scar that the original game had left in me, and replaced it with a tiny flower, with a string ensamble orchestra accompanying it.

[h1]Updated Comments for 2020 (Post Origins Update)[/h1]
Look, at this point I don't even know how the work Hello Games is doing on No Man's Sky is even remotely commercially viable. 

But I appreciate the heck out of it, and it is amazing to look back at how the game was at launch vs. now. There was a period there, near the beginning, where my earlier thoughts on NMS being akin to an Early Access Title were looking like they wouldn't pan out. Progress was non-existent (so far as we could tell). When an update did come, it was small in scope and imagination.

Since then?

Broken promises from launch have been met -- including with the latest Origins update, the Sandworm shown in the earlier trailers. Almost any system you can think of has been expanded, improved or otherwise touched upon in some way.

There is still plenty of room for growth to be sure. I'd love to see further updates to the trade system for example, maybe something new in the area of combat missions too.

But even so, I am happy to be able to turn my thumb upside down and give this a hearty recommendation. It's at such a point now where if HelloGames came along and announced NMS 2 I could actually be excited by the prospect, rather than roll my eyes.

[h1]Original Review from Launch:[/h1]
[b]Feels like an early access title[/b] - and in fact if it had been released under that platform we'd probably not be seeing the extent of negativity we are.

We'd instead be seeing the review of type, 'Not recommended right now - only get if you're wanting to support the devs in their development of the game or see the development unfold. I'll update this over time as more updates are released'. You know the type.

Given the stated plans to continue patching in additional features and content I'm inclined to think about No Man's Sky in this light even though it has officially launched under the guise of a final release. It's an adequate [i]base[/i] of a game. It has a solid foundation (technical issues many are experiencing aside) to be built upon which shows promise for another day, perhaps.

But the sentiment being expressed quite commonly of the game being a mile wide and an inch deep is an accurate one. 

Each planet - no matter the size - has only a single biome on it.
The 'trading' element has no real depth to it given the swings in pricing (for the most part) is so minor that there is no real benefit to be had in bothering to transport beyond where you are right now - an issue compounded further by the limited inventory management game NMS wants you to play. There is no indication provided either through remote scanning, setting up probes or the like of supply/demand in other systems nor is there any real context provided when checking out a star system what it might 'produce' or have a need of. 
The crafting is rudimentary and hindered significantly by the aforementioned inventory issues.
Aliens, and interactions with the worlds in general are generic and meaningless.

So many things, and so little of it offering any satisfaction. 

And yet - at the time of writing this review I've put in about 8.8 hours and couldn't tell you categorically I'm 'done' with the game, even in it's current state. 

There is something here to be sure, I just hope the grand success of this release (deserved or otherwise aside) allows Hello Games to deliver on some of the implied promise. Get the space stations and freighters talked about in the last patch notes out in a satisfactory way - add more depth to their trading setup, flight controls, planet diversity and more.

We could get that one day - or it could end up down the route of Spore, a similarly ambitious yet ultimately shallow game that in the end could only disappoint.
